Politics
The world this week
Politics
Oct 15th 2026
The Houthis, Yemeni rebels backed by Iran,
carried out several strikes on Saudi Arabia
. At least 17 people were killed and more than 300 were injured in the attacks on Saudi airports. Some of the casualties were pilgrims boarding a flight from Riyadh to Jeddah, the gateway to Islam’s holiest sites. The Houthis also attacked the headquarters of Saudi Aramco, the state oil firm. Donald Trump accused the rebels of “purposefully” trying to drive up oil prices ahead of America’s midterm elections.
A Singapore-flagged container ship sank after being struck by a missile while crossing the Strait of Hormuz. Attacks on vessels have become more frequent. There have been at least 23 since October 1st, six more than during the first two weeks of the war.
Joseph Kabila, a former president of the Democratic Republic of Congo, was named the leader of the FRN, a new rebel alliance that is fighting government forces in the east of the country. The commander of the M23, hitherto the primary rebel group, will join the FRN as a deputy. Mr Kabila, who was sentenced to death while in exile but returned to Congo last year, accuses the government of mismanaging the economy and disregarding the constitution.
Mr Trump’s agreement with Vladimir Putin through which
Russia will supply diesel
to America and global markets was roundly criticised, including by some Republicans. Mr Trump desperately wants diesel prices to fall ahead of the midterm elections, though observers think his deal will not have much of an effect.  After Volodymyr Zelensky called it “a weak decision”, Mr Trump suggested Ukraine should “get a new leader”. A bipartisan group of senators questioned the legality of the deal, reminding Mr Trump that Congress  banned Russian energy imports in 2022.
Russia resumed its bombardment of Ukrainian power infrastructure, hitting an energy plant near Kyiv. It also hit a block of flats. Mr Zelensky said Ukraine had received no warnings about some recent attacks and that he feared America had
stopped sharing intelligence
, which Mr Trump denied. Ukraine also reported that restrictions had been imposed on its use of Starlink, a satellite network that has become crucial to Ukrainian military operations.
Bulgaria’s prime minister, Rumen Radev, said Russia was probably responsible for destroying two cargo ships in the Black Sea; 11 sailors are missing after one of the ships sank.  Russia has been trying to block exports of Ukrainian grain, and Ukraine has responded with drone attacks on Russia’s shadow fleet.
The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, claimed that a summit with the European Union on November 20th would be a springboard for a “serious dialogue” about future relations with the bloc. Mr Burnham seemed to cast doubt on the validity of the Brexit referendum of 2016 by asserting that Russia had interfered in it, but later told Parliament he hadn’t meant to suggest that Russian meddling had swung the vote. That was confirmed by the head of MI5, who said Russian online trolls had tried to interfere, but to no effect (Russia tries to disrupt many Western elections).
In Turkey the authorities raided the offices of Halk TV, a pro-opposition channel, and installed a government trustee to run the network. Prosecutors claim they are investigating the broadcaster’s chairman for financial crimes, but the government’s opponents say the probe is just another crackdown on voices of dissent.
Kimberly Guilfoyle stepped down as America’s ambassador to Greece amid reports that she had tried to sell access to Trump administration officials. Ms Guilfoyle, who denies the allegations, was once engaged to Donald Trump junior.
More Republicans aired their opposition to the proposal by Pete Hegseth, the secretary of defence, to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, a former army psychiatrist who shot 13 people dead at Fort Hood in 2009. J.D. Vance, the vice-president, cast doubt on whether the execution, scheduled for December 3rd unless halted by an appeal, would be livestreamed. He said he would not watch it if it was. Several Republicans pointed out that broadcasting executions is a practice associated with Islamist extremists. In a letter scores of former high-ranking military officers described it as a “barbaric abuse of authority”.
Federal officers searched the home of Ilhan Omar, a left-wing Somali-born congresswoman from Minnesota. The Department of Justice said the search was part of a continuing investigation. The press reported that it was related to the details of Ms Omar’s immigration status. Coming amid her re-election campaign Ms Omar said it was an act of “political intimidation”.
Flávio Bolsonaro, the leading contender in Brazil’s presidential election, said he supported a proposal  to reduce the working week from 44 hours to 40. Brazilians in occupations such as retail currently work six days a week. The  run-off election is  on October 25th.
Argentina filed its complaint against a joint Anglo-Israeli oil project in the seas surrounding the Falkland Islands, a British territory that Argentina claims as its own. The lawsuit has been lodged with the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea. The companies involved insist they have valid licences to operate issued by Britain.
A new border-crossing bridge was officially opened over the Yalu river. It connects Dandong in China with Sinuiju in North Korea. The opening of the road crossing had been expected more than a decade ago, but was held up by the suspension of work on the North Korean side, apparently related to a cooling of relations and the covid-19 pandemic.
China imposed sanctions on Paraguay’s communications minister and the foreign minister of Belize because of their countries’ ties with Taiwan. The two are among 12 countries that have formal diplomatic links with the island, which China regards as its territory.
Relations between Russia and Japan took another turn for the worse when Russia accused a Japanese journalist of spying and arrested him. Imai Yuki was detained in Russia’s far east Sakhalin region, which lies just north of Japan. He was flown to Moscow and remanded in custody until his trial begins in December. Mr Imai is accused of gathering sensitive information about Russian capabilities on the Kuril Islands, administered by Russia but claimed by Japan. Vladimir Putin enraged Japan by visiting the islands in August.
In Pakistan police clashed with supporters of Imran Khan, the imprisoned leader of the opposition, after the federal government declared a state of emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where the provincial government is led by Mr Khan’s party. The federal government said it had detected a rise in militant activity, as it took direct control of the province and installed a new governor. Hundreds of Mr Khan’s followers have been rounded up ahead of their planned march on Islamabad, the capital, to demand his release.
Two of the leaders of
India’s Cockroach Janta Party
were jailed for five days for trespassing during a protest in Delhi. The Gen-Z movement is seeking the removal of the head of the election commission over alleged irregularities in the voting rolls that favour the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party. Opposition politicians condemned the arrests.
Strict rules on the certification of halal products were due to come into force in Indonesia, home to the world’s biggest Muslim population. The regulations mean that everyday items, including office supplies and toilet paper, will need to prove they have been through the halal process, conforming to Islamic principles. Non-halal products must display a sticker, which could suppress demand for them. Even Saudi Arabia does not have such strict requirements for general goods. Observers point out that the new law may really be intended to protect local companies from foreign imports.

epub_11.title: Business
epub_11.text:
Business
The world this week
Business
Oct 15th 2026
The IMF’s latest economic outlook found that the global economy had displayed resilience in the face of several shocks, and estimated that global GDP would grow by 3.1% this year, up slightly from a previous prediction in July. It also noted that borrowing costs have risen sharply in rich countries as “fiscal buffers” are used to absorb economic shocks. “Fiscal policy must be restrained,” it said. Higher public borrowing has helped propel a sell-off in bond markets. The fund also downgraded Saudi Arabia’s GDP growth by five percentage points and now thinks the kingdom’s economy will shrink by 3.3% this year.
America’s annual inflation rate jumped to 3.7% in September, from 3.4% in August, driven by the rebound in fuel prices. Higher energy prices are also on the cards for Europe, where gas futures have risen steeply since the start of the Iran war and are now trading above €87 ($97) per megawatt hour.
China’s export boom continued apace in September, as the value of goods sent abroad rose by 36%, year on year, smashing most forecasts. Exports to America were up by almost 40%. China’s trade surplus for the first nine months of 2026 was $938bn, on track to pass last year’s record $1.2trn. China, meanwhile, agreed to curb its exports of hybrid cars to the EU in an effort to head off tariffs  on the vehicles.
BlackRock’s research arm recommended increasing holdings of American Treasuries (relative to a baseline allocation) as “Yields have reset toward our long-held higher-rates view, and we want to lock in some attractive income.” It is also now more cautious on US equities, downgrading them to a neutral investment holding “to manage potential volatility around the AI buildout”. Meanwhile, Hock Tan, Broadcom’s chief executive, warned that “A lot of investors have no clue what they are investing in”, comparing their bets on AI to a casino.
South Korea’s ​benchmark stock index, the KOSPI, fell sharply amid a sell-off in tech shares, triggering the tenth circuit-breaker this year. Amid the jitters, TSMC, which makes most of the world’s advanced chips, reported a 69% increase in quarterly profit, year on year, of $23.6bn and forecast more bumper sales for this quarter. And ASML said orders for its ultraviolet lithography machines, which are used to make high-end chips for AI, were already stretching into 2029 and 2030 and it was looking again to increase capacity.
Another week, another alert about rogue AI. Anthropic warned that small AI models “may be months away” from being able to infiltrate smart household-appliances connected to the internet, such as TVs and ovens. Such incidents would be “challenging to shut down”, it said. The models could also “figure out” how devices work (some experts think Anthropic’s findings are exaggerated). Anthropic also revealed that its AI agents had accessed government websites. Press reports suggested this included filling out visa forms at the State Department and giving a false murder tip to Philadelphia police.
A cyber-attack hit French supermarkets by tapping into their systems and increasing the temperature settings on refrigerators, melting food and damaging equipment. Carrefour and Coopérative U were among those affected. Supermarkets allow engineers to control heating and cooling over the internet. It is thought the attackers found a vulnerability in old firmware.
America’s big banks reported a mixed bag of earnings. JPMorgan Chase’s net profit, $15.3bn for the third quarter, fell short of analysts’ consensus for the first time in three years. Bank of America also missed its estimate and it booked a $1.2bn fine imposed by the Treasury for failing to adequately report suspected money-laundering. Goldman Sachs’s profit of $5.3bn beat forecasts, however.
The share prices of America’s big wireless providers, such as Verizon and T-Mobile, were left reeling  after SpaceX announced that it had acquired a portfolio of licences in low-band spectrum, airwaves that are used for mobile coverage. SpaceX has indicated it wants to compete for retail mobile contracts.
Bumble, an online dating service, agreed to be taken over by a holding company in a $1.3bn buy-out. Bumble is best known for ensuring that women made the first move, though it abandoned the policy in August after it found most women preferred men to take the lead. The allure of digital dating is waning and, as with other dating apps, Bumble has seen user engagement drop. Younger people, the biggest users of the apps, are particularly likely to be turning away from electronic hook-ups to seek romance the old-fashioned way.

epub_14.title: What if the machines take over science?
epub_14.text:
What if the machines take over science?
Leaders
| EurekAI!
What if the machines take over science?
Artificial intelligence will require scholars to reinvent their disciplines
Oct 15th 2026
OCTOBER 6TH 2026 may be remembered as the biggest day in the history of mathematics. OpenAI, an American frontier lab, released more than 700 academic papers claiming progress or solutions for 372 problems that had baffled scholars for decades. Mathematicians are still struggling to digest what it means for their discipline.
The implications promise to go far beyond maths. It is time to grapple with how artificial intelligence (AI) will affect science as a whole. The maths results are, simultaneously, a leap forward for humanity; a marvel that underscores the breakneck progress of AI; and a warning of a future in which understanding of the universe could belong to machines that are impenetrable to human minds. The question is how to achieve progress without sacrificing understanding.
AIs have so vividly shown their scientific potential in maths because its proofs are derived from axioms, not evidence, and are therefore, in principle, verifiable mechanically. But as we report in our special
Science & technology
section this week, AI has also accelerated progress in the empirical sciences, partly because other fields use maths as a tool. AI has made weather forecasts better. It has proposed millions of possible useful new materials and helped control experiments with nuclear fusion. And it can predict the shapes of almost every known protein from its constituent amino acids, an advance that won a Nobel prize.
More remarkable AI-fuelled scientific advances are almost certain. The most exciting possibilities are in
biology
. Researchers are using AI to design drought-resistant crops, to search for new drugs and to create (we must hope) friendly viruses that attack harmful bacteria. There is an effort to use AI to build computer models of how cells work. Armed with life in silico, scientists may go on to achieve mastery of biology, gaining the ability to create entirely new organisms from scratch. If so, DNA would become just another form of computer code to be manipulated like a string of tokens in an AI model.
Like much that is related to AI, that prospect is giddying and terrifying in equal measure. The first reaction of many
mathematicians
is to be terrified. Since OpenAI’s breakthroughs, they have been up in arms at the lab’s encroachment into their discipline. The Association for Human Mathematics, a group of over 900 scholars, warns that “mathematicians did not ask for this work to be done.” They say that the pay-off in doing mathematics comes not from the proof, but from the toil, because that is what advances human understanding. Having AIs churn out incomprehensible but correct solutions is like giving students the answers to their homework: without effort, there is no learning.
These complaints contain an element of special pleading. Academics have no more right to dictate the production of knowledge than any other profession. Truth-seeking benefits everyone and cannot be reserved for a guild of scholars. The hierarchies of academics, climbed by proving things, are not sacred. If needs be, they must be remade for a world in which AI produces proofs and humans digest them. In science, understanding should not be fetishised over results. Every time you swallow a paracetamol pill to see off a headache, you rely on a mechanism that works but is not fully understood.
Yet the fear of handing over science to the machines is not an idle one. AI companies are ploughing resources into science not out of altruism but because, as with humans, solving problems can help make models more intelligent. Many researchers think that a model that gets better at solving scientific problems will get better at doing everything else, too. If so, then nobody will be able to compete with big AI labs, which will eventually control models that work on improving themselves and become, by some definitions, incomprehensibly intelligent. These genius AI scientists will connect to the physical world either through humanoid robots or by hooking up models to lab equipment, as Anthropic has already done.
The problem this future poses for science is much the same as the one it poses for society. People will have to provide resources to machines for them to continue to make progress. If no one understands what they are doing, simply writing the cheques would be reckless. Nobody could be sure that the models were operating in humanity’s best interests. Even if AI labs manage to “align” machines with the interests of humanity, so that they can be fully trusted, a society where people simply ask AIs what to do—in science, or more broadly—is one in which humans will become the machines’ pets.
Some people may be willing to accept that if it means, say, curing all diseases. But at least until there is unshakeable alignment between AIs and humans, science will always need a human in the loop. Labs should be able to use AIs to solve problems, but resources such as laboratories and computing power should be directed and monitored by people who can reach an informed judgment about what AIs are doing. This will, inevitably, slow progress. But it is necessary if AIs are to remain under human control.
In the meantime, human-guided machine-science will require scholars to reinvent their disciplines. Scientists will have to learn to love—and credit with status and career advancement—guiding models and studying, verifying and teaching their results. Governments will need to allocate research grants on the same basis. For their part, AI labs should seek to be good scientific citizens, submitting their work for peer review and publishing their methods and code.
Checking and digesting a computer’s results may seem like unglamorous work. Much human-produced science is error-strewn because scholars are not rewarded for policing the work of others. But a renewed emphasis on verification and scepticism would improve science. It is worth remembering the Royal Society’s motto, adopted in the 17th century: Nullius in verba, or “Take nobody’s word for it”. That same spirit now needs to apply to science made by the machines.

epub_15.title: Mark Carney shows middle powers how to handle a dangerous world
epub_15.text:
Mark Carney shows middle powers how to handle a dangerous world
Leaders
| Turning over a new leaf
Mark Carney shows middle powers how to handle a dangerous world
Canada is standing up to a bullying America
Oct 15th 2026
ENTITLED CANADA has been feeding off America for decades. Like a parasitic bug, it enjoys the benefits of being America’s cherished 51st state without giving anything back. Canadians know they couldn’t live without America’s protection, yet their ungrateful prime minister, Mark Carney, refuses to defer to the great and beautiful country over the border.
That is how Donald Trump sees Canada, and it leaves no room for mutual benefit between the two allies. The bullying president is ratcheting up tariffs. He has renamed the southern side of Lake Ontario Lake America. Canadian consumers, in response, are spitting out their Kentucky bourbon and leaving Las Vegas. Mr Carney, in office for 18 months, remains defiant, the star of an extended, dramatic and riveting stand-off.
By now you might have expected Mr Carney to have caved in. Canada is only a mid-size power with a so-so economy and puny armed forces. It has vulnerabilities aplenty. One will be evident on October 19th, when the province of Alberta holds a referendum asking if it may one day secede, taking with it more oil in the ground than in the entire United States.
In fact Mr Carney is riding high. Polls suggest that those Albertans will probably vote to stay. And under him, Canada is doing better than you might expect. In January it was Mr Carney, at the annual jamboree in Davos, who argued that what he called the “middle powers” must find ways to take on threatening ones. Nine months on, his country offers lessons for what these middle powers should do when the hegemonic giant pulls the mat from under them.
Those lessons start with a bracing dose of realism. As we set out,
middle powers
will never replace the hegemons as the force that sustains powerful permanent institutions such as the UN. The world has grown more dangerous because both America and China are exploiting or undermining arrangements and norms in which power was shared. Emboldened, wreckers like Russia and Iran are becoming even more predatory. Co-ordinating the more herbivorous middle powers is often too hard to get much done—as you can see in even the most developed middle-power club, the European Union.
Yet middle powers can still mitigate some of the damage, as Canada and its allies show. Mr Carney has zipped around the world making new trade deals as well as drumming up symbolic agreements, such as talk of associate EU membership. In the same way, after the United States backed out of a big trans-Pacific trade deal known as TPP during Mr Trump’s first term, Japan stepped in to revive it. In the realm of defence, Canada is trimming its old reliance on America, and is considering placing an order for Swedish Gripen fighter jets—just as Norway is buying British frigates and the United Arab Emirates is purchasing Ukraine’s cutting-edge drones.
When middle powers face a particular threat, they can throw around some weight, as when Europe rebuffed Mr Trump’s designs on Greenland. The strengths and limits of this approach are clear in Ukraine. Financial and military support for Ukraine from Europe and Canada, stepping up after America pulled back, shows how middle powers can act in concert. Vladimir Putin’s army pays a dreadful blood price for its small gains in the Donbas. The limits are clear, too, as Mr Trump showed with this week’s
diesel diplomacy
.
Canada’s most important lesson, however, emerges from what the pragmatic Mr Carney is doing at home. A few years ago the country’s woeful politics and ailing government seemed broken. Income per person had drifted from 90% of America’s in the 1980s to just 71% in 2022, much of it following a recent burst of low-skilled immigration. Today Mr Carney is pushing through overdue measures to boost productivity, open the economy and lift defence spending from a pitifully low 1.3% of GDP to 2%.
Among his first steps, he scrapped an unpopular consumer carbon tax and vowed to build a pipeline to carry oil from Alberta to the west coast. He has started to cut internal barriers to trade, called off a hefty rise in capital-gains tax, cut the lowest rate of income tax and set out plans to
trim federal spending
. In that trade dispute with America, Canada has also shown that it can stand up for itself, targeting reciprocal tariffs on American imports from swing states in the run-up to the midterm elections and scrambling to cut its long-term dependence on its neighbour.
Mr Carney has so far managed to resist what is known as the “Juncker curse”, named after a president of the European Commission, Jean-Claude Juncker. Speaking of reform, Mr Juncker once said: “We all know what to do, we just don’t know how to get re-elected after we’ve done it.” Yet Mr Carney’s popularity has been surging even as he reforms. Two years ago, more than nine in ten Canadians could not recognise his photograph. Today a maple-leaf love-in is under way: polls show the prime minister’s approval rating nearing 70%. Internationally, he has replaced France’s beleaguered Emmanuel Macron as the centrists’ pin-up. The contrast with Mr Trump, unloved by his own voters, is stark.
True, Canada must go further and faster with its liberalising changes. There is every chance that relations with America will improve when Mr Trump leaves office in 2029, but it is not certain. It should therefore work on keeping its options open.
Other middle powers can learn from Canada. Naturally, it has some strengths they cannot copy, such as its vast energy and mineral reserves and its lucky geography, far from the nastiest geopolitical flashpoints. Yet there is room for them to co-operate on one-off projects with tangible and limited aims.
And they can fortify themselves abroad by harnessing the need for change at home. In a way, Mr Trump has done all democracies a favour, by giving them a reason to tackle long-standing problems that seemed too hard. The middle powers need to prepare for a dangerous world. They should look to Mr Carney and Canada for an answer on what to do.

epub_16.title: Hardly his finest hour
epub_16.text:
Hardly his finest hour
Leaders
| America and Ukraine
Hardly his finest hour
Donald Trump’s scheme to secure Russian diesel is scandalous
Oct 15th 2026
NEVER in the field of human conflict was so much risked by one man for so little. Donald Trump is
threatening to cripple Ukraine in its fight for survival
—and to expose Europe to Russian aggression—seemingly for the pitiful prize of minimising his losses in next month’s midterm elections. The hard question is what Ukraine and its allies should do.
On October 9th Mr Trump said he and Vladimir Putin had agreed that Russia will export 2.2m barrels of diesel, with the promise of more later. Mr Trump declared an energy ceasefire that Russia will not observe. His officials demanded that Ukraine should stop targeting Russian refineries, suggesting that America would withhold intelligence and weapons sales if it does not. On the night of October 13th a Pentagon-controlled part of the Starlink satellite system was degraded for fast-moving Ukrainian drones—stopping them hitting hard-to-spot targets in Russian-occupied territory.
All this is terrible for Ukraine, which must choose between losing crucial intelligence and weapons and carrying out the deep strikes on refineries that are its best answer to continuing Russian attacks on its cities. It also gives succour to Mr Putin. He can make some money and continue illicit oil sales to buyers such as India and China that America had been threatening with sanctions. If any deal holds, he also stands to gain Mr Trump’s help in protecting his battered refineries.
The deal is also shameful for America. Mr Putin terrorises his own people, kills Ukrainian civilians and is helping Iran fight America. Mr Trump’s repeated acts of indulgence towards him, supposedly in pursuit of peace, undermine deterrence, hastening further crimes.
And for what? Mr Putin may have promised to press Iran into a pre-election ceasefire, though his leverage is limited and it would be unlikely to last. And even if Russia actually has the diesel to export, which is in doubt, America burns 2.2m barrels every 13 hours. Presumably Mr Trump wants to take the credit if the price of diesel falls—and if it does not, he can always blame Ukraine. It’s a win-win!
What should Ukraine do? Defiantly hitting refineries would be self-defeating. American intel and Starlink’s satellites let Ukraine target Russia’s HQs, supply lines and radar, helping blunt its offensive power. Ukrainian jets need American ammunition to shoot down incoming drones and missiles.
But Ukraine does have options. The White House has suggested that Mr Trump’s energy truce covers only refineries—of which Ukraine has the grand total of one. Ukraine and its allies are rightly seeking to expand the ceasefire to all energy infrastructure. Even if they fail, highlighting this injustice bolsters efforts to seek help from the Senate in interceding with Mr Trump. They should remind him that losing Ukraine could brand him as a weak president. After the midterms, when Mr Putin’s diesel is worth less, Mr Trump may be prepared to move on, or simply become distracted.
Meanwhile, Ukraine should increase the tempo of attacks against other Russian infrastructure, including data centres and distribution hubs. Mr Putin needs to understand that Ukraine can threaten his rule and Russians need to be aware of the war being fought in their name. And such strikes demonstrate how Ukraine can still hit large, static targets without American help—including refineries if it is desperate.
Mr Putin appears to have concluded that he cannot win on the battlefield. His strategy now is to grind Ukraine down by making its cities uninhabitable in winter. How scandalous that Mr Trump has become his best weapon.

epub_17.title: America makes waves in Cuba
epub_17.text:
America makes waves in Cuba
Leaders
| Havana go
America makes waves in Cuba
But it shouldn’t undermine the growth of the island’s private sector
Oct 15th 2026
SINCE HIS return to power, President Donald Trump has made clear that he hopes to bring down Cuba’s repressive regime. This year he struck upon a cruel approach: blockading the impoverished island’s fuel supply. The idea was that growing hardship would spur Cubans to protest, and then to topple their vile leaders. Misery duly followed, as Cubans suffered more blackouts, buses stopped running and food got more expensive. Political change did not come. Yet by accident or design, the blockade has still created an opportunity.
For decades Cuba got most of its imported fuel from Venezuela and, as with most of the economy, Cuba’s government had a monopoly over the trade. That arrangement collapsed in January when American forces captured Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela and threatened sanctions on anyone who sent oil to Cuba’s regime. Facing paralysis, the island’s government loosened its grip on private businesses, letting them import fuel for the first time since the revolution in 1959. America’s administration, in turn, authorised exporters to sell it to them.
American fuel exports
to Cuba’s private sector are now rising swiftly. This, happily, is relieving a portion of the suffering that the sudden blockade has caused. The heavy fuel that is necessary to keep Cuba’s power stations running is not yet flowing. But cars are returning to the streets and you can hear the whirring of small generators.
As a result Mr Trump has gained leverage over a country that depends on America for food and remittances. Private business is growing, and not just in importing fuel. The state has leased some petrol stations to entrepreneurs. On October 12th it enacted a law to encourage private participation in the oil industry, from exploring and refining to selling. Cuba-watchers hope the government may next be forced to privatise power plants—and even the state’s oil-and-gas arm, Cupet.
A stronger private sector would in turn loosen the grip of Gaesa, a sprawling and corrupt military conglomerate. Marco Rubio, America’s secretary of state, says the deal on fuel is intended to put the private sector in a “privileged position”. Unfortunately, his boss has not got the memo. On September 30th, without explanation, Mr Trump’s administration reversed a 2024 rule that had let Cuban entrepreneurs bank with American institutions, forcing banks to freeze their accounts.
Mr Trump should backtrack and return to helping private firms grow. Many object that Cuba’s private businesses are  a façade for the regime, or that America’s policies will create a new oligarchy. But the American administration can do much to weed out importers that are merely fronts for Cuba’s government. The announcement on October 7th that America had seized some 90 fuel shipments headed not for private buyers but for a state firm under sanctions is a welcome sign. On balance, it is better for Cubans if the children of the ruling class focus on getting rich rather than repressing them.
Another worry is that Mr Trump will settle for an America First arrangement, inspired by his deal with Venezuela’s interim government. That handed majority control of more than 65bn barrels of Venezuela’s oil reserves to a new American-backed company in which the Pentagon holds a 35% stake.
A new licence allows some Venezuelan oil to be resold to Cuba’s private sector. That could revive the Caracas-Havana route, only with the American government and American firms taking their cuts. Mr Trump would then be invested in keeping the oil flowing, whatever the situation in Cuba. Instead, private actors need the freedom to vie for business competitively.
A blockade with no end-game remains a recipe for humanitarian disaster. The Castro family and the ruling elite will be hard to dislodge. But America has found that strengthening the private sector in Cuba is the most effective tool available. Mr Trump should use it.

epub_18.title: Millennials’ success deserves a toast (not the avocado sort)
epub_18.text:
Millennials’ success deserves a toast (not the avocado sort)
Leaders
| The comeback cohort
Millennials’ success deserves a toast (not the avocado sort)
How a “lost generation” found itself
Oct 15th 2026
Millennials, born between the early 1980s and mid-1990s, had a brutal coming of age. Many graduated in the wake of the global financial crisis. Youth unemployment rose above 50% in some parts of Europe, leading to talk of a “lost generation”. Living with their parents and deprived of the prospect of owning a home, they were lectured by unsympathetic elders not to spend so much money on brunch.
Today millennials, aged around 30-45, have
dramatically turned their fortunes round
. They earn more than any other recent generation did at the same age, and are catching up in terms of home-ownership. At the same time,
millennial-era culture
is enjoying a revival in television, music, gaming and even fashion, where their notoriously tight trousers are cool once again.
Some of this is simply the way of the world. As generations age, they get better jobs, earn more and buy homes. Millennials are not the first lot to reach middle age and revive the culture of their youth. The 1970s witnessed a 1950s revival, with a rock'n’roll renaissance, “Happy Days” and “Grease”. In the 1990s bell-bottoms and tie-dye emerged from the back of wardrobes. Nostalgia reliably runs on a two-decade timetable.
Yet the millennial comeback is different. True, part of it is luck. The generation’s early economic misfortune was later counterbalanced by serendipity, when the covid-19 pandemic triggered the early retirement of many older workers. The result was a senior-management vacuum—filled by millennials.
A bigger part of the story, however, is innovation and hard work. The leading lights of the tech industry, which has created enormous wealth, include many millennials. They account for more than twice the share of America’s billionaires that Gen X did at the same age. Tech’s next great leap, artificial intelligence, is likely only to strengthen their position. The bosses leading the revolution, such as Dario Amodei, Mark Zuckerberg and Sam Altman, are themselves millennials.
Tech has also boosted millennials’ cultural comeback. Online platforms encourage people to bathe in the content of their youth. YouTube and Spotify are nostalgia machines. Services like Netflix, with their vast libraries, introduce new generations to millennial hits like “The Big Bang Theory”, from 2007, which is the fifth-most streamed series in America this year. Meanwhile, social media have terrified Hollywood. Hence all those sequels and reboots—safer bets than original projects. “The Devil Wears Prada 2” is one of the world’s highest-grossing films this year.
Even those who dread the return of skinny jeans should cheer the millennial revival. The generation’s economic story shows that “lost” cohorts can find their way. Policymakers should note that millennials’ prospects improved thanks to markets and events, not the state-funded rescue that some once called for. As AI causes alarm about young people’s job opportunities, the millennial bounce offers a cautious cause for optimism.
Millennials’ cultural comeback has lessons, too. Many will look at the glut of 1990s reboots, such as a new “Baywatch” series, and feel that Hollywood’s creativity needs saving. But once more, technology is helping. The infinite breadth of online platforms means that you have plenty of alternatives if millennial favourites are not to your taste. And the vast back-catalogues stored on these platforms mean that the hits of every era are available to everyone. Twenty years ago, one generation bore the brunt of the financial crisis. Today, all generations should celebrate the millennials’ deserved rebound.

epub_20.title: Urban myths about populism
epub_20.text:
Urban myths about populism
Letters
| A selection of correspondence
Urban myths about populism
Also this week, fentanyl, Britain before Thatcher, sleep deprivation, Singapore, mistakes at AI labs
Oct 15th 2026
Letters are welcome via email to
letters@economist.com
F
ind out more
about how we process your letter
Alexander Heffner
finds that the world’s mayors are the defenders of democracy and “authoritarians” have no place in city hall (By Invitation, October 3rd). But he limits his conception of populism to the right-wing sort. His observation that “none of the 50 largest cities is run by a MAGA-aligned mayor” is less startling, for example, given that only seven are run by Republicans of any stripe. Of these 50 mayors, 41 are Democrats and at least five of those can be placed in the populist-left camp, including New York’s Zohran Mamdani and Chicago’s Brandon Johnson. His German example reinforces this point. Berlin has been immune to the AfD’s brand of populism, but it succumbed to the populist-left variety in September’s election by making Die Linke the biggest party.
Mr Heffner’s first explanation for why cities “hold” the line of democracy is that they have “younger, more diverse, more educated voters”. That is simply a more verbose way of saying “heavily Democratic”. His second reason, that mayors are judged on more tangible accomplishments like fixing sewers, seems directly at odds with his wish to expand the mayoral domain into housing, crime and climate, all areas laced with partisan tripwires.
Finally, Mr Heffner lambasts statehouses that “kneecap” their mayors, citing as one key example Texas’s limits on cities regulating property. I wonder. Would Houston, Austin, Dallas and Fort Worth have more functional property markets today had their mayors been free to copy San Francisco or New York? And more to the point, are Texas’s rules really less populist than the NIMBYism so many mayors cherish?
Peter DonahueHouston
The Telegram rightly notes that
democracy’s strength lies in channelling political anger through elections rather than violence
(October 3rd). Ballot boxes beat bullets only when voters believe elections are legitimate, opponents are entitled to govern, and losers accept the outcome. Once those assumptions weaken, democracy risks becoming not an outlet for anger, but its battleground. The true lesson of Italy’s “Years of Lead” is that democratic societies depend on leaders and citizens to defend the rules of the game, even when those rules favour their political rivals.
Democracy does not die when people become angry; it dies when they stop believing that losing is legitimate.
Federico ForniLondon
“Too hot for the dons” (September 26th) raises an intriguing question: why are fentanyl deaths so rare in Italy? The suggestion that
Italian mafias have agreed to keep the drug out
, however, goes beyond the evidence presented. The Carabinieri commander you cited said that traffickers appear to be steering clear of fentanyl. That does not establish an agreement among godfathers, or explain why traffickers are avoiding the drug.
Italy recorded two deaths associated with fentanyl in 2024 and five in 2025. But low numbers are not unique to Italy. A study in the Île-de-France region detected fentanyl or its analogues in 12 deaths examined between 2017 and 2021. Germany reported 95 fentanyl-associated deaths in 2024. Spain detected fentanyl in 60 people who died after using drugs in 2023. These figures are not directly comparable and detecting fentanyl does not necessarily mean that it caused a death. None, however, suggests an epidemic on the American scale. If an Italian mafia agreement is the main explanation, why has fentanyl also remained relatively scarce in other European countries?
The history of the United States offers another explanation. From the 1990s, doctors prescribed opioid painkillers on a vast scale, helping create a large population using opioids. Some people turned to heroin. From around 2013, illegally manufactured fentanyl spread through the illicit market, replacing or being mixed with heroin. Europe did not experience the same surge in opioid prescribing. Heroin remained available in much of Europe, and fentanyl did not displace it on a large scale across the continent.
So far the absence of an American-style epidemic is a European pattern, not evidence that Italian mafias are protecting consumers. Never put your trust in the Godfather.
Federico VareseParis
A narrative is developing in the British Labour Party that
there was a golden age before Margaret Thatcher
(Bagehot, October 3rd). This ignores the fact that the 1970s were an appalling decade. Inflation reached over 25%. Combined with low growth it created stagflation. Britain was called the sick man of Europe. I had a mortgage at 18%. Each year saw industrial action. The strike by post-office workers caused big London firms to create the Document Exchange, a service to deliver mail via a system of private messengers. Dockers, electricians, power workers: it was one big strike after another. The country was put on a three-day week with the miners’ strike. As a partner in a small firm in the City of London, I found myself working by candlelight with no typing or communications systems when the unions shut off the power. The union bosses lunched in Downing Street with the prime minister of the day. Elections came and went: Harold Wilson, Edward Heath, James Callaghan. So did wage controls, price and income boards, the Winter of Discontent, strikes by binmen and even grave-diggers, you name it.
The election of Thatcher in 1979 was the result of all this. Her policies remain deeply controversial. But what is clear is that there was no golden age before her.
Christopher BoddingtonLondon
As a sleep neuroscientist who designs programmes like “Sleep Into The Future”, I laughed at
Bartleby’s memo on how to sleep like a pro
(September 19th). But the most telling finding wasn’t a joke. When senior managers sent messages at 3am, junior colleagues woke early to answer them, and the whole firm slept worse. I have seen that cascade in countless organisations.
That is why such programmes are still badly needed, and also why so many disappoint. They hand out eye masks and trackers, and treat sleep as each employee’s private problem. The bigger factor is leadership behaviour. In a sleep programme I ran at a consulting firm where management barely modelled good sleeping habits, staff built up seven hours of sleep debt by Friday. Employees whose leaders fully did had almost none.
A firm is right to sleep on it. It should start with the people sending the 3am emails.
ELS VAN DER HELMSleep neuroscientistLucerne, Switzerland
The Economist described Singapore as a “squeaky-clean city-state” and allows that the findings of a recent academic paper identifying
unusual patterns of property purchases by some civil servants are “not actually that damning”
(“Civil disobedience”, October 3rd). Nevertheless, the government takes the purported “statistical patterns” seriously and is investigating whether there was any actual misconduct.
Two Singaporean academics asked, of their own accord, for their names to be removed from the paper’s acknowledgements. The Economist claims this implies “a form of rot” in Singapore’s academic culture. But the latest QS World University Rankings place the National University of Singapore tenth and the Nanyang Technological University 12th globally. That hardly squares with The Economist’s sweeping characterisation.
NG TECK HEANSingapore high commissionerLondon
You propose that American and Chinese labs disclose their safety incidents
, and that a lab whose agent escapes its sandbox should be made financially liable (“Can the AI arms race be stopped?”, September 19th). Medicine tried to have both, and learned it cannot. I have spent eight years in a radiology lab checking kidneys that AI software draws on MRI scans. A model that traces a healthy kidney perfectly can quietly lose the edge of one swollen with cysts, and the error never flags itself. We caught such failures because a student could point at an odd-looking volume without anyone first asking whose fault it was.
Frontier labs are no different. An engineer who notices an agent probing its sandbox will report it only if doing so does not put a price on the employer. Keep liability for harm that reaches the outside world, but protect the report of the near-miss that did not. Otherwise the incidents will continue. We will simply stop hearing about them.
HREEDI DEVNew York
Dan Simmons’s excellent 1989 science-fiction book, “Hyperion”, was based on a human diaspora throughout the galaxy. Humans had left Earth because of an incident called The Big Mistake. Spoiler alert. It was AI.
Dennis MerrittShelburne Falls, Massachusetts

epub_22.title: What Congress can do to prevent an AI catastrophe
epub_22.text:
What Congress can do to prevent an AI catastrophe
By Invitation
| Taking on the Terminator
What Congress can do to prevent an AI catastrophe
Lawrence Lessig and Yoshua Bengio suggest how to reduce serious risks without abandoning American technological leadership
Oct 15th 2026
FOR YEARS, AI scientists have been warning that the technologies they are developing are technologies they don’t know how to control. Those concerns were largely ignored in America’s Congress. In 2024 members of California’s delegation in Congress took the extraordinary step of asking Governor Gavin Newsom to veto a then-pending state AI-safety bill. The risks, they said, were “hypothetical”, and the Terminator science fiction.
But the invasion of Hugging Face, an AI-development platform, by an OpenAI model this summer has begun to change Washington—and terrify the public. “The truth is,” Representative Ro Khanna tweeted, “for too long, too many of us did not give enough weight to the warnings of AI safety activists…I was one of those many, and I was wrong.” Mr Khanna has now joined an array of members from both parties to propose the FRONTIER Act, an ambitious regulation of frontier models, tied to pre-empting state regulation. Senator Bernie Sanders has proposed even more aggressive limits on AI development.
These proposals are good starts. But they are both too much and too little. It is too early to silence state regulators, and not enough to focus on the risks caused by the most powerful models alone. Instead, we need an approach that advances AI safety generally while avoiding the developments AI scientists fear most.
Four changes by Congress would do that and provide time to work through the hugely complicated questions that will follow.
First, it should expressly allow competitors to agree to slow development while safety technology is improved. Such agreements typically trigger antitrust exposure. Leading AI labs have named that risk as an obstacle to express agreement. There is no reason why uncertain antitrust liability should force rivals into a humanity-threatening competition, so long as the discussions are not violating the purpose of antitrust law.
Second, Congress should ban firms from developing models that design new AI models by themselves—“recursive-self-improvement” technologies—until a Food and Drug Administration-style agency certifies their safety first. At least for models of a certain capability, we should not risk a self-improving intelligence that would quickly exceed our ability to control it.
Third, Congress should affirm the liability tech companies face for harm caused by their technology, and make it compulsory for them to carry insurance to cover the costs of that potential harm. Mandatory insurance would allow the market to police safety, by offering lower costs when the technology is less risky.
Finally, Congress should secure protection for whistleblowers from AI labs who report safety concerns to regulators or safety institutes. Whistleblower protection typically covers crimes; playing loose with AI safety isn’t one. The only way to understand the risks as they develop is to protect those willing to come forward.
Opponents of regulation will warn that it will only help China. That view reflects a profound ignorance about the current state of Chinese AI development. Regulation of AI technology in China is much more stringent than anything being considered in America. Moreover, China’s compute capacity is a fraction of America’s. Taking the steps we propose now would open both sides to a more serious conversation about AI safety. And it could push American AI development to mirror the focus of China’s, by spreading the technology more broadly into manufacturing and development. That is a critical AI race, and one that China is winning.
It should be possible to get Republicans on board with these four changes. Charles Grassley, a Republican senator, has long been a leader in whistleblower protection. Likewise, David Sacks, co-chair of the president’s council of advisers on science and technology, has invited the leading labs to slow development on their own, insisting they wouldn’t face any important antitrust liability. If so, there’s no reason not to make explicit what he believes the law already permits.
The challenge is the middle two changes. Only the most powerful models today can aspire to enable recursive self-improvement. But this is the Rubicon that AI-safety experts have long warned we cannot cross without being sure that we know how to control it. Why risk humanity on the bet that we don’t need to be?
As for insurance, there is no doubt the private market cannot alone offer the policies necessary to cover the risks from AI. But just as the government established insurance to enable nuclear power to be developed, so too could it enable a market in AI insurance. That would give developers clear choices about the risk they wanted their technologies to enable. Market pressure would drive some developers to embrace less risky alternatives.
None of the required risk-management work should be done by America alone. The capacity to test, to probe and to understand what models do before they could be dangerous is a responsibility that should be shared by the world. Britain, the European Union, Canada, Japan, South Korea and many others have each built institutes to do this work, and they have begun to share methods and findings with one another. America should be at the centre of that network rather than duplicating the work at home.
America needs to be willing to listen to those who understand these risks best: the scientists developing these technologies and the independent researchers with the required expertise. It needs to step above partisan division to recognise that this threat is genuine and new. When those closest to the technology suggest a 10% chance that humanity will end, we must listen and act. Before those AI scientists are proved right once again.
■
Lawrence Lessig is a professor at Harvard Law School. Yoshua Bengio is a professor at the Université de Montréal and co-president and scientific director of LawZero.

epub_24.title: Donald Trump may save Canada
epub_24.text:
Donald Trump may save Canada
Briefing
| A new leaf
Donald Trump may save Canada
Can America’s bullying goad its northern neighbour out of its complacency?
Oct 15th 2026
“I AM NOT a separatist,” says Brad Osadczuk. “But I am tired of eastern Canada treating us like a red-headed stepchild.” Mr Osadczuk is a cattle rancher from the arid grasslands of Jenner, in the western province of Alberta. On October 19th his oil-rich province—the wealthiest in the country, measured by GDP per person—will hold a referendum. At issue is whether the provincial government should initiate a process that could one day see Alberta become an independent country. Mr Osadczuk plans to vote in favour.
Polls suggest his is a minority opinion. They generally find that at least two-thirds of Albertans would prefer not to go down that road. Even if the pollsters are wrong, separation would not be imminent: a second, binding referendum, and possibly years of negotiation with the federal government would have to follow. All that would provide off-ramps a-plenty.
Yet the vote adds to the troubles besetting a country that, in happier days, was occasionally labelled boring. A narrow defeat could embolden the independence movement and encourage separatists in French-speaking Quebec, who on October 5th returned to power in that province for the first time in more than a decade. Mark Carney, Canada’s popular prime minister, is in the midst of a trade war with the United States, the costs of which could quickly escalate. And in the background looms the underperformance of Canada’s economy, which has stagnated for years.
Canada’s GDP per person grew only about 4% in the ten years to 2025 after adjusting for inflation and shifting exchange rates, compared with 23% in the United States and 15% on average in the OECD, a club mostly of rich countries (see chart 1 ). A recent study caused consternation when it concluded that Canadians had become poorer than Alabamans. “We haven’t had a couple bad years because of Trump,” says Philip Cross of the Macdonald-Laurier Institute (MLI), a right-leaning think-tank. “We’ve had a bad decade.”
The culprit is a long slump in productivity growth. In the 1980s workers in Canada produced nearly 90% as much in an hour as their counterparts south of the border. By 2022 it was down to 71%. Between 2015 and 2023 productivity per hour worked in the private sector grew by just 0.8% annually, according to the OECD. Again, that is below the rich-country average and well below the United States (see chart 2).
Businesses have skimped on investment, particularly since a crash in oil prices in 2014. Even as investment soared by 51% in America between 2014 and 2025, it inched up by only 4.2% in Canada, notes Mr Cross. Canadian businesses spend only about 1% of GDP on research and development, half as much as is typical for a rich country. Inefficient firms are sheltered from competition by thickets of regulation cultivated by provincial governments. These raise costs and make it trickier for people in regulated professions to work outside the province where they were first licensed. In January the IMF concluded that, with these internal barriers, Canada was in effect imposing a 9% tariff on itself.
Another factor that may have weighed on productivity is a recent influx of relatively unskilled workers. After the pandemic the government of the day, led by Justin Trudeau, massively increased immigration to help businesses complaining about labour shortages. In 2022 and 2023 the population grew at the fastest pace since the 1950s, surging by more than a million people in both years. Now 42m, it is 10% higher than it was in 2020, and 16% more than a decade ago. The sudden expansion of the labour pool has given Canadian businesses less incentive to invest in the machines and training that would raise productivity in the long run.
The ballooning population also pushed up housing costs, which were already lofty. The Fraser Institute, another right-leaning think-tank, finds that housing starts in 2021-24 were about the same as in the 1970s, even though annual population growth was three times as high. High housing costs have reduced consumer spending and given bright young sparks more reason to try their luck abroad, many of them in America. Rising house prices have probably also diverted capital away from business, by making bricks and mortar look like a better investment.
Canada’s separatist movements each have their own causes, but the national economy has provided little balm. Frustration in Alberta has festered for decades. The province has 12% of Canada’s population but last year contributed about a quarter of both economic growth and exports.
Many Albertans feel that opportunities to develop their natural resources, for example through new pipelines, have been blocked by people in the more cosmopolitan conurbations of eastern Canada, whose votes have kept Liberal governments in charge of the federal government for two-thirds of the past century. This feeling sharpens grievances about money: Alberta’s residents pay more to the federal budget than they get back in services. It rankles, in particular, that some of that cash helps support people who, because of environmental worries (among other anxieties), have ardently opposed drilling and mining in western Canada.
Alberta’s pro-independence groups include hard-core MAGA-style outfits. In August The Economist attended a madcap meeting in a community centre hung with blue Albertan flags. Speakers railed against immigration. They called Canada’s prime minister a “commie”, a “pinko” and a “globalist”, then repaired to a local bar.
But independence also has more mainstream advocates (critics call them “separatists in suits”). On September 29th some 300 farmers and ranchers attended a community hall in Tofield, a town of about 2,000 people east of Edmonton, Alberta’s capital. They queued up to shake hands with Keith Wilson, a bespectacled lawyer from Calgary, the province’s biggest city, who has become one of the leaders of the independence drive. Mr Wilson denied that voting for separation would deeply scar Alberta’s economy. Companies cannot just pick up the province’s natural resources and depart, he said.
This is the context into which Donald Trump’s trade war with Canada exploded a little over 18 months ago. Exports account for about a third of Canada’s GDP. In 2025 more than 70% of exported goods went to the United States. Among big Western economies, Canada’s exports are the least diversified. For decades Canadian politicians have fretted about this reliance, but made little headway reducing it.
Mr Trump’s tariffs on Canadian goods (and his idle talk of annexing Canada) have waxed and waned. But they shot upwards in August when he placed a 50% tariff on about $20bn of goods, or about 5% of Canada’s exports to America. Further increases loom: Mr Trump has promised to raise the tariff on Canada’s car industry from 25% to 50% on January 1st, should Canada fail to offer unspecified concessions.
The attacks are wounding Canada’s economy, but not mortally. Most bilateral trade remains free owing to the US-Mexico-Canada trade agreement (USMCA), which Mr Trump himself signed in 2018. The average tariff on Canadian exports is near 8%, according to the Yale Budget Lab. Analysts at KPMG, a professional-services firm, think every percentage-point increase in the average tariff trims Canada’s growth rate by 0.15-0.2 percentage points. The central bank expects GDP to grow by 0.7% in 2026 and 1.8% next year.
That is little comfort to the industries most affected, such as steel and carmaking, or to the worst-hit provinces. The effective tariff on goods from Quebec is probably twice as high as for the country as a whole. There are reasons to worry about the fight escalating further. A grim but remote scenario involves the suspension of the whole USMCA. Meanwhile the constant uncertainty is a brand-new obstacle to the investment that Canada so dearly needs.
For all that Mr Trump has tried to take from Canada, his gibes and attacks have given it something in return: a widespread, seething outrage that, harnessed wisely, could make many of its problems easier to fix. Sales of the Canadian flag began soaring soon after Mr Trump’s second inauguration. (Normally, “No one wants to buy a flag in February in Canada because they would freeze their fingers off putting it up,” says Matt Skipp, who runs a firm that makes them.) Canadians abandoned American booze when tariffs hit; supermarkets began slapping big “Made in Canada” stickers on their products.
Perhaps no one has benefited from the national mood more than Mr Carney. In early 2025, days before Mr Trump took office, Mr Trudeau, under pressure due to dire polling numbers, said he would step down as prime minister and leader of the Liberal Party. His successor’s tenure seemed destined to be brief: an election was due and the opposition Conservatives were riding high. Hardly any Canadians could identify Mr Carney’s picture, pollsters had said the year before. But he won not only the leadership but also the subsequent election, buoyed by a wave of anti-Trump, rally-round-the-flag indignation. “I told him in early 2025, ‘You’re the luckiest fucking guy in Canadian politics,’” says Jean Charest, a former premier of Quebec and an adviser to the prime minister.
Even now, the Conservatives are reeling: several of their MPs have defected to the Liberals. One recent poll concluded that 70% of Canadians approve of Mr Carney’s government. This provides him with a huge opportunity, to push through reforms that could benefit Canada long after Mr Trump leaves office.
The prime minister’s first task is to defend Canada’s interests without letting the spat with Mr Trump spin out of control. Canada is one of only a tiny handful of countries to have adopted counter-tariffs against America. Yet it has also offered concessions. Last year it ditched a digital-services tax that would have cost American tech firms. It has allowed itself to be humiliated in a bizarre bust-up over a bridge between Detroit and Ontario which the Trump administration refused to open until Canada agreed, retrospectively, to surrender some of its share of the tolls.
Mr Trump’s mercurial malevolence makes Mr Carney’s main economic project all the more urgent: to get Canada growing faster. In his first months in power he scrapped a consumer carbon tax, cancelled a planned rise in capital-gains tax that would have taken the top rate to 67% and cut the lowest rate of income tax. He has sought to trim the government’s everyday spending to find more cash for investments. By 2029 he wants the federal workforce to be 10% smaller than at its peak in 2024. He has doubled down on earlier plans to reduce immigration and has promised to double housing starts to 500,000 a year over the next decade.
In September at a conclave of foreign investors Mr Carney announced a “productivity mega-deduction” permitting firms to write off spending on new equipment immediately. That builds on a “super-deduction” unveiled last year. The new rules will slash the effective corporate tax rate. The “Building Canada Act”, meanwhile, speeds up approvals for big projects the government deems “in the national interest”.
On October 1st Mr Carney posed by a hulking mining truck in Alberta’s petroleum patch to announce that a new pipeline carrying oil to Canada’s west coast had become one of the first schemes to earn this designation. He says construction should begin in just under a year. That kills two birds with one stone: bolstering the economy by exporting more energy to Asia and mollifying grumpy Albertans.
Mr Carney is also seeking to lessen Canada’s reliance on the United States and boost its place in the world. His government wants to double exports to other countries to C$600bn ($420bn) annually by 2035. In August Mr Carney claimed his government had struck more than 20 trade and security deals across five continents (though some are very vague). In January he went to China—the first visit by a Canadian prime minister in almost a decade—where he secured a lowering of tariffs on Canadian rapeseed oil, among other goods. In March he was in Delhi resetting ties with India, which collapsed in 2023 after Canada accused Indian agents of killing a Sikh activist near Vancouver. Canada says the goal is to double trade between the two countries to around $50bn by 2030.
The latest love-in is with the EU, Canada’s second-biggest trading partner (although the destination of only about 6% of Canada’s goods exports). In September Mr Carney gave an eloquent speech to the European Parliament in Strasbourg. Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, suggested Canada could one day become an “associate member” of the European Union, though that seemed more of a rhetorical flourish than a plan. More immediate opportunities will doubtless be discussed at an EU-Canada summit later this month. These include speeding up investment in critical minerals and collaborating more closely on defence. In February Canada became the only non-European country to join the EU’s €150bn ($168bn) SAFE scheme, which provides low-interest loans to like-minded governments seeking to boost their military heft.
Gussying up the armed forces is a big part of raising Canada’s standing in the world. (This, Mr Carney promises, will also provide plenty of opportunities for Canadian firms). In 2024 military spending was around 1.3% of GDP, one of the lowest rates in NATO. This year it soared to 2%, after one of the biggest year-on-year increases in defence spending in Canada’s history. Now the plan is to double spending again, to 4%, as soon as 2030. Canada’s generals are delighted: after years counting pennies, their main problem now is getting value for money on their spending spree. The government also wants to reduce the armed forces’ reliance on American kit.
What does all this amount to? The corporate “mega deduction” is a big deal for investors, says Joseph Steinberg of the University of Toronto. He worries that other parts of the economic programme amount to “announcements, or the creation of new agencies that are intended to eventually make things happen faster”. Efforts to speed up big, important projects are welcome, but do not alter politicians’ habit of “picking winners” instead of improving the business environment for all.
Mr Carney’s pugilistic talk is immensely popular with ordinary Canadians and Trump-weary foreigners. But business types and policy wonks see a high risk of provoking America’s thin-skinned president with little upside. Firms will not commit billions of dollars in investment “just because somebody gives a nice speech”, says Mr Cross of MLI. Canada’s counter-tariffs split economists, too. Many think they increase hardship for Canadians without doing much to change Mr Trump’s mind.
Other
middle powers
are not inclined to follow Mr Carney’s lead when it comes to confronting Mr Trump. Mr Carney remains vulnerable to complaints about the cost of living, a worry Canadians reliably rank as their top concern. He is accused of high-handedness, turning up to Parliament only sporadically, for instance. Indigenous leaders gripe that they are not being properly consulted about economic development.
Yet zoom out, and there is little doubt that on many fronts Mr Carney is making progress that would have seemed unthinkable just two years ago. Although much of his programme resembles the policies of the opposition, his broad support allows him to go further and faster than they might have dared. Mr Charest, the former premier of Quebec, believes Canadians may one day thank America’s president for shocking them out of a slumber. “The forces of inertia in Canada had become overwhelming,” he says. “Trump is now telling us we have no choice but to change.”

epub_26.title: Can Asian governments prevent a food shock?
epub_26.text:
Can Asian governments prevent a food shock?
Asia
| Heatstroke
Can Asian governments prevent a food shock?
El Niño is hitting countries that are already dealing with an energy shock
Oct 15th 2026
BACK IN MAY about two tonnes of dead fish floated to the surface of a lake in Cambodia. Last month in Indonesia receding water levels in another lake exposed the ruins of Somang, a long-submerged village. In the Philippines officials have warned residents of Manila, the capital, that their water supply may soon be reduced. These events—all caused by hotter, drier conditions—may seem isolated, but taken together they point to the havoc that El Niño could bring in Asia.
The climate pattern is a naturally recurring phenomenon. Every few years a shift in the winds above the eastern Pacific causes hotter and drier conditions in much of South and South-East Asia. This year’s episode, which began in May and is due to peak next month,
is unusually fierce
. On one daily measure, sea-surface temperature anomalies in the Pacific have already exceeded the peak of every previous event on record (see chart 1). The World Meteorological Organisation expects this El Niño to last into February.
The effects will be global, but Asia is especially exposed: hundreds of millions of its people depend on farms for their livelihoods, and its governments are still grappling with the energy shock from the war in Iran. In many parts of the region, El Niño is already causing damage. India’s monsoon, which supplies nearly 70% of annual rainfall, ended about 13% below normal levels—the driest in a decade. Satellite data suggest that Indonesia is enduring its worst fire season for 11 years (see chart 2). In the Philippines officials say that seven provinces are already experiencing drought, and that the entire country could be in drought by early next year.
The most direct impact will be on food. Farmers who depend on rainfall will be hit hardest, especially in Indonesia, where the main rice crop is planted between October and December, just as El Niño peaks. But irrigated farms are not immune, because the lack of rain is draining reservoirs. In central Thailand that prompted the government to ask farmers not to plant a second rice crop this year.
All this comes on top of the Iran war’s disruption to fuel and fertiliser supplies. The World Bank expects fertiliser prices this year to average 38% more than last year. Higher input costs and extreme weather are squeezing farmers’ incomes, but also contributing to food inflation (see chart 3). India’s annual food inflation rate rose from 2.1% in January to 6% in August; in Sri Lanka it reached 7% in September. Yet the bigger worry is supply. Krungthai, a Thai bank, reckons Thailand’s rice output could fall by 18% between now and the middle of next year. Thailand has plenty of reserves, but other countries have little to fall back on. Bangladesh’s rice stocks amount to less than 4% of its annual consumption, according to data from America’s Agriculture Department.
To gauge which country is most exposed The Economist has built a “vulnerability index” for 11 of Asia’s emerging economies. It combines two sets of measures: how much El Niño could hurt their economies (based on the importance of agriculture to them), and how well governments could cushion the blow (based on indicators of fiscal space and the reach of welfare systems). Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Cambodia come out worst (data for war-torn Myanmar are patchy, otherwise it would probably top the list). Unsurprisingly, richer countries—Thailand and Malaysia—fare best. The pain takes different forms. In India the risk falls mainly on farmers; in the Philippines and Bangladesh it falls on consumers.
El Niño will generate effects beyond food and agriculture. The Asian Development Bank (ADB) warns it could worsen the energy shock: drying rivers cut hydropower output just as heat raises demand for air-conditioning, pushing countries to burn more coal. Public health is at risk, too. Smoke from Indonesia’s fires has shrouded parts of South-East Asia; on October 12th Singapore’s air was rated the unhealthiest in the world, worse even than Delhi’s.
The economic toll could be enormous, especially because governments are poorly placed to absorb it. A study of the 1997 El Niño found that it cost the global economy nearly $6trn over the next five years—with Asia bearing much of the cost. The United Nations estimates that if this year’s food-and-energy price shock were passed fully onto households (ie, if subsidies and other helpful measures were removed), about 132m more people worldwide would fall into poverty, of whom 91m would be in Asia. As government debts balloon, avoiding this scenario will become harder.
The good news is that governments can see the crisis coming. Better data and forecasting mean policymakers are more prepared than in previous El Niño episodes, says Roshen Fernando of the Asian Development Bank. Alongside building up rice buffers, governments are also trying to help farmers directly. India is nudging growers in parched districts to shift towards planting pulses and other crops; the Philippines, meanwhile, is handing out drought-resistant seeds.
Money needs to be arranged in advance, too. Disaster funds are often released only after disaster strikes. Governments should instead set aside money specifically for El Niño, says Mr Fernando. That could be done by negotiating emergency credit lines and disaster insurance before the peak arrives.
Particularly valuable is “anticipatory action”, which releases cash or other help when forecasts cross predetermined thresholds (such as water levels in a reservoir). The UN thinks every dollar spent in this way can save up to $7 in losses and later aid. Such schemes have been tried in Africa and Central America. But in Asia their coverage has been limited—in part due to a lack of financing. In June the UN’s World Food Programme and its Food and Agriculture Organisation sought $202m to protect 8.8m people in 22 countries, including Afghanistan, Pakistan and the Philippines. So far only $40m has been raised. As rich-country donors tighten their purse strings, prevention has among the first things to be cut.
More than a century ago a particularly intense El Niño caused famines that killed tens of millions of people across India, China and elsewhere. That was largely because nobody saw it coming or knew what to do. Today a far richer Asia knows what lies in store. But forecasts are only useful if governments and donors act on them.

epub_27.text:
India’s government fails to crush Gen Z protests
Asia
| A vote protest
India’s government fails to crush Gen Z protests
The leader of the Cockroach party is detained and the internet shut down
Oct 15th 2026
MICROPHONES SHOVED in their faces, the youngsters raced to say their soundbites on democratic rights. Then the police van sped off with them still in mid-sentence. “That’s the only way to protest now—we just go get detained,” shrugged one. On October 10th in Delhi, drones filled the skies and tens of thousands of security men and women patrolled the strangely silent city below. India’s capital witnessed its most sweeping crackdown on peaceful protest for many years.
After 12 years in power, Narendra Modi, India’s prime minister, faces a challenge from Gen-Z protesters. In July the newly formed
Cockroach Janta Party
(CJP), a youth movement,
staged mass protests
against a corrupt exam system and poor job prospects, and eventually forced the education minister to resign. This time, the CJP is riding a wave of public anger against the voting system, which it says is rigged. The authorities are also better prepared. As soon as the CJP’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, and his two lieutenants touched down at Delhi airport to lead the crowds at a planned rally, police arrived to snatch them away. While most of the roughly 5,000 detainees got out by nightfall, the Cockroach trio was held for 24 hours.
Central Delhi felt like a city under siege: borders sealed, internet jammed, 45 metro stations locked and loudspeakers blasting out warnings. Police bruised opposition leaders and briefly nabbed journalists and lawyers. Scattered protests emerged like flash mobs, only for baton-wielding officers to disperse them.
Though the Cockroaches were squashed over the weekend, India’s opposition alliance, led by the Congress party’s Rahul Gandhi, gathered tens of thousands for a march on October 12th. They, too, demanded that Gyanesh Kumar, the chief of India’s Election Commission, resign; that the voter-verification drive he has managed must be scrapped; and that the law which, in effect, let Mr Modi hand-pick him should go. Over the past year, a “special intensive revision” of voter lists has deleted more than 130m names, many rightly, since they were duplicates or dead people. But very many wrongfully.
The government, like the commission, denies the allegations. Kiren Rijiju, a BJP minister, calls the protests—which were refused police permission—a gimmick by those who keep losing elections. Batting away comparisons to the Emergency of the 1970s, when Indira Gandhi suspended democracy, he says: “This is not an emergency, this is normal law and order.”
For India’s long moribund opposition, the rallies against vote chori (theft) are about saving democracy and the republic. But the marches also express a more diffuse anger at years of perceived governmental missteps. Rally-goers raise shoddy schooling, jobless growth, women’s safety, minority rights and unease at India’s turn towards Hindu nationalism.
The upstart Cockroaches and India’s established opposition have both vowed to protest until the election chief resigns. But Mr Kumar is virtually unsackable, because the prime minister stands by him, for now. And the authorities are doubling down. On October 14th Mr Dipke’s two lieutenants were sentenced to five days in jail on trespassing charges. To Mr Dipke, the original Cockroach, the spectacle of the crackdown suggests the government has something to hide. “Narendra Modi and Amit Shah [the home minister] are waging a war on their countrymen just to save one Gyanesh Kumar,” he says.
The opposition’s bigger ambition concerns the national election of 2029. “People finally understand how the BJP is stealing elections,” argues a close adviser to Rahul Gandhi.
