epub_28.title: Two Japanese towns offer lessons for shrinking countries
epub_28.text:
Two Japanese towns offer lessons for shrinking countries
Asia
| Demographic doubts
Two Japanese towns offer lessons for shrinking countries
Only some places can hope to grow; others must learn to manage decline
Oct 15th 2026
LESS THAN 40km separates the towns of Nanporo and Yubari, on Japan’s northernmost island of Hokkaido, but their fates could hardly have diverged further. Nanporo, a tranquil commuter town east of Sapporo, the regional capital, is growing its native population at one of the fastest rates in the country. Yubari, a former coal-mining hub that went bankrupt in 2007, has seen its population decline by 95% from its peak. Their contrasting trajectories offer lessons for local life in an era of demographic shrinkage.
Start in Nanporo. The town’s population fell from around 10,000 in 1998 to fewer than 7,400 over the next quarter-century. But in recent years the trend has reversed: by last year, the population had ticked back up to 8,400. Nanporo was one of only nine out of 179 municipalities in Hokkaido to see population growth in 2020-25.  It was the only one of those nine to do so without substantial foreign immigration. Meanwhile, Japan as a whole lost some 3m people over the same period.
A sense of optimism is palpable at the Hareppa indoor playground in the town’s central park. Sunlight streams through the new building’s floor-to-ceiling windows, lighting up a gaggle of children clambering up a wooden playhouse under a vaulted ceiling. In the adjoining café and library, a mum and young son peruse a shelf of children’s books: “The Very Hungry Caterpillar”, “Library Lion” and a popular Japanese series called “The Encyclopedia of Big Crises”.
A combination of structural advantages and targeted policy initiatives has helped Nanporo solve its own big crisis. While offering the peaceful capaciousness of the countryside, the town sits comfortably within the economic orbit of Sapporo, less than an hour’s drive away. Local leaders recognised that could appeal to young families, and implemented several incentives to attract them.
Many municipalities elsewhere in Japan have tried such measures, but Nanporo’s have been effective because its efforts were sustained and unique, reckons Saito Takashi, an official. Couples where both partners are under 40 years old, or with children of middle school age or younger, can receive up to ¥2m ($12,500) towards home construction; unused plots of land held in a prefectural land bank are sold at a steep discount. Parents also get 10kg of rice every year, a meaningful treat when rice prices have caused  national anxiety.
The Tatsuki family are among the new arrivals. Aoi and Yamato moved to Nanporo with their young son last year, drawn by the combination of proximity to Sapporo and support for young families. They built a home and opened a café on its ground floor, where they do brisk business serving lunch sets of grilled fish and freshly-baked desserts. “It would have been super-expensive to do the same in Sapporo,” Mr Tatsuki says. After seeing the conditions, Mr Tatsuki’s older sister decided to move to Nanporo as well.
Yet Nanporo’s growth has come from migrants moving in, rather than a baby boom. Last year the town still saw twice as many deaths as births. With the national population shrinking, one municipality’s gain is another’s loss. There is a “competitive dynamic”, Mr Saito acknowledges. Not everywhere can be Nanporo.
Many places will be more like Yubari. Its population peaked in 1960 at some 117,000. (Though the size of a town now, it still carries the city designation as a relic of its past glory.) After the last coal mine closed in 1990, Yubari tried to reinvent itself as a tourist destination; mismanagement left it bankrupt. As part of a nationally administered restructuring plan, officials closed schools, halted bus routes and shut the local museum. Cutting services only speeded the decline, laments Yubari’s current mayor, Atsuya Tsukasa.
Since 2022, when Nanporo’s tide began to turn, Yubari has seen its population shrink from around 7,000 to just 5,600. More than half the remaining residents are over 65. “Almost no one is moving in, everyone is leaving,” says Noda Masaru, an entrepreneur. “And when you know the population is going down, you aren’t going to start a business, you’re going to close it.”
Yubari’s case is extreme, but hardly unique. The Population Strategy Council, a group of business and civic leaders, reported in 2024 that some 40% of Japan’s municipalities  risk disappearing, given the outflow of young people. “I don’t see any prospect for reversing the trend—it’s not just Yubari, look at small towns across Japan,” Mr Atsuya says. “The question is how to survive in that context.”
While Nanporo, thanks to its favourable location near a regional hub, can realistically pursue revitalisation, for Yubari the task is to manage an inevitable further decline, for instance by becoming more compact. “We need to live in a more connected way,” Mr Atsuya says. In an era of population shrinkage, growth can no longer be the only measure of success.

epub_29.title: Myanmar’s dictator tries diplomacy
epub_29.text:
Myanmar’s dictator tries diplomacy
Asia
| Charmless offensive
Myanmar’s dictator tries diplomacy
He has a few cards to play
Oct 15th 2026
MIN AUNG HLAING is keen to get into the world’s good books. The dictator, who seized power in Myanmar in 2021, underwent a makeover earlier this year. He quit the army and made himself president following a rigged election. Now he has gone on a diplomatic blitz within Asia and is talking to America. Calls to end military atrocities have gone unheeded; but the despot has some cards to play.
One is taking back those who have fled Myanmar’s war and economic collapse. This won Mr Min Aung Hlaing a visit on October 7th-8th to Malaysia, formerly his biggest critic in the region. Anwar Ibrahim, Malaysia’s prime minister, received him in return for a deal on repatriating thousands of Myanmar nationals, a bid to fend off local anger about the migrants.
Mr Anwar pleaded pragmatism, but the dictator’s red-carpet welcome was a step towards his rehabilitation among leaders of the Association of South-East Asian Nations (ASEAN). The Malaysia visit followed ones in the past four months to Cambodia, Laos, Thailand and Vietnam.
Other cards include fighting online scams and selling rare earths. These have helped lure America into talks with the regime. Michael Vance, the State Department’s intelligence chief, met Mr Min Aung Hlaing in September. Mr Vance’s visit was ostensibly to secure the release from prison of Adam Castillo, a businessman. But the budding dialogue is focused on scam centres and extracting minerals.
A rapprochement would be key to lessening Myanmar’s reliance on China, which has propped up the regime amid its heavy losses to rebels. That help has come with high-handed orders to close scam centres targeting Chinese citizens.  It is unlikely that America will have any more luck than China in getting them closed. Scam profits have allowed the centres to buy off regime officials, allegedly including the former head of its anti-scams committee.
Myanmar’s rare-earth deposits, meanwhile, are largely beyond the regime’s reach, in areas controlled by ethnic armed groups, and are locked into Chinese supply chains. American officials may simply be using the minerals to get noticed by Donald Trump. “Everyone knows the White House and president are fixated on rare earths,” says a former Washington-based official with Myanmar experience. “That’s what everyone, including me, would throw out in meetings to get attention.”
Mr Min Aung Hlaing is also holding his strongest card in reserve. The trading of Mr Castillo shows an appetite for hostage diplomacy—and there is one prisoner who far outranks the rest. Aung San Suu Kyi, who led Myanmar between 2016 and 2021, has been detained since the coup. If freed, odds are that she would be barred from politics. But her release might provide the symbolic win that ASEAN and others need to wash their hands of Myanmar’s atrocious human-rights record and get back to business as usual.

epub_30.title: The limits of India’s diaspora power
epub_30.text:
The limits of India’s diaspora power
Asia
| Ashoka
The limits of India’s diaspora power
As the West closes its doors, India must make staying home more attractive
Oct 15th 2026
THE INDIAN diaspora, which numbers around 37m, is the world’s biggest. It may also be the most successful. It has a compelling case to make, especially in America, home to more than 3m people born in India. The median Indian-American household earns $151,000 annually, around 75% more than the figure for America as a whole. And many Indian-Americans occupy top jobs in business, technology and politics—think of Sundar Pichai, Satya Nadella, Zohran Mamdani and Kash Patel.
Such achievements are celebrated back in India, not just by relatives but also by a proud nation. Newspaper reports and WhatsApp forwards diligently catalogue the accomplishments of anyone with an Indian connection, however remote. Recent examples include Navi Pillay, the South African judge awarded this year’s Nobel peace prize, whose ancestors left India in the 19th century, and Anil Menon, the world’s first Malayali astronaut, a reference to his parents’ origins in the south of India.
The state encourages such enthusiasm. For years after independence, India tended to look down on its diaspora, disparaging emigrants for deserting the homeland and contributing to a brain drain. But as their numbers grew and the economy boomed, the relationship changed. In the 2000s, during the Bharatiya Janata Party’s (BJP) first term in power nationally, the party sought stronger ties with Indians abroad as a way of advancing India’s interests and boosting its own coffers (overseas Indians are believed to be enthusiastic donors to the party). Under Narendra Modi, those efforts have become more intense. The prime minister’s foreign trips often include rallies in stadiums packed with adoring non-resident Indians (NRIs).
To the BJP and indeed to many Indians, the success of NRIs is yet another indicator of India’s inevitable rise. But, viewed differently, it is also an indictment of the country’s inability to hold on to its talent. A study in 2023 found that of the 1,000 highest scorers in the 2010 entrance exam for the Indian Institutes of Technology, the country’s top engineering colleges, 36% were living abroad eight years later. Among the top 100, the share was 62%.
Similarly, the accomplishments of Indian-origin bosses abroad reveal dysfunction at home. Given the size of India’s economy, its businesses punch well below their weight. Of the world’s 500 biggest firms by market capitalisation, India is home to only eight. China has 41, America 234. One reason is that many Indian companies, whether small or large, are run as “lala” operations,
family fiefs
lacking professional management. Another is that the state has failed to create the conditions—from infrastructure to regulation—needed for them to flourish.
Emigration makes up for some of these failures. Remittances amount to 4% of India’s GDP (compared with 0.2% in China) and support millions of households. During crises, including the recent shock from the Iran war,
diaspora cash
has been particularly helpful. Migration has served as a social safety-valve, easing pressure on the labour market by giving educated Indians a chance of outward mobility.
It may now be shutting. The Trump administration has clamped down on migration. On October 8th it suspended tech firms, including several Indian ones, from sponsoring workers for permanent residency, accusing them of immigration fraud. Australia and Canada are restricting student visas. And it is not just potential migrants who are being targeted. Racism and resentment are fuelling hate campaigns on social media, especially in America.
The diaspora can do little to stem the hate, let alone advance India’s interests. In America it has failed to persuade the Trump administration to adopt policies favourable to India. Indeed just last month Congress in Washington passed legislation allowing 100% tariffs on India for buying Russian oil. The diaspora may be large and even influential, but it is no diplomatic corps.
Mr Modi has hailed his overseas audience as rashtradoot, or emissaries of India. But for all their attachment to India, few in the diaspora want to return to a country where decent jobs are scarce and cities unliveable. Those are the same factors contributing to frustrations among youngsters in India who are increasingly expressing their anger on the streets. Celebrating success abroad may feel good, but a real reason for national pride would be for Indians to flourish at home.

epub_32.title: China is turning trash into treasure on a vast scale
epub_32.text:
China is turning trash into treasure on a vast scale
China
| The recycling superpower
China is turning trash into treasure on a vast scale
EV batteries, especially, will help it secure supplies of critical minerals
Oct 15th 2026
The European Union worries about China’s vast exports of cheap electric vehicles. On October 12th it said that in December a quota of 350,000 a year would be imposed on hybrid-EV imports from China. This is expected to keep their market share below 10%. But the bloc also frets about China’s dominance over critical minerals used to make these vehicles.
A fast-growing number of EVs will soon be scrapped and replaced. Shredding their batteries yields “black mass”, a powder from which valuable metals such as lithium, cobalt and nickel can be recovered and reused. From next month the EU will make it harder to export this waste. The aim is to encourage more processing of black mass close to home (currently most is shipped to Asia). In August America, which has banned Chinese EVs but still imports lots of Chinese batteries, blocked all black-mass exports.
China, however, is unlikely to suffer. Black mass might meet 20-30% of global demand for battery metals by 2050, says the International Energy Agency, a forecaster. So China is supercharging its recycling industries to shore up supplies not just of battery metals, but also of rare earths and much else. The goal is to make the country’s economy less “linear” (where raw materials are made into products that are then thrown away) and more “circular” (closing the loop so recycled waste replaces raw materials).
Once recycling efforts were driven by concerns about pollution. Now, amid a global scramble for the materials needed to build a high-tech economy, security has become a primary motive.
The country has hard-earned experience in managing rubbish. It produces more than anywhere else: about 15% of the world’s municipal detritus (everything from the contents of household bins to street sweepings) and more than one-quarter of its industrial waste (such as demolition debris, factory effluent, scrap metal, slag and ash).
In the 1980s China started to import waste, taking the hardware, paper and plastic that richer countries did not want. A sprawling informal recycling sector emerged, led by scavengers picking through rubbish piles. Much ended up in landfills or burnt in the open air, leaching toxic chemicals and creating poisonous smog. A Chinese documentary in 2011 found that organic waste from dumps around Beijing was being turned into oil and sold to restaurants.
In 2013, wary of mounting public anger, China declared a “war on pollution” and released its first comprehensive national plan to create a circular economy. Electronics were directed to new “urban mining” zones to be scrapped safely; household rubbish was sent to specialised plants to be burned for power; the proportion of waste dumped in landfills started to fall. In 2017 China launched “Operation National Sword” to stop most imports of plastics (in 2021 all imports of solid waste were banned). State-run media trumpeted that the country was “no longer a dumping ground”. Over the past five years most of China’s cities have rolled out mandatory sorting of household rubbish.
China is still well behind squeaky-clean European countries when it comes to waste management (though it is hard to say how far, as it does not publish detailed national data for recycling). Its poorer rural areas are still often strewn with rubbish. But officials have made China’s big cities, at least, cleaner and more pleasant to live in. Now their focus is shifting to the use of recycling for the sake of security. In July China released a plan for the development of the circular economy until 2030. “The importance of resource security has become increasingly prominent, while geopolitical dynamics…have grown complex and severe,” the plan noted.
That judgment rests on two considerations. First, China wants to
dominate high-tech manufacturing
in everything from robotics to wind turbines. And second, to achieve this, it must secure supplies of raw materials, connect more power lines and build more data centres. Massive amounts of aluminium, copper, battery metals and rare earths are needed. While China controls the bulk of the global refining capacity for these materials, it relies on imports for most of the ores. Meanwhile many Western countries want to reduce reliance on China’s factories. Officials worry they may try to squeeze its supplies. Last year a researcher at a state-owned research facility said that, without recycling, China would “keep facing strangleholds in the future”.
China wants to use recycling to supply 510m tonnes of industrial materials annually by 2030, about one-third more than the current level. The easier part will be scaling up the recycling of steel, copper and aluminium: this kind of work is already a mature industry. Recycling more plastic is a little trickier, but worth it to help China reduce imports of oil. The hardest bit will be managing a growing tsunami of electronic garbage. By 2030 China expects to generate 0.5m tonnes of waste from wind turbines, 1m tonnes from EV batteries and 1.5-2m tonnes from solar panels every year—big shares of the global total.
The fact that China already makes vast quantities of these goods should make recycling simpler. Factories can tweak designs so that products are easier to dismantle later. And many battery-producing techniques (such as using acids and heat to isolate valuable metals) are also used in recycling them. Take CATL, for example, the world’s largest battery-maker. Most of the Chinese firm’s sales are domestic, and will end up being processed by a CATL subsidiary called Brunp, which is the world’s biggest battery-recycler. Such arrangements have helped China build 85% of global battery-recycling capacity.
Still, big challenges remain. Much of China’s recycling capacity is unused because too many batteries end up with informal scrap dealers (who waste much of the good stuff inside them) or are just dumped. In recent years several gangs have been busted for running illegal battery-collection rings. Solar panels and wind turbines, which are often used in remote parts of the country, present an even bigger collection problem. Valuable materials they contain (silver, for solar panels; and neodymium, a rare earth, for wind turbines) are present only in small quantities, making extraction trickier.
As ever, China hopes its tech-enabled state can overcome such difficulties. In 2024 it set up a new state-owned company called China Resources Recycling Group to co-ordinate and streamline recycling efforts, with a focus on cleantech products. Recycling plants have started using artificial intelligence to sort waste more efficiently. In April battery- and EV-makers were required to give their products digital IDs to track them through their life cycle on a state-run platform. They have also been made legally responsible for recycling the batteries they produce.
China says recycling already accounts for 10% of its supply of rare earths. It is trying to make the process more efficient. At present it is far more costly than extracting them from raw materials. Still, Chinese rare-earth companies, which are almost all state-owned, “do not rely on economic viability in all cases”, notes Corby Anderson of the Colorado School of Mines.
And to make sure its recycling plants are fed, China is also quietly reassuming its old role in the waste trade. It is selectively rolling back restrictions on some foreign waste. In 2024 it eased curbs on imports of some scrap copper and aluminium. Last year it started allowing imports of black mass. In January it slashed duties on the stuff from 6.5% to 3%. Officials have pledged to continue to increase imports of “high-quality” recycled materials over the next five years.
Now that America and Europe want to keep their valuable waste, could they eat into China’s recycling dominance? Zhang Yuping, the deputy general manager of GEM, a big Shenzhen-listed battery-recycler, thinks not. “From the perspective of national security, they might have some justification,” he says. But the cost of recycling outside China would be high and scaling up difficult. Europe, at least, “can’t digest” such a challenge, reckons Mr Zhang. “They would pay a heavy cost.”

epub_33.title: China has captured the market for hobbyist 3D printers
epub_33.text:
China has captured the market for hobbyist 3D printers
China
| Manufacturing mould
China has captured the market for hobbyist 3D printers
Amid Western wariness, it is struggling to do the same with high-end machines
Oct 15th 2026
The fastest-growing industrial product in China today is not the electric vehicle, lithium-ion battery or even humanoid robot. It is the humble 3D printer for hobbyists. Once geeky curios, 3D printers have quietly become one of China’s most successful consumer electronics. Exports of the machines grew by 90% in the first half of this year. In the past decade China’s global market share has risen from 19% to 96%, ending the dominance of Western firms.
The personal 3D-printing market is now split among the “four little dragons of Shenzhen”, says Chris Connery of Context, a London-based market-intelligence firm. Creality, Anycubic, Elegoo and the industry’s leader, Bambu Lab, reign supreme globally (see chart). Their success shows, yet again, how fierce competition in China combined with generous government support can help improve quality and drive down export prices, making Chinese products hard to beat.
The printers work by building objects layer by layer, usually by extruding molten plastic. Invented by Chuck Hull, an American, in 1983, they long remained expensive, unreliable and difficult to use. Today they routinely sell for a little more than $500 and have the sleek aluminium finish of an Apple computer. Comparable entry-level printers from Western firms start at more than double the price. Artificial intelligence allows users to create print designs for such things as tools, parts or toys by describing them in natural language rather than using complicated design-software. Just as Chinese factories helped to turn drones into recreational devices (as well as game-changers in warfare) by achieving large-scale production at low cost, so they are now doing with 3D printers.
Price wars have eaten into the printer dragons’ profits even as sales boom. But the firms still excite investors. Bambu Lab was founded in 2020 by alumni of another Chinese company, DJI, the world’s leading dronemaker. The printer-maker is reported to have a private valuation of about $10bn. Last year DJI itself invested in Elegoo, a Bambu rival. Creality listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange in May. It boasts a market capitalisation of HK$12bn ($1.5bn).
The government cherishes 3D-printing firms. The business featured in its “Made in China 2025” industrial plan, which was launched in 2015 to ensure domestic strength and self-reliance in high-tech manufacturing (much to the West’s concern). Officials see 3D printers as a way to produce components of aerospace, health care and military equipment, for which China often relies on Western suppliers. Policymakers have directed research institutes and state-run firms to buy them.
Some competitors say Chinese firms have profited from Western open-source printing software. Last month an American court ruled that Bambu Lab had infringed on four patents held by an American company, and ordered it to pay $27.6m in damages. Although Chinese firms have captured the consumer market, they have struggled to do so for industrial 3D printers. Firms are wary of relying on Chinese products if it involves feeding them with sensitive designs (though Britain’s defence ministry has been using Bambu printers, its government admits). Outside China, top-of-the-range machines are still mostly supplied by American and European outfits. They can sell for millions of dollars.
Undeterred, Chinese suppliers are creating a new form of manufacturing at home and abroad. They are pioneering “3D-printing farms”—facilities with as many as 5,000 desktop 3D printers that operate like factories. Several have been built in China this year. Printing farms can mass-produce trinkets for zany consumer trends in short order, replacing expensive and slow injection-moulding techniques. Like the printers themselves, their output will be higher quality and cheaper than what came before.

epub_34.text:
China is channelling much more money to poor countries
China
| Up in alms
China is channelling much more money to poor countries
It wants a greater say in organisations that hand it out
Oct 15th 2026
Chinese diplomats often talk about the threat of a “Thucydides trap”, named after the Greek historian who described how an incumbent power, Sparta, fought to resist the rise of an upstart, Athens. In the realm of foreign aid, however, such fierce rivalry has been sadly absent in recent years. Another trap, identified by Charles Kindleberger, an economic historian, looks dangerous, too. He described what happens when a stabilising superpower cedes its global role before the emerging power is ready or willing to assume it. America was slow to fill Britain’s shoes in the interwar years of the 20th century. And there is now a similar gap in the realm of multilateral giving.
America has tired of the international institutions it helped create. Last year the aid it channelled through multilateral organisations like the World Bank and the UN fell by half. It has withdrawn from the UN’s World Health Organisation—and it still owes the WHO money.
China could have rushed boldly into this void. And it has indeed stumped up more cash. But its approach lacks Athenian assertiveness. “China is not currently either willing or able to fill the financial gap that would be left behind by US withdrawal,” points out Beata Cichocka of the Centre for Global Development, a think-tank in Washington.
With her colleague Ian Mitchell she has tried to add up China’s contributions to multilateral aid, channelled through development banks, UN agencies and 26 “vertical” funds that collect money for specific problems such as climate change. China itself founded some of these institutions, including the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, based in Beijing, and the New Development Bank in Shanghai.
China’s giving to these bodies has increased steeply over the past decade, from about $1bn in 2014 to more than $3bn in 2024 (see chart 1). China has, for example, become the largest donor to the WHO among its member states, promising an extra $500m over five years. It has backed Song Li, a Chinese health official, to become the organisation’s boss when the position opens up next year.
China has also pledged more money to the International Development Association, a World Bank outfit that provides aid and cheap loans to 78 of the world’s poorest countries. China was itself once one of those hard-up countries, receiving almost $10bn in soft loans from 1981 until it ceased to be eligible in 1999. China’s “transformation from major borrower to significant donor represents one of the most remarkable trajectories in multilateral development finance”, as the report points out.
This transformation is all the more welcome given the remarkable retreat of other donors. But much of China’s extra multilateral giving is mandatory, not voluntary: it must pay more dues because of its economic growth. Even the $500m pledged to the WHO mostly reflects an increase in membership dues, judging by the patchy information available. China is doing its bit. But it is not going far beyond its duty.
Perhaps this should not be a surprise. China’s GDP per person is still middling by world standards. It has only just reached the income threshold at which countries typically “step up their contributions”, points out Mr Mitchell. And China’s increased giving has not been matched by a comparable increase in voting power or voice within the institutions it finances. China’s government is “seized [by] this feeling that they pay and therefore they should have [a] say,” says Courtney Fung of Macquarie University. Its voting share in the World Bank remains at less than 6%. According to formulas the bank has used in the past, it should be more than 12%.
China’s share of UN staff is also tiny: 1.4%, ranking only 20th (see chart 2). It is trying to change that by funding more junior professionals and other entrants. China contributed 773 interns in 2022-23 compared with America’s 532. But the country’s civil servants still struggle with language barriers and unfamiliar work habits.
Some obstacles are self-imposed. China, for example, screens its candidates for patriotism (which includes political loyalty). And civil servants who have spent too long abroad worry that their home networks are “going stale”, says Ms Fung. Perhaps the Athenians felt the same way.

epub_35.title: China’s hidden levies are becoming more visible
epub_35.text:
China’s hidden levies are becoming more visible
China
| Chaguan
China’s hidden levies are becoming more visible
Taxpayers now owe more. But is more owed to taxpayers?
Oct 15th 2026
Among tax evaders, from Al Capone to Cristiano Ronaldo, Wu Huatao hardly stands out. Still, the small-time salesman deserves recognition for his brazenness. According to Shanghai’s tax bureau, Mr Wu earned about 550,000 yuan ($82,000) per year but reported just 9,000 yuan. He also claimed an exemption as an ocean-going seafarer when he was, in fact, a landlubber. Then, when tax officials called him, he blocked their numbers.
The authorities ultimately got their man. After they had subjected Mr Wu to what they caringly described as “face-to-face education” on income-tax policy, he fessed up to his misdeeds and paid his taxes and fines. This is just one of many similar cases as China cracks down on evasion. A big deadline looms on October 22nd, when wealthy Chinese must comply with a new tax on offshore trusts or face penalties for late payment.
The heightened enthusiasm for tax collection naturally raises economic questions. Does it reflect a state that is strapped for cash? Probably. Extra revenue is needed to plug gaping budget holes. Might the rules spook Chinese investors? Possibly. But many are captive in their home market. Who will benefit most? That is easy: tax advisers.
Yet there is a separate, more combustible angle to consider: whether the Communist Party faces any political risk from pushing too hard on taxation. No one is throwing green tea into Ningbo’s harbour for now. But Chinese taxpayers, like those anywhere, want to know that the government is not wasteful. And demands for budget accountability are discomfiting for a regime allergic to popular representation. So the trick for Chinese officials is to ensure that cash flows into state coffers without prompting people to dwell on their putative rights as taxpayers.
China’s fiscal system has long been calibrated to do just that. Personal income tax is equivalent to about 1% of GDP, compared with an 8% average in rich countries. Thresholds are so high that only 65m people—a tenth of the workforce—pay any at all. China makes up for this partly with indirect taxation, especially a value-added tax (VAT) that is baked into prices for consumers. It also has non-tax revenues, mainly from land sales. Taken together, these let China extract resources so thinly that people do not feel the pinch. Zhang Changdong of Peking University has argued that the vast majority do not know what they pay in taxes—blissful ignorance as far as the party is concerned.
Yet the system has flaws. When consumption taxes are relied on so heavily, they hit poor people hard because the less well-off spend a bigger share of their incomes. The wealthy technically face much higher income taxes but have many loopholes to reduce their bills—including, until recently, offshore trusts. More pressing for the government, the tax structure no longer raises enough revenue. Local authorities, which had relied on land sales for much of their income, now face widening budget deficits amid a prolonged property slump.
That is what makes the new taxation drive so significant. Previously officials went after the odd celebrity, such as Fan Bingbing, an actress ordered to pay a whopping 883m yuan in 2018, to show that the wealthy are not a law unto themselves. Now China’s taxation efforts are much broader. Virtually every transaction is digital, and authorities have honed their technology for parsing the data—a system known as Golden Tax Phase IV. They comb through bank statements and transactions on Alipay and WeChat, China’s main digital wallets. All this monitoring is buttressed by co-operation with tax agencies in many other countries.
Over the past year people with foreign accounts have received alerts in their income-tax apps warning them to comply with laws. The ultra-rich could owe mammoth sums, enough to unsettle financial markets. Shu Ping, a co-founder of Haidilao, a hotpot chain, sold a nearly 5% stake in September, worth about HK$2.75bn ($350m). The firm cited personal funding needs; analysts suspected a tax bill. Haidilao’s share price fell by more than 10%. Other bosses—especially those whose foreign listings suggest wealth offshore—may also be in line for hefty back taxes.
A private-equity manager recently moaned to Chaguan that his tax bill had blindsided him. The government’s new rule on overseas trusts did not exempt existing arrangements; it had applied the tax retroactively. But he had to resign himself to paying up. The government is counting on a couple of things. The rich do not really have anywhere to run, short of changing their citizenship and abandoning their businesses and assets in China. And most of the population will remain untouched, and indeed might enjoy seeing more fortunate compatriots pay up.
Yet Mr Wu, the hapless tax-evading salesman, is a reminder that the dragnet does not stop at tycoons. Anyone with side income or a foreign brokerage account is now visible to tax authorities. That describes many middle-class Chinese, precisely those who are likely to wonder what they are getting in return. In the early 2000s state media occasionally spoke approvingly of “taxpayer consciousness”—the idea that those paying taxes ought to have some oversight of public budgets. Such talk has faded as the state has tightened its grip on the media. Instead of taxpayers’ rights, the emphasis has been on their duties. Beijing’s tax office recently listed managing public sentiment as a key part of the new reforms—a euphemism for nipping criticism in the bud.
Fiscally, a shift to more direct taxation is right for China, promising a system that is fairer and more sustainable. Politically, it is a calculated gamble. China is making the taxman a bigger, and more intrusive, presence in everyday life. People who pay more tend to ask for more.

epub_37.title: America’s election officials are ready for trouble
epub_37.text:
America’s election officials are ready for trouble
United States
| On guard
America’s election officials are ready for trouble
Donald Trump has failed to change voting rules. Cities and states are preparing for mischief anyway
Oct 15th 2026
On a fine day in Florence, a city near Phoenix, staff at the local voting centre are doing a tabletop exercise, the euphemism to describe training for election hell. The point is to imagine calamities—fire, power cuts, bomb threats—then have a Plan B, C and D. Officials have always made some doomsday preparations, but this year’s exercise is more thorough, and the range of threats broader. What, for example, should they do if federal law-enforcement agents show up at the polls?
The staff run through the protocols. Monitors from the Department of Justice (DoJ) can stay if they have an official letter, and indeed the government has said 1,000 will be dispatched across the country. Any other agents must leave unless they are themselves voting; Arizona law mandates a perimeter of 75 feet (25 metres) around precincts. “If they refuse to leave, that’s when the scenario becomes a scenario,” says an election worker in the recorder’s office in Pinal county, of which Florence is the seat. In other words: call the sheriff.
Pinal is a Republican county. A portion of it lies in Arizona’s 6th congressional district, one of several dozen competitive House races in the midterm elections on November 3rd.
Our forecast
suggests Democrats will flip the House and possibly the Senate, too. The nagging concern is that Donald Trump may try to subvert the election’s legitimate results.
His effort to overturn his loss in 2020 alerted everyone to the many pressure points in America’s decentralised election system, and the lengths he might go to squeeze them. So far, his many attempted interventions this year have amounted to little, with Congress and the Supreme Court blocking his efforts to rewrite voting procedures. States, not the federal government, run elections, and their rules are mostly unchanged from past cycles. However, the executive branch has shifted from being a force to support electoral integrity to one undermining it, and in November the system will be tested once more.
Some changes represent not active interference, but the removal of help. Last year the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) stopped covering localities’ costs to join a service for sharing cyber threats. Membership in the programme is down by around two-thirds. The upshot is that cyberattacks are more likely to proliferate, reckons Geoff Hale, formerly of CISA. “If a jurisdiction faces one and gets compromised or repels it, but if they’re not sharing information about that attack, then other election jurisdictions remain equally vulnerable.” Similarly, the FBI is said to have no plans to activate its election command centre, which in past years monitored threats and co-ordinated with local officials.
However, election administrators increasingly view the federal government as a threat, too, says Jonathan Miller of Public Rights Project (PRP), a litigation group that represents local governments. Earlier this year the DoJ said it would prosecute officials who let non-citizens vote. Such voter fraud is extremely rare, but the spectre of voting by non-citizens propels the myth of election theft. It is the reason that MAGA activists want immigration enforcement at the polls.
Their presence would be illegal: federal law prohibits government officials from sending armed agents to precincts. On behalf of the city of Denver, PRP has sued the Department of Homeland Security, seeking to pre-empt anything like that on election day. The Trump administration says it has no intention of patrolling precincts, but that it may take targeted action, such as serving warrants against anyone suspected of being an illegal immigrant. Democrats fear that even the threat of agents near polling places will dampen turnout by minorities, who tend to vote Democratic. In a survey by UC San Diego, a third of Hispanics said they anticipate being questioned at the polls despite being citizens. Nearly half say they expect some form of intimidation.
Election experts’ nightmare is that Mr Trump might try to seize voting equipment or ballots. That would break the “chain of custody”, the controls that set out who can handle ballots and where they go, ensuring all are accounted for. Losing custody would make it hard to know whether ballots had been manipulated. “I would feel very uncomfortable about validating those ballots,” says Stephen Richer, a former recorder in Arizona’s Maricopa County. “Then you start going down the dark road of, like, do you have to call a new election?”
Two incidents concerning past elections have primed Democrats to the possibility of meddling. In January the FBI raided an election office in Fulton county, Georgia, and carted away material from 2020. Then in March, Chad Bianco, a Republican sheriff in Riverside, California, seized ballots that had been cast in a statewide referendum last year. Both the FBI and Mr Bianco cited misinformation in their requests for warrants.
Could there be a similar ruse in November’s midterms? The previous incidents occurred long after elections were over, not in the middle of one. Ed Martin, a MAGA agitator, says that the president met this month with Tina Peters, a former county clerk who had gone to prison for giving a fellow election-denier unauthorised access to voting machines in 2021, and whose sentence was then commuted by Colorado’s Democratic governor. Mr Martin, who described Ms Peters’s meeting to an interviewer, offered this cryptic assessment of the midterm elections: “The president’s going to have to do what he’s going to do.”
State and local officials are on high alert. Colorado now requires county clerks to log everything, so that they have clear records if a judge ever orders material removed from their custody. One county official in Arizona says she has made sure her voting-machine vendor has extra supplies, so they are ready if the feds seize equipment. Gabriella Cázares-Kelly, the recorder in Pima County, along the Arizona-Mexico border, says lawyers there have restraining orders drafted if immigration agents show up. “They would plug in a few things, hit print and physically run the document over to a waiting judge.”
Such scenarios remain very unlikely. Yet officials must also contend with election-denial activists, who routinely file nuisance public-records requests and challenges to voter registrations. In swing states such as Georgia, they have also managed to win positions on local boards, with some aiming for statewide office this November. As administrators prepare for “what if” scenarios, there remains the not insubstantial task of getting the basic mechanics of elections right, which can be challenging enough, says Eslir Musta of Arizona’s Coconino County. In his case, that means preparing a mule caravan to serve voters who live at the bottom of the Grand Canyon.
Just half of Americans tell pollsters they anticipate a free and fair midterms. The tighter the margin in either chamber, the more uncertainty there will be to exploit in November. Lawsuits and recounts are now standard in close races. This year control of the Senate may come down to one or two states, including some that are famously slow to count, such as Alaska. A lengthy or contested count requires patience and restraint on the part of candidates. Those are not qualities often attributed to Mr Trump.

Vivek Ramaswamy is too MAGA and not MAGA enough
United States
| Adrift
Vivek Ramaswamy is too MAGA and not MAGA enough
A candidate once considered a rising star gets stuck in Ohio
Oct 15th 2026
A covered picnic area in a park on a damp, blustery day is hardly an ideal spot for a political rally, so it was difficult to fault the members of the Delaware County Republican Party for their muted enthusiasm. At an event in a suburb of Columbus on October 10th some 75 people sat through an hour of speeches by candidates and local police officials. The highlight of the show was Vivek Ramaswamy, a pharmaceutical billionaire and former presidential candidate who is the party’s candidate for governor. He promised to be an even-handed and independent leader. “You don’t just tell [people] what they want to hear,” he said.
No more than 15 yards away, it was easy to find views that Mr Ramaswamy’s crowd did not want to hear. In an adjacent children’s playground Jared Hessler, a 39-year-old technology worker who was with his young son, explained that he will not be voting for Mr Ramaswamy. Mr Hessler used to vote Republican, but over the past two elections he has pivoted towards the Democrats and is enthusiastic about Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate for governor. “I would say that the main driving force is just being
so sick and tired
of Trump,” he says.
That sentiment is a problem for Mr Ramaswamy. Mike DeWine, Ohio’s term-limited Republican governor, won 62% of the vote in 2022 and Donald Trump has won the state in three consecutive presidential elections. Now most polls show Dr Acton with a slight lead. Mr Ramaswamy is proving too MAGA for Ohio’s moderates and not MAGA enough for many Republicans.
Delaware County is the richest and best-educated in Ohio. Not long ago it was also at the heart of Republicanism in the state, with its residents favouring George W. Bush by 32 points in 2004. But as it has become more built up and diverse, it has shifted Democratic. By 2024 Mr Trump’s margin was less than seven points.
Mr Ramaswamy has some traits that would, presumably, appeal to the suburban Republicans who have become sceptical of the president. In his speeches, he emphasises cutting business taxes rather than deportation. The son of Indian immigrants, he celebrates people who come to America legally and backs immigration reform. Last year he issued a stark criticism of his party’s nativist wing in an article for the New York Times. Many of his campaign staff previously worked for John Kasich, a moderate Republican who served as Ohio’s governor from 2011 to 2019.
In practice, however, he remains tainted by his links to an unpopular president with whom he has appeared at two rallies in the past month. At a party on the outskirts of a recent Ohio State football game (as close as a secular event can come to being sacred), former Republicans were easy to find. Voters for Mr Ramaswamy were not. “I am going Democrat all the way, even though I’m a Republican,” said one enthusiastic middle-aged tailgater named Debbie. Mr Trump is the reason why. “The insanity of this particular administration has just put me over the top,” she explains. It is Dr Acton, who led the state’s response to the covid pandemic, who is seen as the moderate. In 2020 Mr DeWine called her a “hero”. Mr Trump is trying to rebrand her as a “radical-left lunatic”.
Mr Ramaswamy has another problem, too, on his right. In the primary election his opponent, Casey Putsch, holding a rifle, invited Mr Ramaswamy to “play cowboys versus Indians”. He also attacked him for being “a HINDU man!” Mr Ramaswamy beat him handily, but Mr Putsch still managed to win 18% of the vote. Nick Fuentes, a white-nationalist podcaster with a devoted following, said last year that his main goal for 2026 was “to deny Vivek Ramaswamy the governorship”. This month he endorsed Dr Acton, calling Mr Ramaswamy an “anchor baby”.
Pinched from both sides, Mr Ramaswamy is resorting to an exceptionally ugly campaign. His adverts and those of the superPACs supporting him centre almost exclusively on Dr Acton. Some allege she is a drunk and a drug addict (based on a police report of her having a shouting match with her husband). Others accuse her of being responsible for the death of an elderly woman during the covid pandemic (the woman had in fact lived and died in Kentucky). Mr Ramaswamy will probably run for president again if he does become governor. But for a man seeking to lead his party, he looks increasingly lost in it.

The impact of data-centre discontent
United States
| The backlash
The impact of data-centre discontent
Democrats are capitalising on voters’ anxiety
Oct 15th 2026
To spot the site of a new data centre, look for the cranes. About a dozen soar over the fields of Saline township, Michigan, visible for miles around. Another hint is the convoy of cement-mixers trundling down the road, loudly and constantly. When the OpenAI and Oracle project in Saline, “The Barn”, is finished, it will consume more power than a midsize city.
Beside it is the Rustic Glen Golf Club, where a few locals are enthusiastic about the project. “They’ve been talking to us, and they’re going to do a lot of nice things for us,” says a cashier. The data-centre developers have bought the club and have promised to inject cash. Fred, a farmer standing atop a tractor across the road, offers a more typical reaction: “There’s nothing good I can say about it…that was a beautiful piece of farmland, and they destroyed it.” Drinkers at a nearby brewery say the same, a little more politely, and grouse that the golfers were paid off.
Across America, data centres are popping up at startling speed. Since last November more money has been spent building data centres—not including the expensive chips inside them—than new offices (see chart 1). President Donald Trump has warned that places opposed to data centres risk becoming “backwards and poor”, but Republican candidates are trying to be more attuned to voters like Fred. In Michigan Mike Rogers, a Republican Senate candidate, supports a pause on building. Such moves may be too late. Our analysis of polling data suggests that, as anxiety over data centres grows, the projects seem to be pushing voters towards Democrats.
We matched almost 150,000 respondents from the Economist/YouGov weekly survey with their nearest data centre, using Compute Atlas, an open-source repository of such sites. Voters across the country are shifting towards Democrats, but for those living within 2km of a data centre the veer has been even sharper. Americans who live near a data-centre site are around six percentage points more likely to support the Democrats than those who live further away (see chart 2). Six months ago there was no such difference.
For Brandon, who is circulating a petition against data centres in Ohio, the issue has turned him from a Republican into a swing voter. Local Republicans refused to help his cause, he says, but “the Democrats have been amazing.” Michigan and Ohio are already home to more local moratoriums than any other states.
Why have data centres caught fire politically? Throughout dozens of conversations, voters seldom brought up AI-related concerns directly. The most common fears were practical ones, about water pollution, higher electricity bills or a hit to house prices. Neither politicians’ promises that the projects will pay their own way nor developers’ efforts to bat away concerns with cash seem to have done much good. Whatever the truth is, practical assurances count for little when voters so deeply distrust both government and big businesses: confidence in each is near 50-year lows.
The real-world effect of all that opposition has, so far, been limited. Maya Barkin of SemiAnalysis, a research firm, finds that only 2.3 gigawatts’ worth of projects are likely to be delayed by moratoriums (see chart 3). But with discontent growing, the political impact is more assured.

Professional sumo wrestling comes to America
Meet the people betting Americans will swoon over Japan’s ancient pastime
Oct 15th 2026
ON A RECENT evening in Peachtree City, Georgia, Katie Hardeman was training her Black Dragon “boys”. For two hours she put the aspiring sumo wrestlers—mostly middle-aged men—through a gruelling workout. Then she invited your correspondent to have a go, strapping her into a mawashi, the Japanese loincloth, and instructing her to charge headfirst into a man’s chest, palms aiming for “tits and pits”. “There’s something electric about it,” says Ms Hardeman, a combat veteran. “We’re trying to overcome the negative connotation in our country that sumo is just fat guys in diapers pushing each other.”
On October 10th the Sumo Championship League held its debut match in Austin, Texas. The league is the first of its kind on this side of the Pacific. Sixteen wrestlers competed until the third-seed, a 21-year-old Floridian, won gold.
Stuart Snyder, the entertainment guru behind the event, was once chief operating officer at World Wrestling Entertainment, which for decades has staged fake smackdowns. After he saw cornhole, in which adults toss bean bags through a punctured plank, go viral online, he decided fringe sports were having a moment—and sumo was next. With $5m in hand, he is betting he can hook Americans on a pastime rooted in Asian traditions.
Many of the league’s aspiring stars are new to it. Jonithan “Jiva” Pilgrim was living at a Hare Krishna commune when he discovered sumo on YouTube. Realising he had “no other nature than to be a warrior”, he joined a club and gained weight on a diet of whey shakes, tofu and ghee. His club-mate Dominus “Domzilla” Davis-Williams, the league’s heaviest wrestler at 450lbs (204kg), is a former player of American football. Sumo “felt familiar”, he says. And it does wonders for his “body positivity”.
To help sumo grow, a few customs may adapt. In Austin some wrestlers went “traditional” and wore just the mawashi, leaving their buttocks exposed. Others snuck shorts underneath. Americans, reckons Mr Pilgrim, will swoon for sumo, but they may not be ready for “that much naked male body”.

Donald Trump turns to Vladimir Putin for relief at the pump
United States
| A slippery deal
Donald Trump turns to Vladimir Putin for relief at the pump
But Russian diesel is unlikely to solve the president’s political problems
Oct 15th 2026
“THE EUROPEANS are still sending money to Russia for energy,” complained Scott Bessent, America’s treasury secretary, in January. “It is so absurd. They are financing the war against themselves.” So too, now, is America. On October 9th Donald Trump—who just weeks ago signed into law a bill requiring tariffs on big importers of Russian oil and gas—said that Vladimir Putin, Russia’s president, would sell millions of tonnes of diesel fuel to America. The deal has sparked a minor rebellion among Mr Trump’s supporters. Worse, it is unlikely to achieve his goals.
Mr Trump’s motivations are mixed. His advisers portray the deal as an effort to pave the way for peace talks; the president also announced a Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire, which was denied by Ukraine and ignored by Russia. European diplomats suspect that some of the president’s aides are desperate to re-establish economic ties with Russia. But a more pressing concern for Mr Trump is rising prices at home. Annual inflation hit 3.7% in September, driven by higher energy costs.
America is a diesel exporter, but a global shortage has pushed up prices everywhere. The main cause is the war in Iran and the disruption of tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. Ukraine’s strikes on Russian refineries have made matters worse. Diesel costs $6.29 per gallon in America, up 72% from a year earlier. That could have political consequences: of seven “toss-up” Senate races in November’s midterm elections, four are in states that use more diesel than average, according to The Economist’s calculations.
Mr Trump seems to hope that more Russian diesel exports will pull down prices before the midterms. But he is likely to be disappointed. Russia is struggling with diesel shortages of its own. The quantity pledged in the deal is tiny relative to global consumption. Moreover, Russia would almost certainly have exported that diesel anyway. And even if Ukraine stops striking Russian refineries, any increase in production is likely to come after America votes.
Opponents of the president accuse him of stretching, if not breaking, the law, citing the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act of 2022. The clear intent of the law is that it should prohibit these imports, says Peter Harrell of Georgetown Law School. The act was implemented through an executive order whose wording might give Mr Trump a tenuous justification for issuing temporary licences. Democrats tried to close that loophole in April but were rebuffed by Republicans. Still, the legal uncertainty may cause firms to stay away. “What company is going to risk liability for importing Russian oil under these circumstances?” asks Dan Fried, who once led America’s sanctions policy against Russia.
The political blowback has been swift. On October 13th a dozen senators, including six Republicans, signed a letter to Mr Trump describing the deal as “a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our allies”. Among them were the independent-minded Susan Collins and the outgoing Thom Tillis, who has threatened to use a military spending bill as leverage to stop the deal. But criticism has also come from Republicans once reluctant to take on Mr Trump, such as Mike Rogers, a Senate candidate in Michigan, and Dan Sullivan, an Alaska senator facing a tough re-election fight. Privately, Republican aides are scathing about what they see as needless folly. “I expect”, says one, “it will go away quietly.”

epub_42.text:
The Jon Ossoff guide to being a Democrat
United States
| Govern moderately, campaign fiercely
The Jon Ossoff guide to being a Democrat
A rising star in Georgia pairs bland governing with hot rhetoric
Oct 15th 2026
Nearly a decade ago a documentary exposed widespread corruption in one of Africa’s top football leagues. The Ghana Football Association was dissolved and dozens of officials were sacked. “Corruption and self-dealing are at the heart of a lot of the dysfunction and suffering in the world today,” one of the film’s producers said at the time.
Eight years on, that producer is a senator from Georgia running for re-election on the same message. At rallies across the state, Jon Ossoff tells a simple story: Donald Trump and his “Mar-a-Lago mafia” have exploited the rot in American politics, enriching themselves while raising costs for ordinary Americans. In a debate on October 8th, Mr Ossoff pressed his case, claiming his opponent, Mike Collins, had “sold out Georgia in his pathetic, childlike devotion to Donald Trump, voting for the tariffs that have sent groceries soaring, voting for the health-care cuts that have doubled your insurance premiums and voting for the war that sent
diesel to its record high
”. In a swing state that Mr Trump carried by two points in 2024, Mr Ossoff leads in every major poll and has raised more money than any other candidate in the country this cycle.
Republicans’ current weakness in the state makes it easier for Mr Ossoff to shine. The president’s net approval rating in Georgia, at -31% according to Economist/YouGov polling, is lower than in any other battleground state. And Mr Collins, a congressman, has been dogged by continued revelations of his ties to white supremacists. But as Democrats consider how to succeed beyond the midterms, Mr Ossoff offers one answer. As a campaigner, he is a firebrand. When it comes to governing, he is deeply uncontroversial.
This is not a combination shared by many other Democrats. As the party wrestles with its identity, two camps stand out. First there are the moderates, such as Roy Cooper and Andy Beshear, one a Senate candidate in North Carolina and the other the governor of Kentucky. Then there is
the populist left
, represented by the likes of Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Zohran Mamdani. The two Democratic Socialists from New York have won campaigns by pairing ample charisma with big, leftist ideas, such as universal health care and rent freezes.
Mr Ossoff straddles both worlds. He was first elected in 2021 at the age of 33, the first millennial to serve in the Senate. Running in right-leaning Georgia, he needs the support of Republicans to win, even when the political environment favours the Democrats. Charles Bullock of the University of Georgia estimates that Mr Ossoff can carry Georgia in November only if he earns the vote of 40% of white college-educated voters and at least 20% of white non-college voters, most of whom are conservative.
So, as a senator, Mr Ossoff is competent and bland. Republican strategists begrudgingly admire how responsive he is to constituents, in both Democratic cities and the ruby-red countryside. At a conference of Georgia mayors a few years ago, a panelist asked the crowd who had received a cold call from Mr Ossoff. Nearly every hand went up. In August two Republican mayors from south Georgia endorsed him. Scott James Matheson, of Valdosta, credited Mr Ossoff with securing $2m for buses in the city and said he was the first politician to visit after a hurricane. The other, Julie Smith of Tifton, told local press: “I’m a Republican, but there are times when a person exceeds the party.”
Mr Ossoff’s Senate record is strikingly uncontentious, focused on reforming foster care, making military housing safer and bringing green-manufacturing jobs to Georgia. “The best word to describe Jon is pragmatist,” says Andrew Feiler, a Democratic political adviser in Atlanta. His only vote that might count as controversial was against blocking federal funding for schools that let transgender women compete in women’s sports. “It’s hard to peg where he actually is on an ideological spectrum and that’s a damn good thing,” says John Anzalone, a national Democratic pollster.
As a storyteller, however, Mr Ossoff prefers to be sharp. He writes his own speeches; his team is adept at splicing his appearances into clips that go viral on Instagram. Mr Trump, he says, is a “draft-dodging crook” and “the world’s most famous sore loser”, his aides are “sycophants” and Mr Collins is “a crumbling little bigot”. This summer Mr Ossoff mocked the president for wanting to “travel with Natalie” Harp, a close aide, on his Qatari-gifted jet rather than do his job.
This has the desired effect. After his comment about Ms Harp, MAGA-world erupted on X. Mr Trump nicknamed him “Pee-Wee Herman”; top advisers called him a “feminine theatre kid cosplaying as Barack Obama” and a “radical, extremist Dumocrat”. The spats keep him in the news and cast him as the fighter Democrats are craving. That, in turn, drives donations. The senator has outraised his challenger by a factor of 12.
Mr Ossoff’s stump speech packs a one-two punch. He argues that America’s political system is “coin-operated”, that Mr Trump and his friends have taken corruption to “spectacular new heights” and that this is why “nothing works for ordinary people”. He then calls on Americans, regardless of party, to take back their government from the corrupt elite. To drive the moral point home, he invokes John Lewis, a lion of the civil-rights movement and Democratic congressman whom Mr Ossoff claims as his political mentor. “He kept reminding us that we all live in one American house.”
That helping of positivity is deliberate. “As Democrats we’ve learned our lesson that we have to present an alternative narrative that politics can do good,” says Jonae Wartel, who ran the Georgia Democratic Party’s runoff effort in 2021, which included Mr Ossoff’s race. The senator, she explains, understands that he can’t just be the “anti-guy”. After the midterms, the question will be whether he wants to be the guy. “I have zero interest in running for president in 2028,” Mr Ossoff said in August. Of the senator’s many claims, that’s his least convincing.

epub_43.title: Republicans need to learn the Democrats’ bitter lesson of 2022
epub_43.text:
Republicans need to learn the Democrats’ bitter lesson of 2022
United States
| Lexington
Republicans need to learn the Democrats’ bitter lesson of 2022
Even if they beat expectations in the midterms, their standard-bearer is an obstacle to their future
Oct 15th 2026
The news rushes ahead so swiftly now that even recent events can vanish in the rear-view mirror, to be recalled dimly, if at all. But cast your mind back, if you can, to four years ago. In mid-October 2022 petrol prices were nearing $4 a gallon, and 30-year mortgage rates were spiking to  7%. Only one in five Americans thought the country was heading in the right direction, and the approval ratings of the president, Joe Biden, were dismal. Analysts noted that Democrats were struggling to defend seats in districts Mr Biden had won by double digits in such reliably Democratic states as California and New York. Not just a red wave but a “red tsunami” was coming, crowed Senator Ted Cruz of Texas. “Tomorrow, its immense swell will make landfall,” the American Conservative, a right-wing publication, predicted on election eve.
The immense swell, it turned out, was in the advance hype. The Republicans won a majority in the House, but it was the Democrats who emerged elated. They had confounded expectations and overcome the historical pattern of midterm elections by losing a net of only nine seats in the House and gaining one in the Senate, where they held  the majority. That outcome should be a caution to Democrats now, as they grow giddy at the hope of their own tsunami next month. But the real lesson is for Republicans:  what seemed like happy news for the Democrats in 2022 turned out to be a disaster for them.
When Mr Biden held a press conference the day after the midterms to celebrate what he called “a strong night” for Democrats, he was asked what he would now do differently. “Nothing,” he replied. Americans, he explained, were just learning to appreciate the great achievements of his administration. “The more they know about what we’re doing, the more support there is,” he said. After the midterms, aides who had privately wondered whether Mr Biden should run for a second term cast their doubts aside, and other party leaders publicly fell into line behind him. At that press conference, Mr Biden declared that the outcome of the midterms meant the MAGA Republicans were “not taking over the government again”. Two years later they did just that.
Do the Democrats have a bigger advantage in 2026 than the Republicans did in 2022? Probably. In 2022  Republican candidates had to contend with anger at the Supreme Court’s Dobbs decision, handed down in June that year, which eliminated a constitutional right to abortion. That energised not only reliable Democratic voters but also a constituency that had drifted away from the party—white women without college degrees. At the same time, though Democrats, then the party in power, were competitive financially  in 2022,  Republicans have extracted an extraordinary advantage during this election cycle. Further, Donald Trump’s push to gerrymander more districts ahead of this election may have added about eight seats to the Republicans’ total.
The biggest difference in 2026 that favours the Democrats is passion. In 2022 voters who described themselves as “extremely motivated” to go to the polls were evenly divided between the parties, according to polling by the Pew Research Centre. In 2026, according to Pew, 59% of such fired-up voters favour the Democrats, while only 35% favour Republicans.
Whence this motivation gap? Everyone knows the answer, but Republicans are scared to admit it. Voters are not inspired by a coherent Democratic legislative agenda.  In contrast to 1994, when Republicans united around Newt Gingrich’s “Contract with America” to win a thumping victory in the House,  and to 2006, when Democrats campaigned on a six-point plan they called “Six for ’06”, no one in this cycle could hope to distil the aims of the opposition party on a notecard. Nor can it be said that even Democrats—let alone the wider public—are thrilled with the party. Only 48% of Democratic voters approve of the job their party is doing now in Congress, according to a poll last month by Quinnipiac University. Among all registered voters, that proportion is 21%.
What Democratic candidates have going for them is, simply, rejection of the Trump presidency. Every midterm election is a referendum on the sitting president, but that appears to be truer this year than ever. Fully 44% of registered voters view their vote for congressional representatives as a vote to oppose him; only 19% want to signal support for him. The election-forecast model devised by The Economist gives the Democrats an astonishing three-in-five chance of winning the Senate, and a 19-in-20 chance of winning the House. But gerrymandering and polarisation make it far harder for a party to achieve the kind of whopping gains Republicans made as recently as 2010, when they netted 64 seats. The Cook Political Report, a sober prognosticator of elections, estimates the Democrats will gain between nine House seats—the same number as the Republicans netted in 2022—and 19 seats.
When Republicans lose, Mr Trump looks for someone else to blame. “If they win, I should get all the credit,” he said of his endorsed candidates in 2022. “And if they lose, I should not be blamed at all.” In 2026 he should get the blame whether Republicans take a shellacking or, by beating the expectations game, eke out the phoney validation Mr Biden claimed four years ago. Mr Trump put his party in a hole by promoting candidates in states such as Texas and South Carolina based on loyalty to him rather than skill and appeal. More important, he has made lousy choices in office that have made him historically unpopular. Yet even more than Mr Biden, this president can be counted on to keep governing as he has, regardless of the midterm result. He cannot run again. But those Republicans who hope to succeed him as president in 2029 should learn from the Democrats’ mistakes and begin, politely but decisively, to distance themselves from him.

epub_45.text:
Entrepreneurs in Cuba are snapping up American fuels
The Americas
| Motors running?
Entrepreneurs in Cuba are snapping up American fuels
Donald Trump’s blockade of the island is starting to have curious effects
Oct 15th 2026
For years Cuba relied on Venezuela to supply much of its energy. Things have changed a lot in the past nine months. Now Cuba is getting all its fuel from the country’s great nemesis, the United States—perhaps as many as 3.2m barrels in July, according to figures recently released by the US Energy Information Administration, a government agency. And whereas the fuel from Venezuela was being bought by Cuba’s government, which at that point monopolised the trade, this time it is (at least in theory) flowing to the Cuban private sector instead.
This changeabout is one result of America’s evolving policy towards the island. Donald Trump and Marco Rubio, his Cuban-American secretary of state, came to power in 2025 promising to squeeze Cuba’s communist government, which has misruled the island since 1959. In January American special forces captured Nicolás Maduro, Venezuela’s dictator, and jailed him in New York; in the wake of that, Mr Trump was able to force Venezuela to stop sending Cuba fuel. America’s president also threatened tariffs on any other country shipping energy to Cuba’s government, which scared off Mexico, too. The idea seemed to be not just that this would make life difficult for the Cuban government but also for its people, increasing the chance that they might seek to topple the regime of their own accord.
The blockade has caused much suffering. The government was already struggling to provide power to the island, because of ageing infrastructure and cash shortages. Apagones (blackouts) have grown so common as to have become the norm. These days the bigger surprise for Cubans are the alumbrones—moments when the power comes on. Additionally, America’s fuel blockade paralysed public transport, prevented distribution of food and other goods, and as a result caused prices for all sorts of things to soar.
Faced with crisis, in February Cuba’s government began letting the island’s private businesses import fuel and started permitting entrepreneurs to lease petrol stations that were previously state-run. The United States likewise gave American sellers permission to export light fuels—diesel, petrol, propane and the like—to Cubans outside government. (A separate, subsequent policy allows American firms to resell Venezuelan crude to Cuba’s private businesses—but no privately owned firm in Cuba has the ability to refine crude or to run a power station, so for now only light fuel is moving.)
These new imports are not fixing the problems with the energy grid, which is managed by the government. People still sit in the dark at night; food still rots in idled fridges and freezers.
But the influx of light fuels has lessened some problems, all the same. Cars are back on the roads; public transport has picked up. People and businesses lucky enough to afford private generators are finding it a bit easier to run them. The price of petrol has dropped to around $2.50 a litre, half the price before the surge in American fuel began. There is even price competition between the petrol stations, says Omar Everleny, an economist in Havana.
The new fuel trade is a boon to Cuba’s downtrodden private businesses. Successive administrations in Washington have said they want to empower entrepreneurs. And for some years Cuba’s government has been grudgingly giving private firms more room, as its ability to meet people’s needs has shrivelled. It legalised freelance work in 1993 and small businesses in 2021. This year it hurriedly passed an impressive-sounding batch of 176 reforms. Largely to appease the Americans, and dig itself out of a hole, it gave somewhat more space to the private sector.
By ending the state fuel monopoly, the government has handed entrepreneurs a new and profitable line of business. “Our policy on Cuba has already caused the largest ever privatisation of Cuba’s economy,” boasts the State Department. The hope is that to get the oil it needs for its power stations, the regime may privatise bits of Cupet, the state oil company, too. On October 12th Cuba passed a law encouraging private participation in the entire oil industry—in the hope of producing more oil itself.
Booming oil sales emphasise how Cuba now depends on a country it still formally considers an enemy. It has not been able to lean on allies, such as China, Mexico and Russia, to help assuage its oil problems. The United States is also Cuba’s biggest single foreign source of food. In three years it has gone from Cuba’s tenth-largest trading partner to its largest, overtaking Spain and China. All this is giving the Trump administration leverage.
Some question exactly how fully the fuel deals are cutting out Cuba’s government. Yes, the state has leased petrol stations to businesses—but its own tankers can be seen filling up at them.  The government is not getting oil for its power plants, but some American diesel may be making its way into the 52,000 government-owned generators that supply power to the grid in some areas. Many Cubans are pleased that petrol has dropped in price, but they warn that the new fuel barons are sons and daughters of bigwigs in government. “The people involved in that business are mainly from the cúpula,” says a Havana resident, using the Cuban term for the ruling elite. There is a danger of merely swapping totalitarianism for oligarchy.
Some United States officials seem not to mind. However much they despise Cuba’s communists, they do not want a humanitarian catastrophe 90 miles (145km) off the Florida coast. And they can at least claim that their policies towards Cuba have been unabashedly “America First”. The fuel trade is helping mint a new generation of Cuban-American entrepreneurs in Florida. And if it becomes feasible for Cuba’s private businesses to import and make use of crude oil, that will come via the United States from Venezuela. In other words, it would be from the same source as before Mr Trump’s oil blockade, but with American business folk now inserted bluntly in the middle.
Muddled policymaking in Washington risks sabotaging some of what is currently being achieved. On September 30th the Trump administration moved to freeze American bank accounts being used by Cuban entrepreneurs—hurting the very people whom its fuel policies have recently empowered. Mr Trump, in trying to topple the Cuban government, may inadvertently have struck upon a policy that can boost the private sector and loosen the regime’s grip over the island’s unhappy people.

epub_46.title: Why do political prisoners still languish in Venezuela’s jails?
