Why do political prisoners still languish in Venezuela’s jails?
The Americas
| Freedom postponed
Why do political prisoners still languish in Venezuela’s jails?
America may see value in permitting it
Oct 15th 2026
RODEO IS A notorious prison near Caracas, Venezuela’s capital. In one of its towers, people who fell foul of the country’s grim regime are held in tiny cells with open latrines. The heat, smell and bugs are unbearable. Televisions play propaganda. And then there is the torture. Wilder Vásquez, 32, who was held there as a political prisoner for almost three years, says the director welcomed him to the prison with a taunt: “Only God can get you out of here.”
In the end, he was sprung by Donald Trump. It is nine months since America’s president dispatched special forces to snatch Nicolás Maduro, the former dictator—only to replace him with his deputy, Delcy Rodríguez. Mr Trump boasts of his control over Venezuela. Mr Vásquez is one of 1,104 political prisoners who have since been released. Yet there are still more than 300 languishing behind bars, many in Rodeo, according to Foro Penal, an NGO. Relatives of these inmates, some of them camping outside the prison gates, struggle to understand why.
The issue underlines tensions at the heart of the new relationship between the United States and Venezuela, says Phil Gunson, an analyst with Crisis Group, another NGO. The Trump administration has extraordinary leverage over Ms Rodríguez. Everyone knows that it could snatch her, just as it snatched her boss. The United States controls Venezuela’s oil exports, too. And yet it still depends on Ms Rodríguez’s regime to run Venezuela day-to-day. “The United States cannot simply remake Venezuela in the way we want overnight,” says Mr Gunson.
America’s priorities in Venezuela are business, stability and democracy—in that order. It does not want to repeat mistakes made in Iraq, where regime change led to civil war. So it has kept the chavistas in power. The regime has churned out economic reforms. But Ms Rodríguez may be arguing that too much political change, too quickly, risks derailing that process. “We are still in Delcy’s world,” says Alfredo Romero of Foro Penal.
Political prisoners are useful for the regime. They are not only chips for bartering with the Americans; their continued incarceration helps make clear to Venezuelans that the regime’s ability to quash dissent remains intact. Venezuelans have been less fearful since Mr Maduro was arrested. Protests are rising: August saw almost four times as many as in the same month last year. The regime needs to retain a degree of “social control”, says Andreína Baduel. Her late father, Raúl Baduel, died a political prisoner in 2021. Her brother Josnars is currently in Rodeo.
Some political prisoners have a specific jailer: a person with a grudge who needs to be convinced to release them. And almost half of those remaining have a military past. Many are senior officers accused of rebellion. Keeping them locked up is a way of controlling the armed forces, says John Polga-Hecimovich, an academic at the US Naval Academy in Maryland. The regime could be worrying that, if released, some of them might talk to United States prosecutors about the regime’s corruption and involvement in drug trafficking.
On October 8th the US indicted Mr Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, for using torture to hold power. Many prisoners tell stories of that. Ms Baduel says the ligaments in her brother’s knees and shoulders are broken. Squatting over the latrine in his cell is agony. Hiowanka Ávila, whose brother was arrested for alleged involvement in an attempt to assassinate Mr Maduro with a drone, says he was beaten, electrocuted and asphyxiated. He was put in stress positions and left hanging from his wrists for days. “And that was just the physical torture,” says Ms Ávila.
Conditions in Rodeo have improved since Mr Maduro was whisked away. Families have been allowed to embrace their relatives during visits. Each prisoner has been given a pillow. The violence against them has abated. The families who camp outside the prison still hope their loved ones will be released soon (a procession near the prison is pictured on the previous page). But they are anxious, too, that something might curtail the political transition. Says Ms Baduel: “This episode of horror for Venezuelans is not totally over yet.”

epub_47.title: Brazil’s gambling wars are only just beginning
epub_47.text:
Brazil’s gambling wars are only just beginning
The Americas
| All bets are off
Brazil’s gambling wars are only just beginning
A country that loves to wager is wrestling with the cost
Oct 15th 2026
A HAPPY TIGER is tormenting Brazil. Wearing a red tang jacket, the fat cat dances across phone screens; it is the mascot for a wildly popular digital slot machine. But late last month Brazil’s government banned the “little tiger game”—along with all online casinos and sports-betting. “People are in debt, killing themselves, and getting sick from a disease called ludopathy,” said the president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, justifying his executive order.
Since it was legalised by a right-wing government in 2018, gambling has exploded in Brazil. Last year the country became the world’s fifth-largest betting market. Punters lost over $10bn, more than Brazilians spent on cigarettes and McDonald’s combined. Though it generates lots in taxes—gambling contributes nearly as much to the public finances as agriculture—many Brazilians have turned against the sector. Businesses blame it for record household and public debt, as well as low spending in shops. Church ministers and doctors warn that gambling firms are ensnaring the poor and the young.
Prohibition has a chequered past. Brazil forbade games of chance in 1946, shutting venues from betting houses to bingo halls. This pushed punters towards the jogo do bicho (animal game), an illegal lottery run by racketeers. Wealthy bicheiros soon infiltrated politics and the formal economy; they tried to seem nice by sponsoring samba schools. When gambling was legalised the idea was in part that this would curb their power. Yet the law that was passed to permit it neglected to regulate the sector. It initially imposed no taxes on the industry, or any rules on advertising.
In 2024 Lula (as the president is known) tried to fill in the blanks. His government limited gambling advertising, began stopping gamblers from betting with credit cards and introduced rules such as age verification. His government also began charging operators a 30m reais ($6m) licensing fee and a 12% levy on revenues. Installing such safeguards was difficult, says Daniele Cardoso of the Secretariat for Prizes and Gaming, the industry’s regulator. Yet officials led by the cash-strapped finance ministry believed they could weaken organised crime, protect gamblers and keep a lid on addiction—all while creating new revenue for the state.
Their efforts seem to have failed. Punters who spent their money gambling, rather than ploughing it into more productive things, chopped 1% off Brazilian GDP last year, estimates Guilherme Klein of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro. That was worse than the impact of Donald Trump’s tariffs on Brazil. The bicheiros have not been edged out: they have simply moved online, where they run both legal and illegal sites, according to Anchieta Nery, an intelligence chief at the justice ministry. More people are wagering high sums and racking up debt, notes Luiz Orsatti of Procon-São Paulo, a consumer-protection agency. In 2025 an academic survey found that some 7% of Brazilians engage in problematic gambling, compared with 2% in Britain, another hotspot.
There is no easy answer. Top football clubs, many of them sponsored by gambling firms, have insisted that permanently outlawing the industry could mean “the end of Brazilian football”. Some of their players have lately taken to the field wearing slogans protesting against the ban. Betting companies are threatening to sue the government for the $500m they have paid in licensing fees; their lobbyists argue the ban will feed an illegal market that already accounted for 30% of the sector.
Lula’s ban aimed to please poor and evangelical voters ahead of the presidential election (the run-off is on October 25th). He, nonetheless, underperformed in the first round. His rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, is said to favour lighter rules—perhaps shutting online casinos but allowing sports bets. It is still anyone’s game.

epub_49.title: Saudi Arabia is increasingly under siege
epub_49.text:
Saudi Arabia is increasingly under siege
Middle East & Africa
| Riyadh attacked
Saudi Arabia is increasingly under siege
The Saudis have no good options against deadly strikes by Yemeni rebels
Oct 15th 2026
SINCE 2014, when Yemen tipped into civil war, the country has become one of the most desperate places on earth. GDP per person has fallen by 58%. Most families cannot survive without foreign aid. More than 2m children under five are malnourished. Yet the Houthis, the Iran-backed rebels who are one side of the conflict, fight on. They care little about governing and extort enough money from areas they control to keep their war machine humming.
Now they are wagering that Saudi Arabia, which supports their opponents, will have far less tolerance for pain. For weeks the Houthis have escalated attacks on Saudi infrastructure. Strikes on Riyadh’s airport have halted flights to the Saudi capital. On October 13th the Houthis attacked the headquarters of Saudi Aramco, the state-run oil giant, in the eastern city of Dhahran. The kingdom feels under siege, just as it prepares to host its flagship investment conference this month.
In public, officials have tried to sound defiant. “The word fear, in the Saudi dictionary, does not exist,” the energy minister told a gathering of oil executives this week. But the Saudis have no good options. They will struggle to defeat the Houthis, and a long war will upend plans to diversify their economy and to make Riyadh a hub for finance and tourism. Yet the alternative is to cut a costly deal that invites, rather than deters, future Houthi threats.
The rebels seized most of Yemen’s population centres in 2014 and still hold them, despite a Saudi-led invasion the next year meant to drive them from power. A ceasefire in 2022 froze the front lines, but the wider Gulf war that America and Israel began in February made the truce unsustainable. By summer both sides were preparing for renewed fighting. Last month the Houthis
launched an offensive
that saw them seize much of Yemen’s south-western coast, including the port city of Mokha (see map).
The Saudis and their Yemeni allies began a counter-offensive this month. Progress has been slow. They have recaptured a strip of the coast, but for now they seem to have halted around the town of Dhubab, 40km south of Mokha. Typically in Yemen, campaigns start strong but soon grind into stalemate. Meanwhile, the Houthis are still trying to encircle Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city and an anti-Houthi redoubt.
They have also resumed cross-border attacks on Saudi Arabia. Airports have been a particular target, with four deadly strikes on the capital’s airport in a single week. The worst came on October 10th, when missiles hit Terminal 3, which handles domestic flights. They killed 13 people and injured more than 300. Some of the casualties were pilgrims boarding a flight to Jeddah, the gateway to Islam’s holiest sites.
It is unclear why the Saudis were unable to intercept the missiles. They have advanced air-defence systems, including American-made THAAD and Patriot batteries. Like many other countries in the region, however, they are concerned about
dwindling supplies of interceptors
after almost eight months of war. The Houthis have also started to employ multi-layered attacks, using a mix of drones and missiles to overwhelm defenders. It did not help that the Saudis recently disabled the mobile-phone alerts that warn of incoming fire, apparently because too many locals found them disruptive (they were reinstated after the airport attack).
Riyadh’s airport is shut until at least October 18th. Though others are open, flights to Jeddah and Dammam are routinely put in hours-long holding patterns, which suggests ongoing Houthi attacks there as well. Many foreign carriers have cancelled flights to the kingdom. Europe’s aviation-safety agency has urged airlines to avoid a big part of Saudi airspace.
All this has disrupted what should be a busy time in the kingdom. October 11th was the start of the World Petroleum Congress, an energy summit hosted this year in Riyadh. The bosses of several big oil firms cancelled their attendance. Organisers still hope to go ahead with the Future Investment Initiative, which begins on October 26th. The annual event, organised by the crown prince, Muhammad bin Salman, and often dubbed Davos in the desert, usually draws a who’s who of global finance. But it is likely to become a “hybrid” event, with many guests joining remotely.
This is Saudi Arabia’s underlying dilemma in Yemen: its government has far more to lose than the battle-hardened Houthis. War will disrupt Vision 2030, Prince Muhammad’s effort to overhaul the economy. Last year the Saudi sovereign-wealth fund inaugurated a new airline, Riyadh Air, hoping to compete with Gulf super-carriers such as Emirates. Its planes were quietly moved out of Riyadh this week for safe keeping. Employees in the capital’s financial district have been told to work remotely until further notice.
Nor does war seem likely to succeed. The Saudis insist they are fighting in Yemen on behalf of its internationally recognised government, which is technically true: the un does not recognise the Houthis as legitimate rulers. But it is also something of a fiction, because the government is a husk. The president, Rashad al-Alimi, was installed in 2022 as part of a shake-up engineered by the Saudis. Ministers spend much of their time in Riyadh.
Yemen’s army exists in name only. Since 2015 the anti-Houthi forces have been a motley crew of militias, from Islamists to tribes to separatists who seek an independent south Yemen (as it was until 1990). Some were sponsored by Saudi Arabia, others by the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The latter were widely regarded as more effective, in part because the UAE was willing to embed special-forces units on the front lines to train and advise its proxies. The Saudis preferred to manage from afar.
But the Gulf powers fell out last year after Emirati-backed separatists seized a chunk of territory from the Saudi-supported camp. The UAE was forced to withdraw its forces, leaving the Saudis to run the war without their most capable ally. The results have been lamentable. As the Houthis advanced on Mokha, their foes fled. If the Saudis continue to wage war remotely, better results are unlikely.
They are eager for outside help. Saudi Arabia has invoked its mutual-defence pact with Pakistan and Turkey. The former has sent thousands of troops but insists they will not fight in Yemen. Prince Muhammad has asked Donald Trump to order American air strikes (so far, the president has demurred). Air power alone will not defeat the Houthis, however: after all, since 2024 they have been bombed by America, Britain, Israel and Saudi Arabia.
The other path is diplomacy. Since 2022 the Saudis have tried repeatedly to reach a deal with the Houthis. Whenever they seem close, the rebels add further demands. Now the Houthis feel they have the upper hand. Their terms will be steep: the Saudis would probably have to stump up billions of dollars and recognise Houthi rule in Yemen. Officials in Riyadh also worry, rightly, that making big concessions now will embolden the rebels to make fresh demands in the future.
Several people who have recently met Saudi leaders believe they will attempt to split the difference: try to retake Mokha, then sue for peace. But the Houthis get a vote too. If they manage to conquer Taiz while pummelling Riyadh with missiles, they may not feel compelled to stop.

epub_50.title: Israel’s Arab parties could be the kingmakers in its election
epub_50.text:
Israel’s Arab parties could be the kingmakers in its election
Middle East & Africa
| The missing link
Israel’s Arab parties could be the kingmakers in its election
They are eager to change the government
Oct 15th 2026
In A campaign video released on October 10th Yousef Jabareen, leader of the Joint List, a slate of candidates from three predominantly Arab-Israeli parties, made a striking announcement. The bloc would “use all the tools” at its disposal to replace the government and “serve as a safety net” for the opposition. For most of Israel’s history, they have stayed on the sidelines, in opposition. But this year, for the first time in an Israeli election, all the parties representing Israel’s Palestinian citizens have vowed to try to change the government.
“This is an existential election for Jews and Arabs,” says Ahmed Tibi, head of the Arab Movement for Change, one of the parties in the Joint List. “The levels of racism and incitement from this fascist government are simply too great. We’ll do almost anything to kick them out.” This should mean Binyamin Netanyahu and his allies can be beaten. The Economist’s poll tracker has his opponents, Jewish and Arab, together averaging 64 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, Israel’s parliament. And yet the Arab parties remain unwelcome.
For decades the parties representing Arab voters, who make up around 20% of the electorate, stayed outside the post-election coalition wrangling. But since the 1980s they have endorsed candidates for prime minister and in 1992, they formed a de facto bloc with centre-left parties to prevent the right-wing Likud party from forming a coalition. In 2021 Ra’am, a small conservative-Islamist party broke away from the Joint List, insisting it wanted to go further, and that it would join any government in which it could have some influence on behalf of Arab voters.
In that year’s election Ra’am passed the electoral threshold of 3.25% of the vote on its own, winning seats in the Knesset. Ra’am’s leader, Mansour Abbas, held talks with Mr Netanyahu about joining his government. Mr Netanyahu’s far-right allies scuppered that plan. But weeks later Ra’am became the first independent Arab party to join a coalition when it voted in favour of a short-lived government formed by Naftali Bennett. In the next year’s poll, Ra’am did even better.
The Joint List, which in 2021 broke with Ra’am because of Mr Abbas’ willingness to consider joining a coalition, is now following its lead. Yousef Makladeh, who runs the Statnet Research Institute, says that in his polls “the overwhelming majority of Arab voters put replacing the government and fighting the crime wave in our communities above all other issues, including the war in Gaza and solving the Israel-Palestinian conflict.” Crime-related murders in Arab communities have doubled during the four years of the current government. Many among them blame the far-right national-security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, accusing him of intentionally diverting policing resources away from their towns.
Ra’am has put a prominent Jewish politician, Yoav Segalovich, a former police commander, on its list. They hope he will boost their crime-fighting credentials as well as increase their appeal to non-Arab voters. The Joint List reckons this is going too far. “Unlike Ra’am, we have conditions, such as a future diplomatic process with the Palestinians,” says one Joint List campaigner. But, he concedes, “a vague commitment will be enough.”
Among Israel’s Palestinians 77% say an Arab party should join the country’s government, according to the Moshe Dayan Centre at Tel Aviv University. And yet among the four main opposition parties only the left-leaning Democrats openly favour an alliance with them. Yisrael Beitenu (Israel Our Home), a nationalist party, is firmly opposed. Gadi Eisenkot, Mr Netanyahu’s main challenger, and Mr Bennett, a former prime minister, who lead the two big centre-right parties, are evasive. Mr Netanyahu’s campaign has accused them of planning to form a government with Israel’s Arabs. Their equivocation reflects their fear that such accusations will be electorally damaging. Since October 7th and the war in Gaza, attitudes among Jewish Israelis towards Palestinians have hardened. According to one poll, a majority of Israelis support barring the Arab parties from even running. The Knesset’s electoral commission tried to disqualify them (the Supreme Court blocked the efforts).
Even if they do not formally join a coalition, the Arab parties could still support a minority government led by Mr Eisenkot, in a confidence-and-supply deal. “There are a lot of things we could do together without joining the government,” says Mr Tibi, though he insists there have been no talks so far with Mr Eisenkot or his party. “There will be time after the election. Why give Netanyahu ammunition?”

epub_51.title: The expat voters who could help unseat Netanyahu
epub_51.text:
The expat voters who could help unseat Netanyahu
Middle East & Africa
| Flying visits
The expat voters who could help unseat Netanyahu
Large numbers of Israelis abroad are flying home to vote, many with an axe to grind
Oct 15th 2026
ROI SARIG is about as Israeli as it is possible to be in London. Born on a kibbutz to a family with roots predating the country’s independence, which he celebrates each year, he follows its news and politics closely, visits regularly and plans to return some day. Yet in the 22 years he has lived in Britain, his wife’s home country, he has not once voted in an Israeli election. “It was never a case of me detaching myself from my Israeli identity,” he says. “But I believed that because I wasn’t living there it wouldn’t be right for me to cast my vote.” This year, however, he will be flying back to do exactly that on October 27th.
He is far from alone. Across Israel’s wide diaspora, the talk around dinner tables and in synagogues in recent weeks has been about who is going home to vote. Under Israeli electoral law only a few limited categories of citizens and their families, such as diplomats and employees of the Jewish Agency, the main body responsible for promoting aliyah—Jewish immigration—can cast their ballots in embassies abroad. Apart from Israelis living in the occupied territories of the West Bank, everyone else must return to Israel if they wish to exercise their democratic right.
It is impossible to know how many will go but numbers appear to be unprecedented. The Aid Coalition, an American non-profit group focused on promoting democracy in Israel, expects over 50,000 expats in America to go back.
The election may be close. Our poll tracker suggests that the Likud party of Binyamin Netanyahu is neck-and-neck with Yashar, a new party led by Gadi Eisenkot.Dahlia Scheindlin, a political strategist and pollster, reckons this year each 40,000 votes a party wins could translate into one of the 120 seats in the Knesset, Israel’s parliament. (The number varies depending on turnout and the party’s vote share.) No one knows how expats will vote, but it is reasonable to assume they will lean heavily to parties opposing Likud because “the major efforts to help people come back are mostly among liberal circles,” she says.
Many returning were involved in protests against Mr Netanyahu’s judicial reforms in 2023, which they saw as attacks on Israel’s democracy. The government’s failures to prevent the Hamas attacks on October 7th 2023, and its prosecution of war in Gaza have added to their anger. “For Israelis abroad it has been like watching a slow-motion car crash,” says Jenny Kananov, an Israeli co-founder of We Democracy, a network in Britain that supported Israel’s pro-democracy movement. “Some people feel this is the last chance to somehow try to make things right.”

epub_52.title: How to make African exports ethical again
epub_52.text:
How to make African exports ethical again
Middle East & Africa
| The green squeeze
How to make African exports ethical again
The continent must reckon with a punishing green squeeze
Oct 15th 2026
Masai farm near Nairobi, Kenya’s capital, is arguably as green as they come. The temperature in its greenhouses is set by natural ventilation. Their proximity to the equator means the flowers get 12 hours of sunshine every day of the year, so artificial light is unnecessary. Any carbon emissions are tracked and reported, says Vincent Terer, the farm manager.
And yet green-minded policymakers in Europe are unimpressed. Each night seven to 18 tonnes of its flowers are flown out of Nairobi, over half on the 6,400km journey to the Netherlands. This puts them in the sights of retailers in Britain and Europe seeking to cut
their carbon footprints
. Some European supermarkets and food companies have of late banned, or said they plan to restrict, air freight from their fresh-produce supply chains. Some are switching from east Africa to places like Morocco, which can send exports by sea.
Low-carbon African exporters like those in
Kenya’s blooming cut-flower industry
contribute next to nothing to climate change. Africa has 18% of the world’s population but is responsible for less than 4% of historic carbon-dioxide emissions. Yet it is especially exposed to what Jodie Keane of odi, a think-tank in London, calls a “green squeeze”: rising costs and shrinking market access as richer countries adopt measures to decarbonise global supply chains. Between 1997 and 2021 the share of trade measures relating to environmental concerns notified to the World Trade Organisation rose from 8% to 19%. Those most heavily burdened include Africa’s small businesses and farms that risk losing vital trade as the effects of climate change start to be felt.
The carbon footprint of sunlit Kenyan flowers is smaller than those grown in heated European greenhouses in winter. East African flower and fruit exports often go as bellyhold cargo in scheduled passenger flights, adding only marginal emissions. Still, “the public has a visceral reaction to aeroplanes which they don’t have to greenhouses,” says David Beer of TradeMark Africa, a non-profit group in Nairobi.
A more immediate crunch for the continent’s exporters is coming in the form of regulation. The eu’s new deforestation rules, which require importers to prove that their cocoa, coffee, rubber, soya, palm oil, wood or cattle products were not produced on land that was forest before 2021, are due to take effect in December. African exporters face losing market access if they cannot provide adequate evidence.
After months of wrangling and two missed deadlines, the final rules have been eased a little. But countries such as Ethiopia, where many farmers grow coffee on tiny plots, are still not ready for the changes, says Ms Keane. She and her colleagues at ODI estimate that Ethiopia could lose almost two-thirds of its coffee exports to the eu, even though just 20 coffee plots have so far been linked to deforestation since 2020. Last year the bloc bought $765m of the country’s $2.65bn of coffee exports.
Another big worry is the carbon border adjustment mechanism (cbam), a levy on imports of certain industrial commodities, such as aluminium and steel. The scheme, which took effect in January, is meant to help clean up global supply chains by making foreign suppliers pay the same carbon price as European ones. Africa’s  renewable-energy resources could give many of its exporters an edge. But African production of most commodities under the scheme is, on average, more carbon-intensive than that of rivals. And no African country outside South Africa yet prices carbon, so exporters pay the full eu price with no deduction for a levy paid at home.
African businesses and policymakers fear a ratchet, as measures like cbam expand to cover more products, and other countries follow suit. “We are beginning to see a new form of standard emerge,” says David Luke of the London School of Economics (lse), so global export competitiveness will increasingly depend on verified carbon performance as well as quality and price. Countries without strong systems for monitoring and verification—ie, most African ones—will lose out. The African Climate Foundation and the Firoz Lalji Institute at lse estimate that if the scheme expands to cover all imported goods, African exports to the eu could shrink by 6%.
Some African exporters are seeking alternative markets. “We’ve got the Middle East, we’ve got India, we’ve got the Far East,” says Tiku Shah, the boss of Sunripe, a Kenyan fresh-produce firm. “They don’t have these standards.” Kenya’s exports of avocados to China surged by over 60% in the first half of 2026. Yet China has its own non-tariff barriers, such as tough phytosanitary rules. And buyers in the Middle East offer unpredictable prices and, at times, fail to pay, notes Wester Schepers of colead, a non-profit that helps African farmers meet European standards.
Many firms therefore have little choice but to adapt. For some less perishable produce such as avocados, sea freight—which can emit up to 85% less carbon dioxide per tonne than air freight—is a viable alternative. TradeMark Africa is helping to introduce electric lorries in Ethiopia, partly in case cbam expands one day to cover transport as well as production. Sian Flowers, the Kenyan firm that owns Masai Farm, is responding to demands from buyers for more precise carbon accounting by building models to estimate emissions from the airport all the way to the final destination.
The eu could do more to help. Robert Byaruhanga of the Uganda Coffee Federation, an industry body, argues that the eu and the bloc’s coffee roasters should share the cost of complying with eu deforestation rules. The requirement for rich countries to do more to decarbonise than poor ones, laid out in the COP21 Paris climate-change agreement, should mean African exporters pay lower carbon prices under cbam. Fatan Agged of the African Futures Policy Hub calls for Africa to set up establish its own trade decarbonisation fund. Africa needs to “really start investing in this adjustment”, she says. The eu buys almost a third of Africa’s exports. That trade partnership is too valuable to squander.

epub_53.title: Gen-Z Kenyans could determine William Ruto’s future
epub_53.text:
Gen-Z Kenyans could determine William Ruto’s future
Middle East & Africa
| #getoutthevote
Gen-Z Kenyans could determine William Ruto’s future
Young activists hope to deny the unpopular president a second term next year
Oct 15th 2026
At the start of this year Allans Ademba, a 26-year-old Kenyan photojournalist, was despondent. A mass uprising against William Ruto, Kenya’s president, which began in 2024 seemed to be fizzling. Protesters' main goal—that the beleaguered Mr Ruto should serve just one term or less—looked remote. After years of falling living standards, “most people were very politically conscious,” Mr Ademba recalls. Yet in the general election in 2027, “nobody was registering” to vote.
A few months later the mood is strikingly different. In March Mr Ademba launched “Niko Kadi”, or “I have my card” in Sheng, the local Swahili-English slang. The viral campaign seeks to get millions of young Kenyans voting in 2027 for the first time. Mr Ademba and his fellow Gen-Z organisers helped register 2.6m new voters in a single two-week period this year (22m people could vote in the last election). Now they are preparing an even more ambitious mass registration drive: enlisting young Kenyans not only to vote but to run for office. The impact on what is expected to be a vicious election could be decisive.
Niko Kadi blends modern online campaigning with more traditional get-out-the-vote efforts. The movement began on social media, notably on TikTok, where activists post cheery videos urging fellow youngsters to collect their voter id cards. Alongside practical advice, such as where and how to register, are jokier tips, such as telling young women to dump their boyfriends if they fail to sign up.
“We found a way to make politics fun, trendy, fashionable—and to some extent sexy,” says Mr Ademba. He attributes much of their success to scores of local groups on WhatsApp, a messaging app. These have helped young Kenyans from across the country spread the word and head to registration centres together.
Activists hope that the newly registered voters will turn out—and vote against Mr Ruto. Kenya’s Gen-Z protests began as a
tax revolt
before becoming a display of the “power of the youth to organise and put pressure on the state”, says Mwanase Ahmed of the Pan-African Solidarity Network, a pressure group. But because the state has since
cracked down
on demonstrations, formal politics are now more important. By one count 6m more young Kenyans will be eligible to vote next year than in the last election in 2022. Many are furious with Mr Ruto because of his repressive tactics and because he came to power on a pro-youth programme which he has failed to deliver. This makes them potential “kingmakers or kingbreakers”, says Martins Kwazema of the Nordic Africa Institute in Sweden.
There are also big challenges. Young Kenyans are a politically engaged bunch; 57% report reading the news frequently on social media, according to Afrobarometer, a pollster. A new study by University College London finds widespread awareness of new laws and policies even among rural youngsters. Yet self-reported turnout among Kenya’s young has been in decline since at least 2013. One estimate put turnout in 2022 among 18- to 25-year-olds at under 40%; overall it was 64%.
Could Niko Kadi buck the trend? Mr Ruto has welcomed the growth in voter registration. But as Ken Opalo, a prominent Kenyan academic, has argued, widespread antipathy towards his administration means the president stands the strongest chance of re-election if turnout is low. Activists therefore expect the state to throw everything it has at them.
Mr Ademba himself was briefly arrested during a registration drive in July. As the election approaches, activists worry most about goons: armed thugs hired by officials to intimidate opponents and terrorise protesters. Under Mr Ruto Kenya has suffered a surge in such violence.
Despite their shared anger at Mr Ruto, young Kenyans do not yet agree on who should replace him. Failure to unite around a single candidate could hand Mr Ruto victory. Legions of enthused young voters would be a sign of democratic health. But they offer no guarantee of change.

epub_55.text:
Donald Trump is squeezing Ukraine’s military lifeline
Europe
| Arms-twisting
Donald Trump is squeezing Ukraine’s military lifeline
To protect his Russian diesel deal, he appears to be withholding vital military intelligence
Oct 15th 2026
UKRAINE’S AIR-raid sirens are the final link in a ballistic warning system that usually begins with American satellite or signals intelligence. They give citizens a few minutes to brace for an attack. But on the nights of October 12th and 13th scores of Russian missiles slammed into Kyiv with little or no warning. Ukraine said there had been no intelligence from its partners. In an interview published in the Financial Times on October 15th, Volodymyr Zelensky, Ukraine’s president, accused America of cutting it off.
American officials have threatened to do so since Donald Trump’s announcement on October 9th of a deal to
let Russia sell diesel fuel
. They demand that Ukraine stop attacking Russian refineries. Arms supplies are at risk as well. The Americans have privately warned that they may pull the plug on the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), the mechanism by which European countries pay for American weapons sent to Ukraine.
Mr Trump insisted on October 13th that intelligence sharing was continuing. Yet Ukrainian officials soon reported that Elon Musk’s SpaceX had restricted the Starlink terminals used aboard Ukrainian attack drones. The terminals began to lose connectivity at speeds of around 160kph, forcing some units to cancel attacks. Mr Musk said it was America’s armed forces that have control over those contracts.
It all added to the grim mood in Kyiv. Amid drone and missile barrages and power cuts, there is no sign of the “energy ceasefire” Mr Trump claims to have brokered between Ukraine and Russia. In a neighbourhood on the city’s left bank on October 14th residents of a nine-storey apartment block collected plywood to board up windows shattered by a ballistic missile. Russian strikes have killed well over 100 civilians so far this month.
Mr Zelensky says he will accept an energy ceasefire if Russia does. To appease Mr Trump, Ukraine suspended attacks on Russian energy targets for three days. But Russia struck dozens of Ukrainian energy facilities during the supposed truce. Mr Zelensky told the Financial Times that attacks on Russian refineries will resume.
The Starlink limits are a serious blow. Ukrainian troops use the system to guide drones in Russian-occupied territory. (The system does not work inside Russia itself.) “Almost all of our mid-range strike capabilities rely on Starlink,” says a Ukrainian military-intelligence source. The timing of the restrictions “cannot be a coincidence”, Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Mr Zelensky, wrote on Telegram.
Ukraine can snoop for itself, using commercial satellite imagery, but its feeds are not as rich as America’s. America also lets Ukraine use cutting-edge artificial-intelligence tools to crunch data. Europe cannot replicate this. When Mr Trump briefly blocked intelligence sharing last year, Britain and France were unable to guide the cruise missiles they had given to Ukraine. And cutting off American intel would badly hurt Ukraine’s ability to shoot down Russian missiles. “Nobody in the world has those capabilities,” says a Ukrainian air-defence specialist.
Ending PURL would also be devastating. Ukraine depends on the programme for 95% of its Patriot interceptors and for many of the missiles its F-16 fighter jets use to shoot down jet-powered drones. The next shipment is reportedly imminent, so Ukraine will know soon if it is blocked. Some Patriot interceptors are coming from European countries, as well as a new generation of SAMP/T air-defence systems from France and Italy. But “PURL is the only solution we have to protect critical infrastructure,” says the air-defence officer.
Dependence on America makes desisting from strikes on Russian oil infrastructure seem the obvious choice. But it is a potent tactic to give up. Burning refineries grab the world’s attention and raise morale. Fuel shortages force Russians to stop ignoring the war. And the damage is cutting into the Russian state’s oil revenues. Our analysis this summer showed that those had fallen 34% short of what would be expected, based on global oil prices.
There are other valuable targets that Ukraine can hit. Figures from Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, a conflict monitor, show only 21% of Ukraine’s strikes into the Russian heartland were on oil-related facilities. Besides data centres and retail warehouses, the vast majority were military-industrial. These are the factories supporting Russia’s war machine, producing the 28,000 jet-powered attack drones it expects to build this year.
There are no practical alternatives to what America provides. Only China and Russia are close to a Starlink equivalent. Europe is years away from American levels of missile production. For all Ukraine’s extraordinary resilience and inventiveness, its war effort depends on outside support.
Ukraine has no alternative to American sensors and satellites, which map Russian spoofing, jamming, and troop movements, helping the Ukrainians plan and conduct drone attacks. Ending such co-operation would cripple Ukraine’s ability to take the fight to Russia. “From the very beginning of any mission we design, there is a really critical element of [American] intelligence,” says a Ukrainian intelligence source. European allies have expanded their own satellite-surveillance capacity, but “the Americans can see inside Russia 24 hours and seven days a week,” says the source. “Without this [intel] exchange, it would be really hard, almost impossible, for us to fight.”

epub_56.title: Russian men are fleeing before the army can grab them
epub_56.text:
Russian men are fleeing before the army can grab them
Europe
| Fight or flight
Russian men are fleeing before the army can grab them
Vladimir Putin looks poised for a huge wave of forced inductions
Oct 15th 2026
On september 18th Dmitry, a 35-year old Muscovite working in advertising, cast his vote in Russia’s sham parliamentary elections. He wrote the word “criminal” on his ballot, slid it into the box and headed straight to the airport, where he boarded a flight to Istanbul. He was one of thousands who have left in recent weeks, fearing that the “special electoral procedure”, as some Russians have taken to calling their elections, would pave the way for a new wave of military mobilisation.
When Vladimir Putin declared a partial mobilisation in September 2022, six months after invading Ukraine, 400,000 Russian men fled the country. This time people are leaving even without any announcement, albeit in smaller numbers. On August 18th 20,000 people crossed the land border between Russia and Georgia, about triple the normal daily number. Russian customs officials reported similar numbers on preceding days. In Armenia, another country that lets Russians in without a visa, high demand for rental accommodation has pushed up prices by 30-50% since the spring. “It wasn’t just because of the mobilisation that I left. I’d had enough of putting up with it, of staying in that atmosphere,” says Yuri, who worked for a tourism firm in St Petersburg.
Grigory Sverdlin of Idite Lesom (Get Lost), a volunteer organisation that helps people avoid forced mobilisation, says the number of requests for help it has received this autumn has risen by half compared with spring this year. Anastasia Burakova of Kovcheg (Arc), a group that helps Russians who are opposed to war to emigrate, says enquiries have gone up eight-fold since July. Compared with 2022, “we are now seeing a smaller but better-prepared wave of emigration,” she says.
Rumours of a new wave of mobilisation have circulated for months. Ukrainian officials have predicted a call-up of at least 100,000 men; on September 24th Emmanuel Macron, the French president, put the number at 300,000. Russia’s own military bloggers think it likely too. Officially, the Kremlin says nothing of the sort is being prepared. “That’s utter rubbish. It’s an information attack on Russia,” Mr Putin said shortly before the elections last month.
Yet Russians, hardened by experience, tend to think that the more emphatically authorities deny planning something unpleasant, the more likely it is to happen. In 2022 the Kremlin denied mobilisation was in the works just a week before it was announced. In any case, no official declaration is needed, since the previous order has never been repealed.
The administrative system has been improved over the years, and includes electronic summonses and communication between recruiters and border officers. This summer there were protests in Penza, 600km east of Moscow, after plain-clothed recruiters grabbed people off the streets. To avoid more unrest, the next wave is likely to be covert. Debtors, the unemployed and failing students may be coerced to enlist. Some believe it is already under way. A military lawyer says DNA samples are being collected from every inmate in a prison in Ryazan, the better to identify their corpses at the front.
Recruitment quotas are being sent to regional governors and bosses at large firms, who will have to take responsibility for any discontent, a practice of “decentralisation” that the Kremlin tested during covid. Nikolai Mitrokhin of Bremen University, a sociologist and analyst of the war, says rich regions are, in effect, buying recruits from poorer ones. The sign-up bonus in the wealthy Sverdlovsk region is 3.1m roubles ($37,000), nearly four times that in poorer Syktyvkar, near the Ural mountains. Recruits travel from poorer regions to sign up in richer ones.
Military bloggers and nationalists are eager. On July 30th Rusich, an ultra-nationalist outfit, called for “the mobilisation of half a million men” to achieve Mr Putin’s war aims. Western analysts have long thought a new wave of mobilisation would be risky and might provoke protests, as it did in Penza. Yet in fact mobilisation can be useful to Mr Putin, allowing him to demonstrate control over the system and to bolster his narrative of national sacrifice, which depends on comparing his war to the epochal struggle against Nazi Germany.
There are important military questions to be answered before additional men are sent to the front. The first is whom to mobilise. Younger, fitter and better-educated soldiers would achieve more than the old, poor and desperate ones Russia recruited in previous drives. The North Korean troops who have fought for Russia proved this: Ukrainian soldiers reported them to be markedly more tenacious and capable than Russian infantry. But the North Koreans first had to learn how to fight the new sort of war that has developed in Ukraine. A second question is how much training and equipment Russia’s new soldiers would get.
If Russia treats mobilised soldiers as cannon fodder, as it has in the past, Mr Putin will get little more than caskets. But if the new recruits are up to North Korean standards, the Ukrainians will have more to fear. A big, well-trained new cohort could make a difference to battles in urban terrain, where drones are less effective. Ukraine has recently pioneered innovative tactics, including use of mine-clearing drones and attacks on drone operators’ bunkers, that have helped it take back Russian-held territory. If Russia copies these, then numerical superiority in troops could recover its relevance. The thin screens of drone-supported soldiers that Ukraine uses to hold parts of the front might no longer be enough.
At the moment Russia’s army attracts mainly low-skilled men with few prospects, argues Vladislav Inozemtsev, a Russian economist. It is even more attractive to those who have little desire to live and want to leave something to their families. Soldiers are paid an unimpressive 200,000 roubles a month, much of which is often stolen by their superiors. But there are large sign-up bonuses and a death benefit of 15m roubles for next of kin, more than ten times the average annual income in Russia. To attract recruits more interested in staying alive, the Kremlin might increase monthly payments and reduce the death benefit.
Dmitry does not want to be part of that calculus. He is looking for a job in Istanbul and hoping his wife and child can join him when he is settled. “I want to live in Russia, but without these kinds of risks,” he says. “It’s hard to believe your own state can just suddenly send you off to be slaughtered, but we’ve already seen it happen.”

epub_57.title: Portugal has limited immigration, and Spain may follow
epub_57.text:
Portugal has limited immigration, and Spain may follow
Europe
| Lessons from Lisbon
Portugal has limited immigration, and Spain may follow
The wave of immigrants in both countries looks politically unsustainable
Oct 15th 2026
Nestled beneath Lisbon’s former Moorish quarter, the Rua do Benformoso is a winding street of decaying buildings faced with azulejos (decorative tiles). It is lined with Indian food shops and stores selling hookah pipes and mobile phones. Piedade, a Portuguese woman who has lived here for over 60 years, dislikes what has happened to it. “There’s drugs and crime,” she says. “I stay inside at home.”
The Rua do Benformoso has become the symbol of a massive wave of immigration. The Portuguese are accustomed to migrants from their former colonies in Brazil and Africa, who speak the language and integrate fairly easily. But between 2017 and 2024 more than 1.1m immigrants took the foreign-born population from 4% to 14% of the total. The new arrivals included 250,000 South Asians, mainly young single men. Many of them speak almost no Portuguese. Immigration became a top public concern. Chega (“Enough”), a new populist right-wing party, won 23% of the vote in a parliamentary election in 2025.
“We were not in control,” says António Vitorino, a Portuguese former European commissioner. It became crucial, he says, to “rebuild the credibility of the migration-regulation system”. The centre-right government of Luis Montenegro, which came to office in 2024, set out to do this. It required immigrants to get appropriate visas, re-established a border force, stretched the time to obtain citizenship to between seven and ten years, and restricted family reunions. It also introduced fast-track visas for key workers. “We’re not a closed-door, ‘remigration’ government,” says António Leitão Amaro, the minister responsible for the reforms. Net migration has fallen from 270,000 a year to 60,000.
Across the border in Spain, in contrast, the Socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has defied the European Union’s consensus on tighter controls. Spain too has seen a spike in immigration, with 3.1m coming since 2021. In 2026 the foreign-born population hit 10.3m, over 20% of the total. Mr Sánchez has stressed not only Spain’s humanitarian values but the benefits of immigration to economic growth. It helped that around half of the immigrants are Spanish-speakers from Latin America.
Earlier this year Mr Sánchez irritated other EU governments by announcing an amnesty for those without papers. The government expected 500,000 to apply; 1.2m did. Portugal, too, plans to regularise up to 800,000. But unlike in Spain, applicants are interviewed individually and 45,000 have been rejected, says Mr Amaro.
Immigration has strained both countries’ public services. Lisbon suffered a shortage of school places this year. In Spain teachers say immigrant children may lack language skills or arrive with a learning deficit. Many schools in Madrid are seen as immigrant ghettos; teachers seek jobs elsewhere. In the health service, waiting lists for operations are at record levels.
The most dramatic impact has been in housing. Mr Sánchez called a snap general election for November 29th on the issue. But the move may rebound. Critics point out that Spain’s overheated housing market is a result of immigration combined with a lack of new building. And the memory of a surge of over 80,000 migrants into Ceuta, a Spanish exclave in north Africa, in late July is still fresh (10,000 are still there).
Spain’s consensus in favour of immigration is breaking. Polls show a majority think there are too many immigrants. Vox, an anti-immigrant populist party, has risen to around 19% in the polls. But immigrants continue to arrive. “They know they can come and sooner or later they will be legalised,” says María Miyar, a sociologist at UNED university. Earlier this year Teresa Garcia-Milà of the Cercle d’Economia, a business group in Barcelona, argued for “a fundamental debate we haven’t had” about “our real capacities of reception and integration”. Cutting immigration can stimulate the economy in some ways: Portugal’s previous lax rules meant “companies didn’t have to improve their efficiency because they got cheap labour,” says Mr Amaro.
In Spain, with polls showing the right likely to win the election, policy seems certain to change. Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s Party, wants a points system and quotas for immigration and priority for Latin Americans. That sounds like the Portuguese approach. Iberia may soon no longer be an exception to the European norm.

epub_58.title: European museums are seeing a spike in high-value art theft
epub_58.text:
European museums are seeing a spike in high-value art theft
Europe
| Going for gold
European museums are seeing a spike in high-value art theft
Forget cat burglars. Today’s thieves smash, grab and run
Oct 15th 2026
LILLI HOLLEIN, the director of Vienna’s Museum for Applied Art (MAK), has just been through the toughest six weeks of her career. On August 27th two armed thieves stole a platinum necklace bedecked with 673 diamonds, designed by Van Cleef & Arpels in 1939 for Queen Nazli of Egypt, from a special exhibition at the museum. Wearing no masks, they entered the neo-Renaissance building on Vienna’s Ringstrasse, bought tickets, wandered into the exhibition and smashed the armoured display case with 41 blows from a hammer they had hidden in their clothes. Snatching the necklace, valued at more than $4m, they made off on foot through the adjacent Stadtpark.
The MAK reopened the next day, having belatedly installed metal detectors at the entrance, securing the doors long after the crooks had bolted. In subsequent weeks Ms Hollein, whose tenure as director had been extended by five years this spring, came under fire for lax security. On October 2nd an independent investigation found that the MAK and its staff behaved properly: had anyone tried to take on the thieves, they might have endangered themselves and the 104 visitors who were in the show. The museum had deployed 185 video cameras, 125 alarm sensors, special safety glass and trained guards. Yet the report concluded that such thefts by professionals cannot be prevented with reasonable measures.
That claim seems bizarre. It cannot be impossible to stop hoods from walking into museums and nicking the art. (Had someone thought of metal detectors earlier, they would have spotted the thieves’ hammer and pistol.) Rather, it seems the threat has risen and the response remains inadequate. European museum directors, Ms Hollein says, are confronted with a new type of violent and brazen theft. The robberies are often smash-and-grab attacks that last just a few minutes. It usually takes four to five minutes for the police to arrive. Global losses from art theft for museums and galleries are estimated to amount to $8bn annually.
“Art theft has always existed,” says Anthony Amore, head of security at the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston, the site of the most notorious art theft since the second world war. (In that crime in 1990, 13 masterpieces worth about $500m were stolen.) Essentially every major museum in the world has been robbed, says Mr Amore, though most thefts are small. But he notes an increase in high-value robberies in Europe, where one finds first-rate art even in small provincial museums. Many European collections are displayed in old buildings that are tricky to secure. In August thieves stole four masterworks by Antonello da Messina, worth up to €80m ($89m), in a provincial town in Sicily. In September two burglars broke into the Renoir museum, in Cagnes-sur-Mer in France, and made off with two paintings valued at €4.2m.
Spectacular robberies, such as
last year’s theft
of jewellery worth €90m from the Louvre in Paris, can create a vicious circle. Thieves may not be cat burglars any more but many are copycats, says Arthur Brand, a Dutch art-crime investigator. Just 12 hours after the Louvre robbery, some 2,000 gold and silver coins were stolen from a museum in Langres in north-eastern France. Thieves increasingly focus on jewellery and gold coins, which can be dismantled or melted down for sale. (Renoirs or Rembrandts are almost impossible to sell, and are taken chiefly for ransom.) In 2017 a massive 100kg gold coin was stolen from Berlin’s Bode museum by members of the Remmo clan, a notorious Berlin crime family. In 2019 other clan members made off with 18th-century jewellery containing more than 4,300 diamonds from the Green Vault in Dresden, worth at least €113m.
Only around 10% of stolen art is ever found. But most of the Green Vault jewellery was recovered after Remmo clan members were arrested and confessed. And this month six people were arrested for the theft of the Renoirs in Cagnes-sur-Mer; the two paintings were recovered. French police used DNA and mobile-phone data to track down the suspects, and arrested them when one visited another museum—probably, the police said, not “simply out of love for art”.
High-tech solutions, such as display cases that drop through the floor when assaulted, are expensive. But few European museums even have metal detectors. Many do not have their own security chief; they may share one with several others. Curators tend to focus on fund-raising and high-profile exhibitions, and pay less attention to protective measures until something goes wrong. Mr Amore says they need to develop multiple layers of protection, equip guards with better communication systems and develop strong relationships with local police. AI-enabled security cameras could deliver better warnings. But there is no way to render museums entirely safe. Displaying art to the public will always make it possible for a thief to grab it.

epub_59.title: Alice Weidel would pull the plug on German support for Ukraine
epub_59.text:
Alice Weidel would pull the plug on German support for Ukraine
Europe
| An interview with the AfD’s leader
Alice Weidel would pull the plug on German support for Ukraine
The populist-right politician says Ukraine has “already lost” against Russia and should sue for peace
Oct 15th 2026
ALICE WEIDEL, co-leader of Germany’s populist-right Alternative for Germany (afd), has good reason to think her moment has arrived. Her party has opened up a wide polling lead and stands on the cusp of running its first-ever government, in the state of Saxony-Anhalt. In the course of a
75-minute interview for The Insider
in a Bundestag meeting room overlooking Berlin’s river Spree (available to watch from 6pm London time), she offers a confident and fluent performance. Nonetheless, working out what Ms Weidel stands for can prove elusive.
What she opposes is clear. Start with German backing for Ukraine’s defence against Vladimir Putin’s invasion. Futile, she says: Ukraine is “too small” and has “already lost”. Germany should apply “pressure on the Ukrainian president” to end the killing. Policy must follow “Germany first” principles, including by emulating Donald Trump’s diesel deal with Russia.
Worse, prolonging the war “endangers Germany” since it could become a target. This is plausible, as Russia’s hybrid attacks on nato allies suggest. And yet Ms Weidel is reluctant to call out Russia as a threat. Germany recently blamed the Kremlin for a failed drone attack at Leipzig airport. But Ms Weidel says she has seen no evidence that Russia was behind this “so-called attempted drone attack”. Anyway, what about the presumed Ukrainian bombing of the Nord Stream gas pipelines?
This rhetorical judo is a habit. Asked for signs that Mr Putin wants peace, Ms Weidel throws the question back: what about Volodymyr Zelensky? She accepts Russia was the aggressor in 2022, but adds, “when diplomacy is at the table, history is sitting there too.” She means that for decades the West ignored Russia’s security concerns, and must stop doing so.
Ms Weidel, a self-styled “libertarian conservative”, fulminates against Germany’s surge in spending, which she says will lead its interest payments to double in three years. Analysts say the afd’s budget proposals do not add up. But Ms Weidel insists that slashing energy subsidies, foreign aid and welfare can pay for tax cuts and debt reduction. She does not include defence, which accounts for the largest share of new borrowing. Indeed, she accepts “we will have to spend more”. But rather than offer details she simply condemns German support for Ukraine.
As for the euro, it is a “myth” that the afd seeks to leave, says Ms Weidel (though its manifesto in last year’s election in effect urged exit). Instead she wants thorough reform such that the European Central Bank stops financing “highly indebted” countries. Marine Le Pen wants “free debt financing, even though France is already in a huge debt crisis”. Europe is “certainly” headed for a bond-market crisis.
Only one question irritates her. Ms Weidel calls the suggestion that the afd harbours extremists “completely unfounded”, although countless party figures have been linked to ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi groups. On “remigration”, a slippery term beloved of the populist right, Ms Weidel says it simply means deporting failed asylum-seekers and the like. Since Syria’s civil war is over, “100% of the Syrian citizens” must return, as must Afghans and the 1m-plus Ukrainians in Germany, once the peace she claims is close takes hold. “Four to five million” will have to go.
“Professionals who want to work here”, by contrast, are welcome. “I love it! Everyone loves it in my party!” exclaims Ms Weidel. So does she disavow her colleagues in Saxony-Anhalt whose recent manifesto railed against “culturally alien skilled workers”? Not at all. Indeed, the foreign workers that Germany should aim to attract are put off by failures of integration.
Behind the bluster lurks a skilled political manager. She forcefully defends Björn Höcke, the afd’s most divisive figure, who has been fined for using a banned Nazi slogan. But she once tried to have him expelled, only to discover he commanded too much support. Ms Weidel has personally failed to capture voters’ affections (see chart). But her ability to pick her battles, suing for peace where necessary, is her most valuable political asset.
Might that extend to other German parties? All mainstream outfits exclude the afd from coalitions under the so-called Brandmauer (firewall) policy. This, Ms Weidel alleges, forces a country that votes for right-wing policies to accept left-wing governments. Yet should the Brandmauer fall, negotiating coalitions would require the afd to compromise, primarily with the centre-right Christian Democrats (cdu). And this is not to Ms Weidel’s taste. “Why should we?” she asks. “On our main points…there are no compromises to be made. The cdu has to move first. And if it doesn’t move quickly, it will perish.”

epub_60.title: Europe has lots of pleasant cities but too few that matter
epub_60.text:
Europe has lots of pleasant cities but too few that matter
Europe
| Charlemagne
Europe has lots of pleasant cities but too few that matter
A tale of too many cities
Oct 15th 2026
Is Paris a big city? It depends on whom you ask. A tourist with only a few days to take in its sights will probably find it dauntingly large. To the French it occasionally feels smothering, the bloated administrative headquarters of an over-centralised country. But after 20-odd centuries of existence, the Ville Lumière has a distinction besides that of top tourist destination or national capital: it is by some distance the European Union’s largest city, a metropolitan standard-bearer for a largely urbanised continent. And seen through that lens it starts looking rather…petite. With one-third the population of Shanghai and less than half the economic output of New York, Paris makes an underwhelming urban flagship for a union of 450m people. Europe has perfected the art of making cityscapes pleasant. Making them mighty engines of economic dynamism is another matter.
Europe’s cities are a wonder to behold. A stroll through Lisbon, Stockholm or Krakow is a fine way to while away an afternoon. The latest ranking of the best places in the world to live, compiled by the Economist Intelligence Unit, our sister company, puts Copenhagen and Vienna at the very top. (Indonesia’s Jakarta, the world’s largest city, with a population of 42m, comes in 132nd.) But what they make up for in charm Euro-cities often lack in size, and thus commercial heft. The ten biggest urban areas in America account for a third of its economic output. In the EU the figure is nearer one-sixth, according to Oxford Economics, a consultancy. Even China and India, with their vast rural hinterlands, have a bigger share of output coming out of their largest cities. Of the 82 urban areas estimated by the UN to have a population of more than 5m people, Paris (in 36th place, with just under 10m people) and Madrid (72nd) are the only ones in the EU that make the cut.
Et alors? some might ask. Who would want a Jakarta-sur-Seine, a Tokyo am Rhein? Economists might. For them, when it comes to cities, bigger nearly always means better. Cramming more humans near each other creates more opportunities to match productive workers with innovative firms. The result is the sort of economic dynamism Europe desperately needs. Doubling the population of a city is associated with a double-digit growth in productivity, according to the OECD, a club of mostly rich countries (even smaller increases make a sizeable difference). In part that is because more productive people will flock to metropolises to seize opportunities. But even accounting for that factor, bigger cities make everyone richer just by making it easier for ideas, skills and opportunities to circulate. World-class amenities, from football stadiums to opera houses, help make up for congestion, high rents and cramped living conditions.
Europeans like their cities big, but not too big—and for there to be lots of them. This is partly for historical reasons. Centuries of weak central states and municipal independence led to a dense lattice of powerful cities. Many gradually seeped out of their tiny medieval boundaries, sometimes despite planning laws designed to protect against unsightly sprawl. In time European conurbations settled into the shape and size that made sense given their respective countries (or regions, in the case of Germany, a place with lots of competing urban centres). Even a city with grand aspirations could not outgrow its immediate national confines.
What is perhaps surprising is that this pattern of urban development has so far survived the past few decades of European integration. In theory businesses and citizens ought to think of their “home” as the EU, rather than individual countries, the better to compete against rivals in China and America. A single market in workers and ideas should have resulted in a handful of megalopolises acting as powerhouses for an integrated EU economy, not just a national one. A few European cities have specialised into continental hubs of global import: Milan in fashion, Eindhoven in semiconductor-manufacturing equipment, Brussels in crafting regulations. But none has the oomph of New York and its role in global finance, for example, or Shenzhen and manufacturing.
The result is the dispersal of riches across multiple midsize cities, many of them national capitals, yet none of them quite up to global snuff (sorry, Prague). In a world of winner-takes-most globalised industries such as artificial intelligence, this is a sizeable disadvantage. A bright graduate from America’s 50th-biggest urban economy (Charleston, South Carolina) with dreams of working in tech will undoubtedly make for San Francisco, the gateway to Silicon Valley. His counterpart in the EU’s 50th-biggest city (Graz in Austria) will have many options. Should she go to Silicon Allee in Berlin, Silicon Docks in Dublin, perhaps the Silicon Sentier in Paris? Such dispersion gnaws at European competitiveness.
Europeans strolling through their souped-up towns might console themselves with two thoughts. The first is that it may be possible to replicate the advantages of metropolises by connecting lots of nearby midsize cities. Could Amsterdam, Antwerp, Cologne and Brussels—all of them a short hop away on high-speed trains—not join forces to create a mega-hub that could turn them jointly into one city of global scale? Alas not: the advantages of being in the same place seem to decay sharply over even short distances (especially if spread across different countries).
The second is that being a pleasant place might matter more than eking out that last ounce of growth. Having lots of middling cities means none is likely to disconnect from its home polities. In an age when plenty of voters feel “left behind” by out-of-touch metropolitan types, that may be worth something. With its dense thicket of wee cities, Europe has no New York or Los Angeles to dominate global industries. But neither does it have vast swathes of “flyover country” for urban elites to sneer at.

epub_62.title: Britain’s new Dad’s Army
epub_62.text:
Britain’s new Dad’s Army
Britain
| State of emergency
Britain’s new Dad’s Army
The government wants its citizens to prepare for crises
Oct 15th 2026
AT A DISUSED hospital in north London, Colin Harmsworth puts his army through their paces. Clad in orange berets, they learn how to strap tourniquets to bleeding limbs and operate drones. Mr Harmsworth founded the Joint Civil Aid Corps to help Britain’s emergency services during a national crisis. Its members, he says, must be uniformed and disciplined: when duty calls, it’s no good turning up in jeans and arguing.
On paper the vision is sprawling, the product of 14 years of deliberations. Mr Harmsworth, a former cavalry soldier, took inspiration from the Civil Defence Corps, which in the cold war was tasked with digging Britons out of whatever remained of bombed cities. He imagines a force of more than 80,000 volunteers, spanning the country, and a budget north of £180m ($240m). There would be roles for medics, quartermasters, meteorologists and a drum corps. For now, however, volunteers number in the low hundreds and must buy their own uniforms. Mr Harmsworth, the “commandant”, is on the hunt for a philanthropist to make his dream reality.
His beret-wearers, meanwhile, are the British state in microcosm. Once dismissed as an eccentric pursuit, the task of galvanising Britons for “whole-of-society” responses to crises now preoccupies Whitehall. Like Mr Harmsworth, officials are adept at producing long policy papers but short of cash. Whether the state is in better shape for a crisis than the Joint Civil Aid Corps remains unclear.
Government ministers are planning a flurry of “big-muscle moves” on the topic. A public-information campaign will soon encourage Britons to stockpile food, water, torches and radios in preparation for emergencies such as bad weather. Similar measures already abound in other European countries, but a government survey found that 32% of Britons have supplies for only a day or less. Next year hundreds of officials and ministers will take part in Exercise Albiston Shadow, a war game to test the state’s reaction to hybrid attacks by a hostile power. The home-defence “war books”, as classified plans are known, are being updated for the first time since 2004.
Ministers are also preparing the Defence Readiness Bill, with provisions for mobilising armed-forces reserves and industries in a crisis. An emergency communications channel, the Resilient Voice System, is being upgraded. ThinkLabour, a think-tank with close government ties, proposes a volunteer National Resilience Corps that resembles groups in the Nordic states (and Mr Harmsworth’s vision).
One threat such measures must guard against is conflict. Sir Keir Starmer, the previous prime minister, warned in the spring that Britain might be at war with a rearmed Russia by 2030. Last week in Berlin Andy Burnham, Sir Keir’s successor, said sabotage and cyber-attacks by hostile states were growing more frequent. The government thinks Iran was behind what seemed to be an attempted attack on RAF Fairford, an airbase in Gloucestershire.
Officials must also plan for natural disasters such as pandemics, floods and wildfires. And Britain’s shoddy infrastructure might give way, too. In the 2026 edition of the National Risk Register, officials updated the odds of a whole region losing its water supply from below 1% to 5-25%. The impact, they said, would be “catastrophic”.
The catastrophising was long overdue. Britain’s state used to fear citizens would scorn advice on how to meet disaster. The ridiculing of the cold-war-era “Protect and Survive” information campaign is still remembered in Whitehall, says Toby Harris of the National Preparedness Commission, a non-profit venture.
Now there has been a “sea change in mentality, at least in the Cabinet Office”, says Elizabeth Braw of the Atlantic Council, another think-tank. During the covid-19 pandemic Britons followed lockdown rules surprisingly strictly; 500,000 signed up to volunteer within 24 hours. A survey found that 84% wanted the state to tell them how to prepare for crises.
Are its plans now sound? One problem is that Britain often uses its armed forces for civilian problems such as security at the Olympic games, wildfires and public-sector strikes. In a conflict, though, all available troops might be engaged in fighting, says Ed Arnold of RUSI, yet another think-tank. And so while the state can respond well to one crisis, it is bad at planning for several occurring at once. Moreover, a “whole-of-society” plan is not much help if society does not know what it is. And here, as in so much else, Britain’s state displays a pathological inclination to secrecy.
Occasional glimpses behind the curtain are not reassuring. Consider preparations at the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (DEFRA) for interruptions to food supplies. Officials fear supply chains are vulnerable—to cyber-attacks on the power grid, for instance. Food is designated one of 13 “critical national infrastructure” sectors. But Defra has “very little confidence” that cross-government governance of such sectors is joined up, and a database of relevant businesses and sites is yet to cover the food industry.
Businesses, meanwhile, have not seen the “playbook” Defra has drawn up for a food crisis. The National Audit Office has observed, drily, that this means the “plans may not work in practice”. The industry has not been invited to Whitehall’s crisis exercises. Nor have Local Resilience Forums, the provincial bodies meant to manage crises, been told what to do when the supermarket shelves are bare.
Money is part of the problem. Ministers boast that Britain will next year hit a new NATO target of spending 1.5% of GDP on “resilience”. Yet it will not spend a penny more than originally planned. Defra officials deemed the cost of a full emergency food plan too steep, opting for a “minimum viable product”. Money frustrates Mr Harmsworth, too. “In my heart of hearts, I know I can make it work,” he says. But only “if I have sufficient funding to do it.”

epub_63.title: Attack drones, meet Britain’s crack clay-pigeon shooters
epub_63.text:
Attack drones, meet Britain’s crack clay-pigeon shooters
Britain
| Skeet and destroy
Attack drones, meet Britain’s crack clay-pigeon shooters
An old hobby trains soldiers for a new type of warfare
Oct 15th 2026
It was a bad day to be a clay pigeon. On a misty morning in Wiltshire, British soldiers gathered for their annual shooting championship. Around 100 shot at 100 targets each—a massacre. Shotguns boomed, and neat clay discs were blasted into bright bursts of colour.
Clay-pigeon shooting was born in the late 1800s to help hunters improve their aim. In the second world war it was used to train fighter pilots. Today Peter Meager, boss of the army’s clay-target shooting team, hopes it can help prepare soldiers for drone warfare. “I think there are huge transferable skills,” he says.
Such skills are needed. Drones are behind 80% of the enemy targets Ukraine destroys. In June Britain’s Defence Investment Plan committed £750m ($950m) to counter-drone protection. Futuristic solutions include acoustic radars and direct-energy weapons.
Victorian ones might help, too. Shotguns are great for hitting aerial targets because their shells contain many projectiles, which spread out in the air. That makes it easier to catch a bird’s wing or a quadcopter’s propeller. But the army trains soldiers to shoot rifles instead.
The two are very different, says Ben Cookson, one of the army’s crack shots. Rifle shooting is about “being as still as possible”. You get in position, aim, breathe in and fire. “If you do that with a shotgun you’re doomed.” Hitting an airborne target means moving with it and judging how far ahead of it to aim. When rifle shooters come to Mr Cookson for tutoring, “we have to completely retrain them”, he says.
Clay-pigeon shooting is a good place to start. Launchers built to mimic the flight patterns of different birds can feasibly simulate those of drones, too. Most can fire clays at a drone-like speed of 50mph, and some at over 100mph.
And so, after Ukrainians told British instructors how useful shotguns were on the front line, the army started using clays to develop soldiers’ proficiency with them. But a shotgun should only ever be “a last resort”, says Mr Meager. A drone within range of one is already too close—much better to down it earlier.
Plenty of questions still hover over shotguns’ use as an anti-drone defence. Spotting the things is hard. In Wiltshire some shooters don tinted goggles to make the orange clays pop. Might whizzier versions help identify a distant, fast-moving quadcopter? Can standard lead shells take down armoured military drones? How widely should the shot be spread when targeting an incoming one?
These are questions for the nerds. At the army’s tournament the focus was on technique: the top score was 94 out of 100. Your correspondent, while not quite managing that, did at least avoid embarrassing himself in front of the troops (”a natural”, said Mr Cookson, a kind man). Spirits were high. But one cloud hanging over the day had little to do with the rain. “I hate drones,” sighs Mr Meager.
