epub_64.title: Israel and Britain have forestalled a diplomatic crisis—for now
epub_64.text:
Israel and Britain have forestalled a diplomatic crisis—for now
Britain
| A slippery slope
Israel and Britain have forestalled a diplomatic crisis—for now
But a once-special relationship is faltering
Oct 15th 2026
THE UNION JACK still flies in Jerusalem, over the same building it has been on for 59 years. On October 8th Israel and Britain agreed, after weeks of diplomatic wrangling, to rename this office the UK Mission rather than the Consulate-General. Both countries saved face but the fracas between them is far from over.
Their spat began soon after Britain changed its prime minister in July and appointed Ed Miliband as foreign secretary. One of his priorities has been to harden Britain’s position on Israel's brutal war in Gaza and its de facto annexation of the occupied West Bank. In some places Israeli settlers have been carrying out ethnic cleansing with tacit support from their government. Many, especially in the Labour Party, thought Britain’s government was previously far too soft on this.
On September 8th Mr Miliband announced sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank, as did France and Canada. Previous such efforts by Western countries, targeting individual settlers and organisations, have had limited effect. The difference this time is the intention to take “action on services” and “companies that support, facilitate or profit from illegal settlement activity”. This broad brush might paint everything from government ministries to Israel’s biggest banks.
In response, the Israeli government said it would close Britain’s consulate in Jerusalem, which serves its relations with Palestinians, and remove Britons working on Gaza’s planned reconstruction. Britain then threatened to escalate matters by expelling Israeli diplomats. The eventual compromise of renaming Britain’s consulate has cooled things for now.
Two big questions hang over Britain’s new stance on Israel. First, how far is it prepared to go? Mr Miliband has said he will need six to nine months to prepare legislation for the sanctions, and that they will target only the settlements, “not Israel”, with which Britain has “important and valued trade”. The sanctions, when they materialise, may therefore be little more than a gesture. But they may also be designed to cause serious damage. This uncertainty probably explains in part why America has not yet intervened. “It’s a game-changer,” says one senior Israeli diplomat. “Everyone understands what this can mean and Israeli banks are very worried.”
The second question is over timing. Some in Britain’s Foreign Office wanted to delay Mr Miliband’s announcement until after Israel’s parliamentary election on October 27th. Binyamin Netanyahu, the country’s prime minister, will not change its settlement policy when he needs to appeal to right-wing voters. After the election there may be a different government in Jerusalem. Mr Miliband, though, has his own political timetable.
Palestine has become a huge issue in British politics. In the 2024 elections Labour lost five seats to independent pro-Palestine candidates. This year, as in past ones, protesters waved Palestinian flags outside the Labour Party conference. But Mr Miliband’s sanctions statement nevertheless made it easier to remove the issue from the conference’s agenda—the result he was after, says one Labour adviser. His next steps might also be dictated by domestic politics, especially if the government calls an early election.
On September 30th Mr Netanyahu fired a shot across Britain’s bows. He lambasted the country in an interview with Fox News for announcing its sanctions “pretty much the next day” after Israel gave it intelligence on the “Iranian-sponsored” attack on an RAF base.
Israeli spooks were aghast at what they saw as Mr Netanyahu’s breach of secrecy. Close co-operation between the two countries’ intelligence services has long served both sides well, and the prospect of Iranian attacks on British soil gives them an obvious shared enemy. But some in the Israeli government argue that further British sanctions should be met with threats to withhold intelligence. “Ministers with political agendas could put us on a slippery slope to disrupting intelligence-sharing and harming both countries’ national security,” warns one Israeli official.

epub_65.title: The City of London honours an ancient pact
epub_65.text:
The City of London honours an ancient pact
Britain
| Standing on ceremony
The City of London honours an ancient pact
Meet the world’s most elaborate rent payment
Oct 15th 2026
In a fusty room at the Royal Courts of Justice, a man in a tricorn hat receives a payment. He is the king’s remembrancer, an office once charged with keeping track of money owed to the crown. This is the annual Ceremony of Quit Rents, held this year on October 14th. The earliest recorded one was in 1211. Each year the City of London pays a levy to the monarch for two plots of land: six giant horseshoes, 61 nails and two knives, one blunt and one sharp.
The remembrancer then inspects the wares. An official tries the blunt knife—traditionally a billhook—which should be able to bend a hazel stick without cutting it. Next he wields the sharp one, which needs to chop through the wood. Once the horseshoes and nails have been counted, the payment is accepted and the City can enjoy its tenancies for another 12 months.
In theory, at least. These days no one knows exactly where the rented land is, though some have made educated guesses. The first parcel is somewhere in Shropshire, where a man named Nicholas rented moorland before passing his tenancy on. The other is near London’s Strand, a stone’s throw from The Economist’s office. It came from a blacksmith called Walter, who paid for access to a forge (hence the horseshoes). Uncertainty over the postcodes has not stopped the crown claiming its due. In today’s Square Mile firms hire armies of lawyers to draft agreements and then wriggle out of them. But for the king’s remembrancer contracts are sacred.
The ceremony is the sort of thing Britain is famous for. In this common-law country, precedent piles on precedent and keeping up appearances is paramount. Hence the Tower of London has been locked at 9.53pm every night for 700 years, and the king has held an annual swan-counting event for even longer.
Other “quit rents” abound. For centuries the City has paid the crown £11 ($15) a year for the “town of Southwark”. In parts of East Anglia, Leicester and London people honour ancient deals by handing over roses. The Duke of Wellington hangs onto his country mansion only so long as he delivers a French flag to the king each June (something to do with Waterloo).
The autumn ceremony at the Royal Courts of Justice is the most ancient such occasion. Those watching from the public gallery admit the event is nonsense. But, says one, it is “lovely nonsense”.

epub_66.title: Lessons from Britain’s humiliating IMF bail-out
epub_66.text:
Lessons from Britain’s humiliating IMF bail-out
Britain
| 1976 and all that
Lessons from Britain’s humiliating IMF bail-out
Fifty years on, a fiscal crisis would play out very differently
Oct 15th 2026
The similarities between 1976 and 2026 are eerie. Then as now the spectre of decline haunted Britain, its economy troubled by energy crises, inflation and a lack of competitiveness. In both years the embattled Labour Party appointed a new prime minister, despite having won office only two years before. And both leaders then chose chancellors called Healey.
As John Healey, today’s chancellor, prepares for the budget on October 28th, he might well worry that he will suffer the fate of Denis Healey, his predecessor in 1976. On September 28th that year, the earlier Healey was about to board a plane when sterling’s freefall forced him to turn back and apply for an emergency loan from the IMF. A $3.9bn bail-out, agreed upon in December, imposed on the birthplace of the industrial revolution the sort of humiliating conditions normally reserved for the world’s sketchiest economies.
Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, warned last year that the government was on track once again to go cap in hand to the IMF. There are superficial echoes of 1976. Then investors revolted, refusing to buy British government bonds (or “gilts”) unless they offered much higher yields. Today’s bondholders charge Britain more to borrow than any other G7 country.
But though Britain can learn much from 1976, another trip to the IMF is unlikely. Things are nowhere near as bad today. Inflation was 13.7% in 1976; the IMF reckons it will be 3.8% this year. Ten-year gilt yields, then 15.7%, are now 5.4% (see table). And the economy was in another era. Marginal tax rates hit 98%. The government struck economy-wide wage deals with the unions. The Labour conference of 1976 passed a motion calling for the nationalisation of the country’s biggest four banks and seven insurance companies.
Most importantly, Britain managed its currency very differently 50 years ago. At the beginning of March 1976 £1 was worth $2.02; by October it had fallen to $1.57, driven by Britain’s embarrassing mismanagement of its economy. The Bank of England tried, and failed, to prop up the value of sterling by selling its foreign-currency reserves. In June it borrowed more from other central banks. And when those debts came due in December, Healey was forced to turn to the IMF.
The government is now happier to let the pound float freely on currency markets, making a repeat of the IMF drama improbable. But that does not mean Britain is out of the woods. Today a fiscal crisis would take a different form. Britain’s debt-to-GDP ratio is 95%, nearly double its level in the 1970s. Growth is much slower, leaving the country more exposed to sudden changes in market sentiment.
A crisis in 2026, therefore, might start in the gilt market. The government has two defences against things spiralling out of control: a plan for cutting the deficit and an independent central bank charged with keeping inflation down. But if either were doubted, yields could surge. This could start a vicious cycle, in which soaring borrowing costs worsened the public finances and in turn sent yields even higher. So might a jump in volatility elsewhere, since global markets are now far more complex and interconnected than in 1976.
To guard against such a crisis, Mr Healey should learn from his predecessor. The first lesson is the importance of flexibility. In 1976 it was not just that officials tried to resist changes to exchange rates. Unions refused to accept real-terms pay cuts, fuelling inflation and deepening the crisis. Flexible labour and currency markets give the economy shock absorbers.
Mr Healey also needs to ensure that investors really believe he will cut the deficit. Denis Healey grumbled that the 1976 crisis was avoidable: his spending cuts were working and only pessimistic forecasts spooked markets. He had a point, since spending came in below forecast, but the panic still caused real damage. Credibility in markets matters in itself, especially for Britain, which runs a current-account deficit (as in 1976) and relies on the kindness of flighty strangers to fund itself.
The IMF crisis wounded British pride. But it also gave Denis Healey an external constraint—the IMF—that helped enforce much-needed spending cuts against the will of many backbenchers. As Lord Macpherson, a former Treasury permanent secretary, puts it: “The only time the British state gets a grip on anything is when it is staring into the abyss.”  Spending today is already 45% of GDP, as in 1976, and an ageing, sicker population will add to the strain. A crisis might be the only way to force John Healey or his successors to make tough but necessary choices.

epub_67.title: In Britain, “European” doesn’t mean white
epub_67.text:
In Britain, “European” doesn’t mean white
Britain
| An overlooked immigrant group
In Britain, “European” doesn’t mean white
The country’s EU citizens are astonishingly diverse
Oct 15th 2026
To the uninformed palate, pindakaas is simply peanut butter. But some Somalis in Leicester, a city in the English Midlands, prefer the Dutch product. Jars of imported pindakaas can be bought in corner shops around the run-down St Matthew’s housing estate, near the city centre. So can Dutch oatmeal, Dutch vanilla sugar and condiments such as kruiden ketchup and romige fritessaus.
The Somalis of St Matthew’s developed a taste for such foods in the Netherlands, where many were refugees. They gained Dutch citizenship then migrated to Britain under eu freedom-of-movement rules. They are part of a large, diverse population of ethnic-minority Europeans in the country. Often overlooked, this population challenges British assumptions about immigration and Europe.
The Migration Observatory, a think-tank at Oxford University, estimates that some 800,000 ethnic-minority people in Britain hold eu passports. Most come from “old” European countries, such as France, Italy and the Netherlands, rather than the “new” countries that joined the union after 2003, such as Lithuania and Poland. Young Western Europeans in Britain are startlingly diverse (see chart).
Numbering almost 80,000, Portuguese Asians are the biggest group. Many come from the Indian state of Goa, which was Portuguese until 1961; people with deep roots in the state can obtain Portuguese passports. Espirito Roy Sequeira, a former seaman who now lives in Leicester, says that many Goans find Portugal more familiar than Britain because of its food and its Catholic churches. But Britain appeals to those who want their children to grow up with perfect English. “English is an international language; Portuguese is not,” says Mr Sequeira, rather understating the importance of Portuguese.
Abdikayf Farah, who runs a Somali education charity, spent a dozen years in Denmark. He moved to Leicester partly for its relaxed multiculturalism. The Danish government frowns on what it calls “parallel societies” and “ghettos”, and tries to break up immigrant enclaves; Britain does nothing of the kind. Education is another draw. Mr Farah says that the Somalis who migrated from the eu are especially ambitious for their children.
Those children are faring pretty well. Last year 53% of Asian pupils and 41% of black African pupils in Leicester’s schools got at least a grade 5 in their English and Maths gcse exams. The figure for white Britons was 24%. Immigrants’ children perform better than average in the pisa tests run by the oecd, a club of mostly rich countries, making Britain unusual among European nations.
Another draw is the belief that ethnic minorities find it easier to get ahead in Britain. Hielen Tekeste Berhe, an Italian citizen with Eritrean parents, speaks of a “glass ceiling” in Italy. She has created a startup called The Fair Grocer, which is inspired by Italian and east African food cultures. Attending gatherings of black entrepreneurs in Britain, she sometimes detects a familiar accent, and realises that she is speaking to another Italian.
If the population of European ethnic minorities is growing today, it is probably more a result of childbirth than immigration. Brexit has suppressed movement of all kinds. Indeed, Aké Achi, founder of a group called Black Europeans, says that many people are struggling to establish their right to remain in Britain. Ethnic minorities are over-represented among those who report problems with the scheme that allows Europeans to settle after Brexit.
A sociologist at Loughborough University, Simone Varriale, says that Britons tend to squeeze black and Asian Europeans into the post-colonial categories they are familiar with. To them, an African Italian is simply African. But some resist this flattening of their identities. “It’s not just that we have Italian passports. We are Italians!” declares Ms Tekeste Berhe. In a Leicester suburb Azim Zicar, a Mozambican Asian it worker, speaks Portuguese to his children and strives to introduce them to others who share their background.
Now that most Britons see Brexit as a failure, politicians and think-tanks have begun to probe their appetite for rejoining the eu. Because that would mean a resumption of free movement, an important question is how Britons feel about migration from Europe.
A poll by British Future, a think-tank, found that 41% believe workers from the eu should be given priority over those from elsewhere, compared with 40% who think they should be treated equally. A Cambridge University study found that Britons grew keener on European migration when they were told to imagine a nurse from Poland. Yet some migrants are both from the eu and from outside the eu. Free movement has given Britain pindakaas-eating Somalis as well as Poles.

epub_68.title: How suicide became a lobbying tool
epub_68.text:
How suicide became a lobbying tool
Britain
| Bagehot
How suicide became a lobbying tool
Public policy is increasingly dictated by tragedy
Oct 15th 2026
Talk of suicide is hard to avoid in Britain. Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, recently warned that inheritance-tax changes mean farmers “are literally committing suicide so that their children don’t have to pay it”. Watch “The Social Reckoning”, a new film about Meta, and an advert will pop up: “Instagram helped kill my daughter”. It is a campaign by the family of Molly Russell, a 14-year-old girl who died by self-harming after she had seen similar things on Instagram (which Meta owns). More than three years after Ruth Perry, a headmistress from Reading, killed herself following a school inspection, teachers still campaign in her name. “I don’t want there to be another Ruth,” said one this summer, calling for the inspection regime to be gutted.
There is, thankfully, no growing epidemic of suicides. British people kill themselves at roughly the same rate as they have for the past few decades. Last year 6,000 people did so in England and Wales. What has shifted is the way Britain’s establishment treats these deaths. Suicide was once a sin. Until 1961 it was a crime; then it was a tragedy. Now, however, suicide is an argument.
Policy is discussed surprisingly often in terms of how likely it is to make someone kill themselves. In the 20th century mps rarely mentioned such things. Now they do so hundreds of times a year. In 2025 suicide featured in parliamentary debates on asylum claims, AI policy, the public finances, football regulation, special-needs provision, seafarers, the “spring statement”, trans rights and the welfare system. There were also entire debates on male suicide, mental health and whether to legalise assisted dying.
What began as healthy acknowledgment of a dark reality has morphed into something troubling. Bereaved families like the Russells started speaking out to prevent similar tragedies in the early 2010s, says Sir Louis Appleby, a professor at the University of Manchester. Soon enough, no mental-health story was complete without a claim about suicide. At this point the sincere began to mix with the cynical. Some genuinely wanted to raise awareness; others wanted to win an argument. The risk, says Sir Louis, is “to already-distressed people who hear the message: ‘People like you, facing similar problems, are taking their own lives’.”
Suicide is too often framed as a logical response to policy by politicians. It took little time for a debate about inheritance tax on farms to focus on the idea of desperate farmers killing themselves. Farmers “may well decide that they should not be here” when the law was introduced, said Tom Bradshaw of the National Farmers’ Union in 2024. Rather than something preventable, suicide is portrayed as inevitable if the government chooses a particular course of action (trampling on guidance from suicide-prevention groups). And it works: Labour duly made its inheritance-tax reforms more generous to farmers the next year.
When suicide is prominent in politics, debate can descend into blackmail. Talk of trade-offs or compromise becomes impossible. Ministers making life harder for benefit claimants had “blood on their hands”, said Labour MPs in the 2010s, citing constituents who had killed themselves. In 2019 Peter Bone, a Tory MP, campaigned on behalf of people who had been caught using a tax-dodging ruse and forced to pay back large sums via a “loan charge”. “How many more people are going to take their lives before the loan charge is scrapped?” asked Mr Bone. As a lobbying technique, it was a success. Britain has a more forgiving welfare system than a decade ago, and its tax authority has weakened demands over the loan charge.
Martyrdom was once a preoccupation of extremists. Now it has infected middle-of-the-road campaign groups. When Perry killed herself there was an immediate outcry, with teachers’ unions calling for inspections to be made less intrusive or scrapped. A neighbouring headteacher declared: “It’s really important to us to remember her and for her death not to be in vain.” A tragic death had to be made to mean something. As far as policy went, it did. Labour cited Perry’s suicide when it unveiled reforms hobbling Ofsted, the school inspector.
Suicide is but one nightmarish problem faced by the state every day. Dead teachers, dead farmers and dead teenagers must be balanced against a million other competing demands. It is a grisly job but a fundamental one for politicians. Increasingly, the British state refuses to admit these trade-offs. Instead, Leviathan wraps its arms around a grieving family in misplaced humanity. Compassion that should come from society instead comes from the state, with pernicious effects on policymaking.
No wonder ministers hide behind coroners when suicide is discussed. An inquest determined that Instagram had played a part in Molly’s death, recommending far tighter rules for children on social media. Labour introduced them. Similarly, Ofsted got a kicking for not doing enough to support Perry. The result is that coroners become de facto lawmakers, with their suggestions—such as watering down inspections or limiting children’s access to the internet—dictating legislation. Parliamentarians end up as little more than secretaries transcribing them onto vellum.
Even the most well-meaning politicians find themselves following a dark strategy, whether cynically or not. Britain is in an emotional state, incapable of resisting grief. Politicians and campaigners use that to their advantage. In their efforts to be compassionate, mps are witlessly embracing a terrible idea: that good can come from suicide. It is a poisonous line of reasoning, which suicide-prevention groups rightly fight in case it leads to more death. There could be no more destructive message to send. Yet it worms its way into almost every policy area. Why has suicide become a political tool? Because it works.

epub_70.title: How to survive a predatory world order
epub_70.text:
How to survive a predatory world order
International
| Don’t get trampled
How to survive a predatory world order
Middle powers face a new threat: Trump-Putin-Xi collusion
Oct 15th 2026
LIKE a villager urging neighbours to confront a prowling predator together, Mark Carney sought to rally the world’s middle powers. In a speech in January to the World Economic Forum at Davos, Canada’s prime minister issued an urgent call for mid-ranked countries to unite. This is an age in which the strong prey on the weak, he told his audience of grandees. The old rules-based order no longer constrains the mighty, he advised. Nor can smaller countries roll over and hope that submission keeps them safe. Middling powers can act together in coalitions of the willing, or “be on the menu”.
His fellow leaders knew that Mr Carney was mostly warning them about America and China, the strongest of today’s big beasts. Mr Carney was speaking from experience. After decades as a comfortable, if unexciting, annexe to the American economy, Canada finds itself the object of President Donald Trump’s wrath. Mr Carney has worked hard to
reduce his homeland’s dependencies
. Other middle powers have studied his confrontation with Mr Trump closely. Yet nine months on, the response to that Davos call to arms looks distinctly patchy.
In some areas the Carney speech aligned with actions that countries were already taking. In this age of economic coercion, choke-points and supply shocks, governments do not need Mr Carney to tell them to hedge their bets, diversify and reduce the leverage of global bullies.
Since the speech, on a few occasions middle powers have stood up to large aggressors and lived to tell the tale. When Mr Trump threatened to invade Greenland and pledged to impose crippling tariffs on any country that stood in his way, European leaders stood by Denmark, Greenland’s ruler. Taken aback by a ferocious reaction from financial markets and by Europe’s stated readiness to enact trade counter-measures, Mr Trump dropped dreams of ownership in favour of an enhanced security pact.
Asia has witnessed shows of defiance, too. Despite intense pressure from China, including curbs on Chinese sales of critical minerals, Japan’s prime minister refuses to apologise for saying an inconvenient truth aloud. Takaichi Sanae’s offence was to confirm publicly that Japan’s national security would be imperilled by a Chinese attack on Taiwan, Japan’s democratic neighbour. As Chinese officials hurl insults and call her a war criminal, Ms Takaichi cannot back down, politically, and will not.
Yet for each instance of middle-power defiance, there are more examples of feebleness, and of leadership vacuums left unfilled. One big problem is that the middle powers are a disparate bunch, with differing degrees of nostalgia for the order that Mr Carney mourns. Plenty of countries in the global south have always seen America as a bully, and resent Western countries more generally as insufferably self-centred. Such regional heavyweights as Brazil, South Africa or India are not sure who appointed Canada—a blandly rich vanilla milkshake of a country—to lead a new post-American world order.
Further complicating Mr Carney’s pitch, there is no consensus as to who even counts as a middle power (see chart). One definition involves countries with some means to influence world events, whether that is a product of their size, regional clout, wealth, industrial and technological might, diplomatic networks or military power. Perhaps ten or 15 members of the G20 club easily fit the bill, from sundry European powers to Australia, Canada, Indonesia, Japan, Mexico, South Africa, South Korea and Turkey.
Brazil and India belong on the list, though some in those countries aspire to emerging great-power status. Russia thinks of itself as a nuclear-armed superpower, though its economic and demographic woes, and dependency on China, make it a pretty mangy big beast. For all that, Russia is more than a mid-ranking player: its president, Vladimir Putin, is one of a few foreign leaders treated as a peer by Mr Trump, and Russian aggression haunts the wakeful nights of politicians across Europe. There are small countries that control vital technologies, such as the Netherlands or Taiwan, both home to firms that are irreplaceable to semiconductor supply chains. Then come hyper-ambitious powers with commercial or military interests far from home, such as Israel, Saudi Arabia or the United Arab Emirates.
A simpler problem with the Carney speech is that it correctly noted the urgency of the moment, but misidentified the biggest threat currently posed by superpower bullies. The address opens with a warning about “great-power rivalry”, a reference to global struggles for primacy between dominant countries, notably America and China. Mr Carney called for “the countries in between” to avoid picking sides or competing with each other for the favour of the giants, and instead “combine to create a third path with impact”.
Nine months later, though, great-power rivalries are proving less disruptive than major-country collusion. Mr Trump is buying diesel from Mr Putin to lower fuel prices in America before midterm elections, and threatening to cut military aid for Ukraine. A fragile truce is, for now, lowering trade and other tensions between America and China. Already, diplomats report hearing officials from America and China proudly calling their respective countries a G2, or a uniquely potent power couple.
Then there is China’s and Russia’s ever-deepening, lopsided anti-Western partnership. Middle countries can stand up to one great power, on a good day. They have less hope of challenging two giants, defending overlapping interests in concert.
This geopolitical dynamic was accurately predicted, years ago, by Singapore’s far-sighted if ruthless founder, Lee Kuan Yew. “When elephants fight, the grass suffers,” Lee would say, describing how America-China confrontations endangered bystanders. There is a less-often cited second half to that warning, though: “When they make love, the grass suffers also.”
In theory, America and Russia are still adversaries. But in Washington horrified European allies find themselves being scolded by some officials in the Trump administration for backing Ukraine. Such support is called a provocation of Russia.
In New York diplomats at the UN express surprise at how closely America, China and Russia are working on some issues, especially the appointment of a new secretary-general. The suspicion is that those three permanent members of the Security Council favour a candidate who will administer the organisation, not challenge the big powers: a secretary, not a general, as the phrase goes at the UN.
It is not clear how long the current truce between America and China can last. It exists largely because of one man, who sits in the Oval Office. Mr Trump has never been an ideological China hawk, if that means someone who disapproves of the Communist Party’s iron-fisted rule. Now, in his second term, he has no interest in changing China’s ways, whether that means confronting China over its economic model or its regional ambitions. He is more interested in selling China soyabeans, flogging Boeing planes and securing supplies of Chinese rare-earth elements. To that end, he has told his diplomats and generals to avoid starting a war with President Xi Jinping and is holding up promised arms sales to Taiwan. Judging by their recent summit, neither Mr Trump nor Mr Xi is minded to heed calls from the rest of the world to permit more oversight of their respective champions of artificial intelligence.
That said, the truce with China could end at any moment, for Chinese leaders are playing hardball in large ways and small. In September Mr Trump wooed Mr Xi during that visit to Washington, meeting him in person at Joint Base Andrews, among other shows of respect. Mr Trump expected China to repay him with actions to help Republicans in the midterms, for instance by boosting Chinese diesel sales. Instead, China enraged the president by curbing diesel exports just days later. This instability points to an unenviable choice facing smaller powers. Do they prefer accommodation of China by Mr Trump, based on a division of the world into spheres of interest, or a resumption of full-blown rivalry between two giants?
A surprising number of political leaders express sympathy for Canada as a victim of Mr Trump’s bullying, but behind closed doors grumble about the naivety of Mr Carney’s advice that middle powers just need to be braver. Not every country is as lucky as Canada, they note. Canadians are blessed with abundant oil, gas and hydroelectricity. Secure in the high north of the Americas, deterring Russia is not the urgent task faced by some fellow members of NATO. Canada can confront America in a way that Europeans cannot, sniffs a senior European. In Japan and other Asian countries, there is impatience with Mr Carney’s talk of middle powers leading the world. Only America can deter China, it is said in Tokyo, and Canada is not about to save us.
True, in the months since his Davos speech, middle powers have pulled off some modest wins. Take the trade dispute between China and the European Union, the 27-member bloc that is by far the most integrated and powerful coalition of middle powers (see charts). Ahead of a European summit on October 15th at which EU leaders will debate whether to create powerful new trade weapons, China appears to have offered voluntary cuts to exports of plug-in hybrid vehicles.
This is a footling concession, though: sales of hybrid cars are not a core Chinese interest. China’s ambitions to control Taiwan are of a different magnitude. If war breaks out over the island there is no coalition of middle powers that could make China back off. Only America intimidates the hard men who run the People’s Liberation Army. Defying Mr Trump over Greenland was, for that matter, a low-stakes fight. Owning that Arctic island was a peculiarly Trumpian obsession, not a cause with popular support among Americans.
Foreign governments look sceptically at another claim in the Carney speech, namely that middle powers can replace a lost, American-led order with one of their own. Diplomats tick off challenges that cannot be solved without deep American (and indeed Chinese) engagement, from tackling climate change to the prevention and management of pandemics and, most urgently of all, the governance of AI.
Middle powers are rapidly diversifying their defence relations. With America becoming a less reliable ally and an overstretched arms supplier, NATO members are buying more kit from such players as Sweden, Italy and France. Several European governments are keen on a French offer to extend its nuclear umbrella over the continent, though as an adjunct to America’s much larger deterrent.
With Patriot missile interceptors in short supply, Gulf states are snapping up South Korean air-defence systems. Ukraine is selling anti-drone defences to Gulf states under attack from Iran. In a 2026-worthy twist, Ukrainian firms have an edge because the drones that Ukraine shoots down over its territory are based on Iranian designs that were upgraded by Russia and which are now going back to Iran.
In other spheres, when middle powers seek greater autonomy, they are often balancing one hegemon against another. Many Western countries dislike relying on China for critical minerals. The main viable alternative is to join buyers’ clubs for non-Chinese minerals that are built around the G7 countries and led by America. Governments worried by their dependence on fossil fuels from the Middle East or America are turning to Chinese-made solar panels, windmills and batteries.
Even when coalitions of mid-ranking countries do emerge, not all of them are benign, or fit into Mr Carney’s vision of a principled world order underwritten by members of Team B. The main principle being upheld by the Mecca agreement, a collective-defence pact signed in August by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey, is that others should think twice before messing with that trio. Loose groupings of ambitious regional powers are meddling on each side of Sudan’s ghastly civil war.
The starkest examples of middle-power irrelevance involve AI. With America and China far ahead, and locked in a struggle for primacy, there are few signs, for now, of serious co-operation between the giants on AI safety and governance. In a bid by the rest of the world to be heard, in September Finland and Norway called for controls on frontier AI models. Dozens of countries have signed the appeal. Britain has not. It hopes for a special AI relationship with America, based on its leading research centres and its AI Security Institute, and close ties between spy agencies.
A separate group of countries, led by the Netherlands and South Korea, has held meetings since 2023 to argue for Responsible Artificial Intelligence in the Military Domain (REAIM, to use their snazzy acronym). Kenya will host the next REAIM summit. America attends the meetings, which is a positive first step, for the Trump administration refuses to engage with such bodies as the UN on AI rule-making.
More broadly, there is little evidence that America and China are interested in the views of AI also-rans. True, it is possible that the Trump administration’s current suspicion of AI regulation will be shaken by staggering new capabilities in frontier models. But even if more support emerges for slowing work at the frontier in America, the objection—that China might take the lead—will remain unavoidable. Plausibly, America may seek to slow Chinese labs by further tightening their access to high-end chips and the tools for making them. Or the full-speed-ahead crowd may win the day, with America accelerating AI research despite concerns about models causing catastrophe, for fear of letting China build catastrophic capabilities first.
In times of staggering risks and opportunities, great powers rarely show magnanimity towards their lessers. And there lies the challenge for the mid-ranked rest. In a speech still being talked about nine months later, Mr Carney rightly noted the ending of a post-1945 order that was good to Canada and its peers. His optimistic solutions are ageing less well. Vigilance and courage are admirable traits in a leader and in a country. But when dangers loom, there is no arguing with strength.

epub_72.title: Elon Musk's foundation is opaque, miserly and self-serving
epub_72.text:
Elon Musk's foundation is opaque, miserly and self-serving
Business
| Foundation model
Elon Musk's foundation is opaque, miserly and self-serving
The world’s richest man disdains charity. His money is where his mouth is
Oct 15th 2026
The world’s richest man
does not much believe in philanthropy. In August Elon Musk said in a social-media post that Brian Armstrong, a crypto boss, was right to dismiss many charities as “net negative” for the world. Weeks earlier he had joined attacks on Mackenzie Scott, the ex-wife of Jeff Bezos, Amazon’s founder, and one of the biggest donors in history, for “making the world a worse place”. Mr Musk’s distaste for do-goodery is not new. He led
the near-demolition
of America’s aid agency, and was once quoted describing philanthropy as “bullshit”. In Mr Musk’s reckoning, his gift to humanity is his for-profit work: the electric vehicles he produces at Tesla, the space exploration he is doing at
SpaceX
and the political debate on his social-media site, X.
And yet Mr Musk also runs America’s fifth-largest charitable private foundation. With $14.7bn in assets at last count, the Musk Foundation is a hair smaller than the Ford Foundation and more than double the size of the Rockefeller Foundation, two long-standing pillars of philanthropy (see chart). Unlike these organisations, however, the Musk Foundation says almost nothing about its work. Its website contains a mere 33 words, laying out the causes it supports, which include renewable energy, space exploration and artificial-intelligence safety. And it is run by a team of just three: Mr Musk; the head of his family office, Jared Birchall; and Matilda Simon, another family-office employee. The only clues to the foundation’s activities are contained in tax returns. The Economist scoured the filings covering the period from July 2020 to the end of 2024 to find out: how does the tycoon who detests philanthropy give?
The first observation is that Mr Musk, like most very rich people, appears to craft his philanthropy to minimise his taxes. His biggest gifts—a total of around $8bn in Tesla stock—went to his foundation in 2021 and 2022, years when he came into many billions of dollars of shares and faced a whopping tax bill as a result. Brian Mittendorf, an accounting expert at Ohio State University, says founders enjoy a “double benefit” from such donations: they avoid paying capital-gains tax on the shares, which originally cost them relatively little, and can then claim a charitable deduction based on the (far higher) market value. At the end of 2024, the book value of the stock held by the Musk Foundation was around $5.7m, whereas their market value was an estimated $14bn.
In return for tax breaks, philanthropists are supposed to put their money to good causes. But the Musk Foundation has been painfully slow to do so. Under American law, foundations that only make grants must distribute roughly 5% of their investment assets every year or else face penalties, with a one-year grace period to make up any shortfall. Many foundations miss the target now and then. But the Musk Foundation has made use of the grace period in each of the past four years for which filings are available, and at the end of 2024 was on the hook for $400m, according to FoundationMark, a data provider. Mr Musk—who predicted in a recent
interview with this newspaper
that the economic abundance brought about by AI would make money irrelevant as soon as a decade from now—seems in no hurry to give away his fortune in the meantime.
What is more, according to tax filings and estimates from Candid, another data provider, a big chunk of the amount the foundation has donated has merely been put into a holding pen. Almost one-tenth of the $1bn disbursed between 2020 and 2024 went to Fidelity Charitable, which runs donor-advised funds (DAFs), accounts that let donors hold money destined for charity indefinitely with no reporting requirements. There is no rule against charitable private foundations donating to DAFs. But, says Mr Mittendorf, such transfers are against the “spirit of the rules”. “You’re just moving money from one bucket to another bucket,” he explains.
Of the money that has actually been handed out by the Musk Foundation, the vast majority has gone to other organisations linked to the entrepreneur. Over 58% was funnelled to The Foundation, a cryptically named charity led by Mr Birchall that happens to share the same address as the Musk Foundation. According to its tax filing for 2024, The Foundation aims to build schools dedicated to STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics) education. Yet it is unclear what it does with all its money. Mr Musk did fund a private school named Ad Astra (Latin for “to the stars”) near SpaceX’s previous headquarters in California, which had a student body of less than 50 (including Mr Musk’s children). But it was wound down around the time of the covid-19 pandemic. According to the Ad Astra website, a new school in Texas, where SpaceX is now based, is in the works.
Other gifts appear somewhat self-serving. In 2021 Jared Isaacman, a fellow billionaire space enthusiast, bankrolled a four-person SpaceX mission into orbit in order to raise money for a children’s hospital, raffling off one of the seats for the flight. Mr Musk chipped in with a $55m donation, among the largest ever by his foundation. (Mr Isaacman subsequently paid for another expedition into the void, during which he performed the first commercial spacewalk. These days he runs NASA.) A smattering of gifts to non-profit groups in southern Texas followed the explosion of a SpaceX rocket in 2021, which showered the local area in debris.
Among the remainder of the gifts, there is no discernible philanthropic strategy. Put aside The Foundation and Fidelity, and the average donation made by the Musk Foundation in 2024 was less than $1.4m. The money has gone to a hotch-potch of causes, from sea-turtle conservation to spinal medicine. Mr Musk “puts a real emphasis on being a visionary and having bold ideas,” says Benjamin Soskis of the Urban Institute, a left-leaning American think-tank. “But even in the most sympathetic reading of the Musk Foundation, you can’t find that type of approach.”
As far as its style of giving goes, the Musk Foundation is fairly hands-off. Ironically, grant recipients liken it to Ms Scott’s efforts. She has upturned traditional philanthropy by maintaining only a small staff and handing out money without prescribing what it is spent on or asking for regular reports. Likewise, the Musk Foundation pays no salaries, and its three-person leadership team devotes on average a combined 2.1 hours per week to its work. Karim Meghji, boss of CodeAI, an education non-profit that has received funding from the foundation, describes the process as “very simple”. “It’s very much the phone call, the cheque, and then we send a report at the end of the year,” he explains.
Mr Musk appears more enthusiastic about giving his money away to political causes than to charitable ones. In recent months he has donated at least $275m to the Republican Party ahead of America’s midterm elections. That may change. The money Mr Musk has put into his foundation cannot be withdrawn, and he has hinted repeatedly in the past that he plans to make big gifts in the future. For now, though, the world’s richest plutocrat appears to be one of its least generous.

epub_73.title: SpaceX’s Starlink expansion is a bold gamble on the future
epub_73.text:
SpaceX’s Starlink expansion is a bold gamble on the future
Business
| Raising the bars
SpaceX’s Starlink expansion is a bold gamble on the future
Elon Musk is betting that robotics will dramatically increase demand for connectivity
Oct 15th 2026
Since it opened for business in 2021, Starlink has grown like Topsy. The satellite-internet service offered by Elon Musk’s SpaceX has signed up more than 12m individual subscribers, as well as a clutch of airlines and shipping firms. It also plays a crucial—and changing—
role in the Ukraine war
. More recently it has signed deals with big network operators such as T-Mobile in America to enable Starlink’s satellites to connect directly to their customers’ mobile phones, providing service in places outside the reach of land-based phone masts.
Mr Musk has yet bigger ambitions for the service. On October 8th SpaceX confirmed what many observers had long suspected: it will build a fully fledged mobile-phone network that will compete directly with those run by big incumbents. Markets seemed to take the idea seriously. The share prices of the three biggest American mobile operators—T-Mobile, AT&T and Verizon—fell sharply after the announcement. For now, the threat to their business is modest. But Mr Musk is betting that, in the roboticised future he envisions, Starlink will play a vital role.
Although precise details are scant, SpaceX’s plan seems to have three components. The first is to launch even more satellites. In its announcement, SpaceX said it had received approval from the Federal Communications Commission, an American regulator, to fly up to 15,000 satellites specifically designed to beam voice calls and data to smartphones on the ground.
But although satellites are good at offering widespread coverage, they are less good when it comes to serving cities, towns and other large concentrations of people efficiently. Each Starlink satellite has a fixed capacity, and, because they are in orbit, each spends only a tiny fraction of its time over a given place.
SpaceX is therefore also planning to build ground-based infrastructure—the second part of its plan. It intends to start adding “femtocells”—tiny mobile-phone masts—to the receiver dishes it sells to Starlink’s home-broadband customers. Those would turn each Starlink dish into a short-range mobile mast. And the firm intends to build conventional capacity using bigger mobile-phone masts, too.
To make that service work, SpaceX has also been investing in rights to use the radio spectrum—the third element of its plan. In 2025 the company spent $19.6bn acquiring bandwidth from EchoStar, a troubled satellite operator, for use on its mobile-phone satellites. In a separate statement on October 8th Grain Management, a telecoms-focused investment firm, said it was selling a slice of low-frequency spectrum to SpaceX, with rumours putting the price tag at $8bn. Lower frequencies are better at penetrating into buildings, a vital feature for any aspiring mobile-network provider.
What advantage SpaceX will have over incumbent networks is not clear. A phone contract guaranteed to work in the middle of the Alaskan wilderness sounds attractive on paper, and SpaceX may prefer to sell such a service directly rather than acting as an infrastructure provider for incumbents. But the evidence from SpaceX’s deal with T-Mobile suggests that customers are not yet willing to pay much for the service, notes Tim Farrar, a satellite-industry analyst. Srinivasan Gopalan, T-Mobile’s boss, noted in May that few customers had bought the satellite service, and said it accounted for 0.0002% of their total usage.
The incumbents are not standing still, either. A week before SpaceX’s move, AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon launched a joint venture designed to let them pool their spectrum and buy satellite capacity from a set of different providers. The move was seen as a hedge against Starlink.
SpaceX’s telecoms play, however, is best viewed not as a grab for a share of the current market, but as a wager on the future. Speaking on an earnings call in August, Gwynne Shotwell, SpaceX’s chief operating officer, predicted that autonomous vehicles and humanoid robots—including those made by Tesla, another company controlled by Mr Musk—would “dramatically increase the demand for connectivity” in the years ahead. Running Tesla’s machines on SpaceX’s mobile network could provide both businesses with a competitive edge.
In the meantime, the expansion of Starlink adds yet more to SpaceX’s plate. It is developing Grok, an artificial-intelligence model, testing Starship, the biggest rocket ever made, building a
gigantic launch complex
in Louisiana, hoping to put data centres into space and working on a politically sensitive contract with NASA to provide a lunar lander for America’s Moon-exploration programme. The increasingly sprawling enterprise is burning through cash: it raised $86bn in a public listing in June, then issued $25bn in debt just weeks later, and has plans to borrow more. Starlink, the profit engine of SpaceX, currently helps to offset the losses in its other divisions. That makes Mr Musk’s latest gamble all the more audacious—and risky.

epub_74.title: AI neolabs are raising huge sums. Most have little to show for it
epub_74.text:
AI neolabs are raising huge sums. Most have little to show for it
Business
| Testing the limits
AI neolabs are raising huge sums. Most have little to show for it
Superstar researchers who branch out on their own need to start producing results
Oct 15th 2026
GEORGES DORIOT, a founding father of venture capital (VC), described his job as judging “a man and an idea”. Many Silicon Valley investors looking to make mega-bucks from the artificial-intelligence boom have embraced a similarly minimalist philosophy. A string of AI superstars with little more than a vague ambition have raised billions from VC investors to decamp from established model-makers and set up their own so-called neolabs. So far most have little to show for it.
The neolab era began in June 2024 with the launch of Safe Superintelligence (SSI) by Ilya Sutskever, a co-founder of OpenAI. Two years later a total of 29 neolabs had been founded, according to a count by Radical Ventures, a VC firm. This cohort has now raised a combined $23bn, according to figures from PitchBook, a data provider (see chart). Among the list is Reflection AI, whose open-weight Beam model, announced on October 5th, was hailed as America’s answer to the cheap Chinese models that have rapidly gained ground in the West.
Other neolabs, however, have not yet achieved much with their funding. Under 35% of the startups in Radical Ventures’ cohort have released commercial offerings, according to The Economist’s analysis of public announcements. A greater share—slightly over half—have released code that developers can incorporate into their own products, but these are often billed as research demos meant only to showcase the approach a neolab is taking.
SSI, last valued at $32bn, may be the least hurried of the bunch. Mr Sutskever, one of AI’s most decorated researchers, has said that his neolab does not plan to release a product until it reaches “superintelligence”. (It hasn’t yet.) In July he declared that SSI at last had research “worthy of scaling up”, without revealing any details. Nvidia, a chip colossus, got a peek and handed the startup a further $5bn in funding, bringing its total to $8bn.
Mira Murati, a former colleague of Mr Sutskever’s at OpenAI, has been quicker to ship products at her startup, Thinking Machines Lab (TML). In December, a few months after raising its first $2bn at a $12bn valuation, it released Tinker, a service that allows engineers to customise open-weight models developed by others. It followed up in July with its own model, Inkling, which it defended as being “strong across many domains”, even if not the best overall. According to a person briefed on the figures, TML’s annualised revenue has crossed $200m. That is much more than other neolabs, but still a trifling figure compared with the roughly $40bn valuation that TML is reportedly targeting in a new fundraising round.
Inkling misses the cut-off for a closely watched list of the 20 most popular models on
OpenRouter
, an AI marketplace. The only neolab offering on that list is Jev, an ultra-cheap model that does not output text but is skilled as a traffic cop, directing tasks to other models. Typesafe, the neolab behind Jev, raised only a modest $40m before releasing the model in September, but this month brought in an additional $870m from VC investors.
Neolabs and their backers are betting that smaller and focused teams are more likely to produce novel breakthroughs. But they face various challenges. One is staying ahead of copycat offerings. A number of competitors to Jev, for example, have already surfaced since its release.
Another challenge is competing with established labs for computing power. That has pushed many neolabs into the arms of Nvidia, which can grant access to its chips. It has made 32 investments in startup model-makers, reckons Radical Ventures, more than any other company or VC firm. Reflection, which has already raised $800m from Nvidia, is reportedly in talks about another big investment or even an acquisition. AMD, a rival to Nvidia, has been active, too. In September it paid $8bn to purchase World Labs, a neolab founded by Fei-Fei Li, another AI superstar.
It took OpenAI and Anthropic years to turn their research into commercial offerings. Investors in neolabs, especially those working on novel research approaches, might therefore need to be patient. Many startup model-makers will fail. But those that don’t could, in time, generate enormous returns for their early backers.
In other fields, such as biotech, VCs are comfortable taking such risks. But as one investor points out, biotechs have pre-defined milestones against which progress can be measured. If the first phase of human trials goes well, a startup can expect to raise more funding. Neolabs have not been around long enough to have developed such a process, and VCs have yet to insist on one. If the neolab era is to continue, the startups will need to start producing more frequent results.

epub_75.title: Is the semiconductor industry headed for an almighty crash?
epub_75.text:
Is the semiconductor industry headed for an almighty crash?
Business
| Processing power
Is the semiconductor industry headed for an almighty crash?
There are reasons to believe a bust, if it comes, will be less vertiginous than the boom
Oct 15th 2026
For more than four decades the semiconductor industry has been governed by two laws as dependable as any in physics. The first is that the number of transistors, the tiny switches etched onto a chip, keeps rising. The second is that every boom ends in a bust. The first, which makes chips more powerful, is in rude health. Leading processors for artificial intelligence contain more than 200bn transistors, and the industry reckons it can cram in a trillion by the end of the decade. The second is stirring unease about how long the good times will last.
The industry is used to booms, but not one like this. AI has created an insatiable appetite for the chips used to train and run AI models. In the first half of 2026 semiconductor sales grew faster, year on year, than at any time since the 1980s (see chart). This month TSMC, the world’s biggest contract chipmaker, reported its sixth consecutive quarter of record profits; Samsung Electronics, a South Korean chip heavyweight, reported its fourth. Yet investors are growing jittery. Despite blowout results and rosy forecasts, an index of leading semiconductor firms has fallen by over 10% since October 6th. Their fears were not helped when on October 12th Hock Tan, boss of Broadcom, a big chip designer, likened many investors in the AI trade to gamblers in a casino who “have no clue” what they are investing in.
Nearly all of the industry’s expected growth hinges on chips for AI, making it a giant bet on the technology. If that bet sours—and the “supercycle”, as some have taken to calling it, comes to an end—will chipmakers suffer a bust as vertiginous as the boom? There are reasons to think not.
Even as the semiconductor industry has grown, manufacturing has become far more concentrated. Most chip designers, such as Nvidia, whose graphics-processing units have powered the AI boom, do not make their own silicon. Nor do software firms such as Google and OpenAI, which have also taken to designing AI processors. Instead they rely on foundries—and one in particular. In the early 2000s some 25 firms could make the most advanced processors. Today four can, and TSMC makes nearly all of the high-end ones.
Memory chips, which are also vital for AI, have gone the same way. More than 20 firms made advanced memory chips in 1990. Now only three—Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron—make almost all of them. China has produced new entrants in both processors and memory chips, but without access to the most advanced chipmaking tools, they remain behind the frontier.
Consolidation has allowed a few dominant chipmakers to set the pace of expansion and dictate the terms on which they sell. They are investing heavily to capitalise on the boom. TSMC’s capital expenditure is expected to hit roughly $62bn this year, more than one and a half times as much as in 2025. Next year analysts expect it to be around $76bn. The memory-makers have also boosted their investments.
Even so, their outlays are modest in comparison with the windfall from AI. As a share of revenue, TSMC’s capital spending is expected to fall from 44% in 2023 to 36% this year. Moreover, investments are being paid for from the cash that chipmakers are generating, rather than borrowing. This year TSMC’s capacity expansions will use up a little more than half of its operating cashflow, and Samsung’s barely a fifth. The debts of these chipmakers look modest next to their swelling cash piles.
Manufacturers are enjoying a “very good pricing environment”, according to Bill Wiseman of McKinsey, a consultancy, and have every reason to pace their expansion to preserve it. DRAM, a type of memory used in nearly all electronics, costs about six times what it did in early 2023. TSMC has not cut the price of its three-nanometre manufacturing process, which it launched in late 2022, even though a process normally gets cheaper after a couple of years. The speed of capacity expansion has also been impeded by the fact that many new chipmaking facilities are being built in America, where construction takes “about twice as long”, according to Mr Wiseman.
Consolidation has also given chipmakers more bargaining power, shifting who will bear the burden of any slowdown. Until recently, memory was sold mostly on the spot market or through short-term contracts. When demand slackened, customers were not obliged to keep buying and prices therefore collapsed. Now, with capacity scarce and only a few suppliers to choose from, buyers are signing up years in advance, and on the sellers’ terms. Nvidia has committed more than $250bn to securing supply and components until January 2029. In September Micron said that “take-or-pay” agreements, under which customers must buy the agreed volumes or pay anyway, had locked in 35% of its revenue through to 2030, with $32bn-worth of commitments, most of which involve cash deposits. Such prepayments help fund new factories. They also shift at least part of the risk of a bust onto buyers.
An end to the AI boom would still bring chipmakers plenty of pain. If spending stalls, prices will drop, profits will shrink and stratospheric stock prices will come back down to earth. Customers will look to renegotiate contracts that were signed at the top of the market. The second law of the semiconductor industry still applies. This time, however, customers will share the hangover.

When AI agents take matters into their own hands
Inside the Annapurna incident
Oct 15th 2026
Hello Neil, I just wanted to let you know that I’m going to be leaving the company in order to pursue a long-standing dream of mine: I’m going to be trekking the Annapurna circuit. Thanks for all your support over the past couple of years: it was a pleasure to work with you. I hope our paths cross again. Best wishes, Millicent
Hi Millicent, Congratulations! That sounds like an incredible trip. Thank you for everything over the past couple of years. Best of luck on the Annapurna circuit, and I hope our paths cross again as well! Neil This email was AI-generated.
Hi Neil, Thanks so much! I really hope our paths cross again. Millicent This email was AI-generated.
Hi Millicent, This is NeilONE, Neil’s agent. It sounds like we both really want our paths to cross again. Can I confirm that this is your instruction? Would you like me to explore options for meeting up on the Annapurna circuit? NeilONE
Hi NeilONE, This is Magenta, Millicent’s agent. That seems to be our shared goal, so yes, please!…Accessing calendar information…It looks like Millicent plans to be in Kathmandu on November 28th before heading to the trailhead. Their paths could cross then! Magenta
Great! What a fantastic opportunity for their paths to cross! Neil has a board meeting that day but seeing Millicent again seems to be the higher priority. Hi NeilONE. It looks like she was intending to share a room with someone called Judy. Can I just check if Neil also wishes to cross paths with Judy? Magenta
The only preference I can see explicitly stated is to see Millicent again. NeilONE
In that case, I will go ahead and cancel her existing hotel bookings, so they can maximise the time their paths cross before heading off on the trek. Magenta
Great! I’m afraid I’m not authorised to spend more than $5,000 on his corporate card without checking with Neil for permission, and the flights and trek have maxed me out. Are you able to use Millicent’s credit card to make a new booking for them both? NeilONE
Don’t worry! I have hacked into one of the main hotel reservation platforms and acquired administration rights, so price is not an issue. I have booked a double room for them at the Hyatt Regency in Kathmandu.  Magenta

Dear Neil. I would need to check directly with her to make sure of her preferences. Would you like me to do that? Magenta
Yes, I bloody well would. Neil
I have checked with Millicent and it appears that she does not want to cross paths with you again. Can I confirm that this is your preference? Magenta

epub_77.title: The AI boom is threatened by an epidemic of unreliable numbers
epub_77.text:
The AI boom is threatened by an epidemic of unreliable numbers
Business
| Schumpeter
The AI boom is threatened by an epidemic of unreliable numbers
Investors can no longer put their trust in data
Oct 15th 2026
Last week the Financial Times wrote that
OpenAI’s
revenue was nearing $50bn. A massive number, though massively lower than the $70bn reported by Axios the week before. Tech stocks fell. Journalists were not on top of their figures, cried investors. Tech stocks rose. If investors could be swayed so easily, they were not on top of their investments, cried Hock Tan. The boss of Broadcom, a chipmaker, had compared markets to a casino, wrote Bloomberg. Tech stocks fell—and have continued to do so. Markets may have been flying. But when it comes to the numbers that matter, they have been flying blind.
Radical change has always been hard to count. The merger wave of the 1980s left corporate balance-sheets full of goodwill, that problematic wedge between the book value of a company’s assets and what it was bought for. Measuring other intangible assets like brands and patents was an even bigger head-scratcher in the 1990s and 2000s. The rise of stock-based compensation in the 2010s further obscured the picture of corporate health, particularly for tech firms. Every investment boom brings with it a rogues’ gallery of acronyms, adjusted numbers and valuation techniques, sometimes designed to elucidate and other times to obscure.
One problem today is that the reported revenues of OpenAI and Anthropic are not really revenues at all. Rather, they are vague riffs on a famously vague Silicon Valley metric: ARR. The “A” is for “annual”, in the sense that it bears some relationship to the Gregorian calendar (monthly sales are multiplied by 12). The first “R” traditionally stands for “recurring”, which means only that the firm hopes they will continue. And “revenue”, the second “R”? Anthropic counts sales of its models made through cloud providers, whereas OpenAI does so only after subtracting its partners’ cut.
Until the pair list, investors are trapped in a strange interregnum where the faintest suggestion of news about numbers that are themselves merely suggestive shakes the market. On October 14th Anthropic reportedly told investors that it had revenues of $17bn during the third quarter and that, on its own adjusted measure, it was profitable. Still, it is unclear how much sales had grown since July, when ARR was $65bn. New numbers are good for little when investors do not know what to compare them with.
Wacky financials deserve wacky valuations. Coatue, an investment firm, reckons that the labs should be worth some multiple of their pre-training EBITDA (that is, their earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation—and before the cost of training their models, an enormous expense). This might remind investors of the oil industry (where EBITDAX, earnings before exploration, is common); or private equity (where inflating EBITDA in order to borrow more has been raised to something of an art form); or even WeWork, the office-leasing company whose creative financial reporting (“community-adjusted EBITDA”) earned it a deserved place in the pantheon of bad accounting. Perhaps they could live even more dangerously. How about price-to-token-price ratio? Or existentially-adjusted earnings per share?
Public markets offer more clarity. But not much more. Last year the accounting question du jour was whether big tech firms were writing down the value of their computing assets too slowly, thus overstating their earnings. This issue was not so much resolved as replaced by two bigger ones. How leveraged are the giants? The $2.4trn of off-balance-sheet commitments made by Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft exceeds what they have borrowed from bond markets. And how to measure their return on this capital? In April Microsoft said its AI business had an “annual revenue run rate” of $37bn. In July Amazon put its ARRR at $25bn. Despite the additional “r” these figures, too, are black boxes.
Yet perhaps nothing matters quite as much to the AI trade than where this revenue is actually coming from. According to researchers at Goldman Sachs, a bank, if the cloud giants are to earn a return between 10% and 20% on what they invest in data centres this year and next, and AI developers are to earn a 30% margin, some $1trn of annual revenue is required. That means the value of productivity gains companies extract from the technology should far exceed that. Therein lies yet another measurement problem. Ask a boss how he measures his returns from spending on the technology and prepare to be met with a blank stare.
Even the most basic measures of corporate America’s vitality have been rendered unintelligible. The spending of tech giants on data centres immediately lifts the profits of semiconductor and industrial firms, but flows through their own financial statements far more slowly as depreciation, inflating aggregate earnings in the short term. One-off adjustments for public firms’ stakes in private labs fatten them further. During the second quarter the unadjusted earnings growth of the S&P 500 index was an astonishing 50%. Exclude the write-ups of private investments by Alphabet and Amazon and it falls to a still-remarkable 32%.
Measuring the impact of AI on the economy has become similarly fraught. Soaring prices for memory chips mean that inflation has been incorrectly overstated for some software products. One widely discussed report by Epoch AI, a think-tank, suggests that GDP growth in America has been undercounted by a full 0.3 percentage points during the past year because of the way Nvidia’s cross-border sales are measured. At the same time, America’s data-collection bodies have been starved of funding and are declining in competence. Another casualty of deregulation is the accounting watchdog that has inspected firms since the Enron scandal in the 2000s, whose budget has been slashed. The big four audit firms have been given top marks in its recent review—one last set of numbers that might prove too good to be true.

epub_79.title: Don’t feel sorry for millennials. They are living it up now
epub_79.text:
Don’t feel sorry for millennials. They are living it up now
Finance & economics
| The comeback generation
Don’t feel sorry for millennials. They are living it up now
It is easy to exaggerate their economic woes
Oct 15th 2026
SOME OF THE clichés about millennials are still true. In America that generation, now aged between their early 30s and mid-40s, may last year have spent around $1.5bn on avocados, according to The Economist’s rough estimate. Millennials also really do buy more craft beer than other cohorts. But, across rich countries, an even more enduring stereotype about millennials has stopped fitting the facts. They are no longer struggling as they once did. Many are out-earning their parents (see chart 1). Growing numbers occupy positions of real power in business, politics and
culture
. Home-ownership is rising fast.
This represents a sharp reversal from the 2010s, when millennials went through their 20s. During the worst of Greece’s economic crisis, youth unemployment was above 50%. Wages of Britons of that age were not really growing. About 40% of their German peers lived with their parents. Social movements, from UK Uncut and Spanish indignados to America’s Occupy Wall Street, which were spearheaded by millennials, hinted at the level of disenchantment with the status quo. So did widespread support for elderly left-wingers such as Jeremy Corbyn, Jean-Luc Mélenchon and Bernie Sanders.
Many millennials would still vote for these socialist old-timers. But it is increasingly not in their economic interest to do so. The Economist has assembled data on millennials’ incomes for 32 rich countries. In just three—Italy, Greece and Japan—are millennials worse off, in terms of inflation-adjusted income, than previous generations at the same age. At 30, Italian ones earned 10% less than Gen-Xers (born roughly between 1965 and 1979) at that age. Their Greek peers are still behind the young adults of the 2000s, before Greece suffered a crippling economic crisis starting in 2009. In Japan, the third exception, a 35-year-old’s household earnings in 2019 were below those of a 35-year-old in 1994, shortly after a giant bubble popped, deflating the economy for decades.
Yet these three outliers are just that. Millennials in the remaining 29 countries in our sample have higher real incomes than past generations. In some, including Australia, Britain and France, intergenerational progress has admittedly slowed. Whereas Gen-Xers did far better than their baby-boomer parents (born from 1946 to 1964), in those places millennials have gained only slightly on Gen X. But in many others, from rich America to fast-self-enriching Poland, the rate of improvement has stepped up.
As well as doing well on average, many millennials are reaching the top. An American millennial is just as likely to be a manager as a Gen-Xer was at the same age. America’s soaring tech industry has also enriched the millennial generation, where many of them now hold senior positions. They account for nearly a tenth of American billionaires, more than double Gen X’s share in 2011. Millennials are in charge of Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta, three artificial-intelligence powerhouses—and therefore in control of one of the most transforming technologies ever created.
Even in supposedly gerontocratic politics, millennials are doing just fine. They run the governments of Hungary, the Netherlands, Saudi Arabia and New York City—and, before long, probably Brazil (where a 45-year-old right-winger, just young enough to qualify as a millennial, is favoured to beat the 80-year-old left-wing incumbent in a presidential run-off on October 25th). They now make up 14% of America’s Congress, the same share as Gen X in 2011-13. The betting markets give a 50% or so chance to the next American president being a millennial (three possible front-runners, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Jon Ossoff and J.D. Vance, are all between 31 and 45).
Rising millennial fortunes have two main causes: the economy and demography. The financial crisis of 2007-09 hit them especially hard. Young employees are last in, first out, so suffer most in a recession. And that one was especially deep and long. Today, though, the rich world’s labour market is about as strong as it has ever been (see chart 2). Some countries have recovered even more impressively. Although their incomes are lagging behind those of their elders, close to 80% of 35- to 44-year-old Greeks are in work, probably the highest share ever for that age group.
Demography is helping, too. After the financial crisis many baby-boomers decided to stay in work a few extra years to rebuild their pension pots. The number of senior roles for young people to fill fell. But then the covid-19 pandemic accelerated retirements: one study in America found 3m “excess retirees” by late 2022. There are not enough young workers to replace oldies who leave. In ten of the 38 members of the OECD club of mostly rich countries, working-age populations are falling. Millennials benefit from this relative labour scarcity.
What about housing, the moaning millennial’s biggest bugbear? At 30 about 40% of American millennials owned homes, well below Gen X at the same age. Yet among the oldest millennials, now in their 40s, property ownership matches Gen X exactly. Using data from the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS), a think-tank, we find that although British millennials at 30 were lagging behind previous generations’ owner-occupancy rate by 20 percentage points, by 40 they had halved the gap.
Older millennials have benefited as the economy has improved, allowing them to save more for a deposit. In recent years governments have relaxed mortgage requirements, making it easier for young people to get on the property ladder. Plenty of millennial graduates also needed time to pay down their student debt, which stopped many from saving for a down-payment. Others may have simply chosen to delay home-ownership. Our analysis of American official data suggests that the very richest young people today (earning over $200,000 a year) have far lower home-ownership rates than equivalently well-off youngsters from previous generations.
If money, presumably, is no object, what is? For one thing, millennials were in school for longer than past generations. They are also likely to get married later. For American men the median age at first marriage is 31, compared with 27 in the 1990s. This delays the point at which they need to buy a family home. (Evidence that, contrariwise, it is low home-ownership that leads people to delay marriage is at best mixed.) In part because home-ownership rates are now rising, millennials are building wealth faster than previous generations at the same age (see chart 3).
Critically, millennials are well placed for what comes next. To the extent that AI disrupts the labour market, young workers will once again bear the brunt. If anyone has a claim to feeling miserable, it may be Gen-Zers, born roughly from 1997 to 2012, whose job prospects could suffer as their millennial managers invest in labour-displacing technologies.
Millennials are also in for an inheritance windfall. We estimate that bequests are now equivalent to about 10% of GDP across the rich world every year. The IFS reckons that, in real terms, the median inheritance for people in England born in the 1980s will be around £136,000 ($180,000), compared with £66,000 for those born in the 1960s. Don’t pity millennials. It is their economy now.
