Another warning sign for China’s economy: falling consumer credit
Finance & economics
| Loan dangers
Another warning sign for China’s economy: falling consumer credit
A crackdown on aggressive debt collectors is good news and bad news
Oct 15th 2026
CHINA’s FRUGAL citizens are getting more so. Lending to households has been shrinking for most of the year. Short-term loans to consumers fell by 8.3% in September compared with the year before, the steepest drop on record. In August the stock of consumer loans was the lowest since China’s harsh “zero-covid” lockdowns (see chart). During a public holiday at the start of October the typical merrymaker spent 2% less than in the same festive period in 2025. China’s retailers have the right to feel disappointed. So does the government, which has been trying to loosen households’ purse-strings since the pandemic.
The Chinese are borrowing less in part because of the prolonged property crash. A collapse in house sales means fewer mortgage applications. Many homebuyers pay back their mortgages early if they can. Given that a home loan is the biggest that most people take out, this prudence has put paid to a rise in households’ indebtedness that had lasted for decades. The ratio of their debt to GDP hit 60% in 2020 and stayed flat until last year, when it declined slightly. (In rich countries as a whole, the ratio is just shy of 70%.)
Yet that does not explain the decline in consumer credit. This may have little to do with shoppers’ frugality—or with the government’s. In a belated effort to boost domestic consumption, last year the ministry of finance began handing out subsidies to banks that let them charge lower interest on consumer loans for big-ticket items such as new cars and home renovations.
Even so, banks are growing more reluctant to extend such loans. And who can blame them? Chinese borrowers appear to be getting riskier. More than 10% of adults may have had unpaid debts last year, up from less than 8% the year before, calculates Gavekal, a consultancy.
The subsidy may be making lenders even warier. When the average Zhou struggles to pay back loans, interest rates on consumer credit should rise, to offset the higher risk to banks, rather than fall. Since refusing the government’s largesse is unwise in China, banks end up underpricing the risk to their loan books. To keep that risk in check, they are screening out more borderline borrowers.
Another reason for banks’ increased risk-aversion is the difficulty of offloading bad consumer debts. They often seek to free up their balance-sheets by selling such sour assets to investors with a higher risk tolerance. These investors pay the banks a fraction of the loans’ face value and then try to recover the full amount from borrowers, which often involves pestering them until they cough up. In early 2021 the average price banks could fetch for overdue consumer loans was around 30% of face value, decent for debts already known to be troubled. By early 2026 that figure had collapsed to 5%.
This is a worrying trend. It seems to indicate that once consumer loans are delinquent, fewer borrowers have any intention of paying them back. And that, in turn, may be the unintended consequence of a government policy that is otherwise welcome—a crackdown on gang-like debt-collection agencies that have been terrorising debtors for years.
China’s debt collectors are certainly a fearsome bunch. With few rules or industry guidelines, small collection companies have often resorted to what the Chinese refer to as “soft violence” in order to retrieve overdue consumer loans and credit-card debts. Common tactics include “calling you to death”, shorthand for ringing debtors, their families and friends hundreds of times a day; releasing credit histories to loved ones or employers; and even creating obscene images that are sent to debtors’ acquaintances. Collectors would often show up on debtors’ doorsteps in the middle of the night.
Such intimidation can have tragic consequences. Stories of debtors who have taken their own lives as a result of it have become common in recent years. The authorities have previously tried to curb loan collectors’ excesses with lawsuits against the worst offenders. This year they went a step further, putting in place national rules to stop bad behaviour. Starting in August the collectors can place no more than six phone calls a day to debtors. They are also barred from contacting family and friends, and from making home visits in the small hours. All interactions between the collectors and debtors must be recorded.
Some analysts have started to connect the steep discounts on consumer-debt sales with the crackdown on collections. The new regulations are meant to protect borrowers from harassment. A side-effect may be fewer borrowers for the collectors to harass in the first place.

A shortage of sulphur could hurt mines and farms everywhere
Finance & economics
| Gunfire and brimstone
A shortage of sulphur could hurt mines and farms everywhere
Another commodity shock from the Iran war
Oct 15th 2026
FOR WEEKS the hottest topic in commodity markets has been the soaring price of diesel. The cause is not a shortage of crude but of refineries able to turn oil into fuel: most Gulf facilities remain cut off from global markets by the war in Iran and many Russian ones are offline owing to Ukrainian strikes. That squeeze has a quieter side-effect. Sulphur, a vital input for mining, farming and chipmaking, is a by-product of fuel production. So it, too, is in short supply. The damage around the world is only beginning to show.
Whereas the global energy system entered 2026 with ample fuel stocks, sulphur markets were tight before the Iran war. Russia had banned exports to preserve supplies for its fertiliser and mining firms, cutting shipments from 4.8m tonnes in 2025—15% of globally traded volumes—to 1.8m tonnes in 2026 so far. Houthi attacks on the Red Sea route used by some Saudi exports and the threat of American tariffs on Canada have not helped. In February Middle Eastern solid bulk sulphur fetched $500 a tonne, up from $340 a year ago (see chart, top panel).
The Hormuz crisis has exacerbated this shortfall. The strait’s closure trapped nearly a quarter of global sulphur production, and half of seaborne exports, in the Gulf. Shipments rebounded in June, when a deal between America and Iran freed cargoes stuck amid the fighting, but fell back again when the ceasefire broke down in July. They remain two-thirds below pre-war levels, notes Ishan Bhanu of Kpler, a data firm (see chart, bottom panel).
Loadings from ports on the Red Sea and Oman’s coast are no higher than before the war, implying little rerouting. Trucking sulphur across the desert is no alternative: a single 30,000-tonne shipment would need around 1,000 lorries. Moreover, existing fleets are mostly built for molten sulphur, a liquid, not the solid kind that bulk carriers ferry. Amba Coombe of Argus Media, a price-reporting agency, expects Middle Eastern exports to fall below 11m tonnes in 2026, from 20.5m tonnes in 2025.
Vanishing Gulf flows have led more producers to restrict exports. Besides Russia, which has extended its ban, India, Kazakhstan and Turkey suspended shipments after the war began. Many restrictions remain in force; despite higher shipments from America and Canada, non-Gulf exports are still 40% below pre-war levels.
Reduced supplies pushed prices of sulphur cargoes from many regions past $1,000 a tonne in June, a record. They have come down a little since, not because supply has risen but because such high prices have crushed demand outside China. Chinese demand has fallen even faster, though for a different reason. The country used to import sulphur, convert it into acid and re-export it, accounting for more than 40% of globally traded volumes last year. In May, however, the government banned acid exports; they are now practically at zero.
Of the buyers, chipmakers are the least affected: they need only tiny amounts of acid. Copper and nickel miners, by contrast, use loads of it to leach metal from ore. Copper producers in Chile and Africa can pay up thanks to the high prices the red metal commands. Indonesian nickel miners, which are exporting their cheap product to the world, are in a tighter spot. Their production costs have risen while their customers—mostly Chinese makers of batteries for electric cars—maintain enough stock and market power to keep nickel prices down. In Indonesia sulphur purchases are down by 75% and miners have brought forward maintenance.
The blow is hardest for producers of phosphate fertilisers: making ten tonnes of the stuff requires about four tonnes of sulphur. Many firms cut output at first, halting or slowing down plants in America, Brazil, Egypt and Morocco. In May Mosaic, a Florida-based firm, described the sulphur crunch as the industry’s most severe since 2008. Many producers then shifted their product mix towards sulphur-sparing variants that deliver fewer nutrients. That, together with the depletion of stockpiles, has helped keep fertiliser exports at decent levels. But prices have surged.
New capacity is due to come online in China and India, but not in time to ease the current crunch. Emerging substitutes for elemental sulphur remain more energy- and capital-intensive. In the short run relief can come only from a resumption of flows from the Gulf, where most of the world’s new projects were planned before the war. “The global market is now seeing sulphur as a strategic commodity rather than a by-product,” Ms Coombe says. One by-product of the Iran war is that the list of strategic commodities is lengthening.

epub_82.title: How Ukraine’s biggest bank is run in a war zone
epub_82.text:
How Ukraine’s biggest bank is run in a war zone
Finance & economics
| A creditable enterprise
How Ukraine’s biggest bank is run in a war zone
PrivatBank is a case study in adaptation
Oct 15th 2026
ONE TUESDAY, recounts Mikael Bjorknert, the chief executive of PrivatBank, a customer called: a maker of cooling equipment whose factory had just been destroyed in a Russian attack. Instead of defaulting on its loan, the company asked: “Can you wait until Friday?” Helped by a repayment holiday from PrivatBank, Ukraine’s largest lender, it found another home quickly (an old installation with a roof but no internal walls), kept its workers on and bought used kit from competitors. Production restarted within three months. Another year on, the bank is considering a new loan for investment.
The tale of the fridge factory is but one illustration of both the peculiarities of running a bank in a war zone and Ukrainians’ remarkable resilience against a ruthless enemy. Mr Bjorknert, a Swede who has run state-owned PrivatBank since January 2025, says that just 2.9% of its core loans were non-performing in the first half of 2026, a ratio he expects to fall to 2.6% by the end of the year. (Around 2% is typical in the peaceful part of Europe; at the peak of Greece’s banking crisis in 2016-17, almost half of loans were duff.) “The payment ethic”, he says, “is very strong.”
So is PrivatBank’s, when it comes to keeping its 1,000-plus branches open. They may, like other businesses, be closed during missile or drone strikes. But closing them at other times, for want of power or connectivity, say, could be interpreted by Ukrainians as a signal that something bad is afoot. To avoid unnecessarily spooking the people, PrivatBank’s outlets are backed up by batteries, generators and Starlink internet connections.
PrivatBank was taken into public ownership in 2016 with a $5.5bn hole in its books, amid allegations of fraud. Only last year did Ukraine’s Supreme Court finally dismiss an attempt by its former owner, Ihor Kolomoisky (who denied wrongdoing), to overturn the nationalisation. Politicians and central bankers have said they would like to see PrivatBank and other lenders reprivatised. If Ukraine is to join the European Union, eventually that will be expected. Mr Bjorknert says PrivatBank’s corporate governance now reflects international standards (for instance, with separate supervisory and management boards). But with war still raging, privatisation will have to wait.
Mr Bjorknert explains that his task is to turn what is chiefly a retail bank, with 18.1m individual customers—almost half the pre-war population—and 945,000 business clients into a universal lender ready for Ukraine’s reconstruction and for European regulation. Progress is impressive: the bank’s loan book grew by 40% in 2025 (around 30% after adjusting for inflation) and at a similar rate in the first half of this year. Growth may continue. Despite Russia’s intensifying attacks on energy infrastructure, ports and much more, the IMF maintained its forecasts for GDP to rise by 1% this year and 3.5% next in its latest outlook, published on October 12th.
Those attacks will yet take a toll in a fifth winter of full-scale war. And whatever comes next, Ukraine’s financial infrastructure is far from fit. “The construction and mortgage markets need clearer rules,” Mr Bjorknert says. “Ukraine also needs a well-functioning domestic capital market.” Reconstruction will require hundreds of billions of dollars, most of them foreign. Ukrainian banks are too small for such a torrent. With assets of 925bn hryvnia (around $20bn), PrivatBank would rank only fourth in Slovakia, a much smaller neighbour.
Foreign banks are sure to be part of the answer. Several have stayed in Ukraine since Russia invaded, and others may be tempted to enter once durable peace returns. But after years of war in a country that has yet to shake off its reputation for corruption, they will need not only sturdy balance-sheets, but also nerves of steel.

epub_83.title: How to lose money betting against Europe
epub_83.text:
How to lose money betting against Europe
Finance & economics
| Buttonwood
How to lose money betting against Europe
In a sovereign-debt crisis, even understanding politics may not be enough
Oct 15th 2026
“THE EURO is like a bumblebee,” noted Mario Draghi, former boss of the European Central Bank (ECB), in 2012. “This is a mystery of nature because it shouldn’t fly but instead it does.” Mr Draghi was a better central banker than entomologist. In the same speech, he vowed to do “whatever it takes to preserve the euro”, a pledge that ended the acute phase of the crisis that had roiled the currency union for three years.
The recent sell-off of French government debt, amid protests in the streets and a yawning hole in the budget, might bring back unhappy memories of the tumult. In early October the yield on ten-year bonds was 1.6 percentage points above that on equivalent German bunds, the widest gap since 2011. When borrowing costs in the euro zone drift apart, it is a reminder of the currency union’s aerodynamic deficiencies.
Europe does not yet face the kind of existential distress of a decade and a half ago. But that near-death experience holds lessons for speculators thinking of betting against wobbly European bonds. Many traders learned the hard way that politics can win out over economics. And even understanding the politics is no guarantee of making money.
Some investors were poorly positioned for the political turning-point in the euro crisis. Days before Mr Draghi’s pivotal speech John Paulson, an American investment titan, was telling clients that he saw a 50% chance that the currency union would shatter. When it did not, his main funds booked double-digit losses that year.
Mr Paulson was not alone. At the time, more than 70% of investors expected an economy to leave the euro zone within 12 months, according to Sentix, a data provider. In the event, troubled countries such as Greece, Ireland and Portugal were willing to bear enormous economic pain to remain in the club, while the rest bent its rules to help them. Fund managers who were right about the economics badly misjudged the politics.
Yet political foresight may not have been enough. A piece of trading folklore states that some traders lose money even with knowledge of tomorrow’s news. In 2023 Victor Haghani and James White of Elm Wealth, an advisory firm, showed there was truth to the adage. They offered 118 graduate students in finance and business the opportunity to make bets on American Treasuries and the stock market with access to the front page of the next day’s Wall Street Journal. The players guessed which way assets would move only 52% of the time.
Some investors who were convinced early in the last crisis that the euro zone would keep bumbling along had their own wings clipped before the bloc landed on a fix. Jon Corzine, a former governor of New Jersey, led MF Global into bankruptcy, largely owing to the broker’s leveraged bets on European sovereign debt. In a congressional grilling after the firm’s collapse, Mr Corzine said he had thought Europe “would take much more forceful steps to avoid bankruptcy or insolvency”. His logic was eventually shown to be sound: none of the bonds ever defaulted. But the intervening decline in their value as collateral was enough to send MF Global to the wall.
Today’s French sell-off has so far been orderly, in contrast to the chaos of 2009-12. It has not infected the country’s euro-zone neighbours too much. And nothing suggests the return of the “doom loop”, where governments borrowed to bail out failing banks, and banks failed because that borrowing depressed the value of the government bonds they held in spades. Share prices of European banks are down in the past month but up by 10-15% this year, after hitting two-decade highs this summer.
France, though, may yet test this orderliness to destruction. In 2027 the presidential race could end in a contest between Marine Le Pen, a populist right-winger who promises, unaffordably, to stop the pension age from rising, and Jean-Luc Mélenchon, a leftist who has threatened a selective debt default.
In such circumstances a wise investor may wish to emulate Alan Howard, co-founder of Brevan Howard, a big hedge fund. In December 2011 Mr Howard explained that betting on the outcome of the euro-zone crisis was a gamble he was “particularly careful to avoid”. Its resolution would ultimately be “a political decision” that his firm had “no real edge in understanding”, he noted. Mr Draghi was wrong about bumblebees: scientists do understand their flight. The euro zone’s volatile trajectory makes for a much harder study.

epub_84.title: A Nobel prize for how to keep economies on even keel
epub_84.text:
A Nobel prize for how to keep economies on even keel
Finance & economics
| Free Exchange
A Nobel prize for how to keep economies on even keel
Two “New Keynesians”, Robert Hall and Michael Woodford, win the highest honour in economics
Oct 15th 2026
How to stabilise an unstable economy? In much of the 20th century the Keynesians, followers of John Maynard Keynes, argued that the government could manage the overall level of demand. That would prevent a repeat of the mass unemployment of the Great Depression in the 1930s. The monetarists, led by Milton Friedman, retorted that the best approach was to fix the money supply. Attempts to boost employment would inevitably lead to ever-rising prices, as in the Great Inflation of the 1970s.
Nowadays most central bankers would place themselves in a third camp, known as New Keynesians. On October 12th the Nobel memorial prize, the top gong in economics, was awarded to two of that movement’s leading lights. The glory (and SKr12m, or $1.2m) will be shared by two Americans, Robert Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University. Mr Hall is best known for his theory of consumer spending and Mr Woodford for modelling how central banks could use interest rates as the main tool to keep the economy steady.
The prize committee credited the duo with rebuilding macroeconomics on “microfoundations”: representing economic outcomes as the result of the behaviour of individuals and businesses. That was an intellectual break from the past. The Keynesians and monetarists built their models top-down, looking at how those aggregates, in the form of economic statistics, influenced each other (how the total volume of money changed the rate of inflation, say). New Keynesians tried to rebuild the models bottom-up from individual decision-making. This followed a critique by Robert Lucas, the Nobel laureate in 1995, that any model not based on the deep features of an economy would be a poor guide for policymakers.
For Mr Hall this meant examining how consumers choose to spend their money. In his model they have views about their future income. Will they get a pay rise? Is a sudden windfall just a passing bit of luck? Because they care about tomorrow as well as today, they “smooth” spending and react to changes in what they see as their lifetime spending power. Track a person’s consumption over time and it should resemble a drunk walking home, randomly straying hither and thither—in response to unforeseen jolts—but staggering in the same general direction.
Mr Woodford looked to Knut Wicksell, a Swedish economist at the turn of the 20th century (he calls his theories “neo-Wicksellian” rather than New Keynesian). Wicksell started from a model of a “pure credit economy” in which all money is created by banks making lending decisions. If interest rates were below a “natural” rate of return on investment, businesses would keep borrowing, leading to an inflationary boom. If rates were above this level, that would cause a deflationary cycle. Rather than fine-tune the economy, as the old-style Keynesians suggested, or the money supply, central banks should strive to bring interest rates in line with this natural rate of return. This rate would emerge not from their choices but from things like technological progress and savers’ willingness to wait to see their investments pay off.
Mr Woodford’s book, “Interest and Prices”, became the bible for many modern central bankers. It built a model of the economy using ideas such as “sticky prices” (the notion that firms do not adjust how much they charge consumers too often) and “imperfect competition” (which allows prices to be sticky). Its publication in 2003 coincided with neither a Depression nor a Great Inflation but with the Great Moderation, a happy spell of low inflation, steady growth and reduced economic volatility.
There are niggles. The natural rate of return can shift in short order: a boom in investment for a new technology can raise demand for capital (as is happening with artificial intelligence), calling for a higher neutral rate of interest. And this neutral rate cannot be observed. Jerome Powell, a former chairman of the Federal Reserve, once quipped that central bankers could only “know it by its works”. Nor do the models account for the financial sector or the influence of interest rates on investors’ tolerance for risky bets. The Great Moderation ended in the financial crisis of 2008.
Mr Hall’s model of consumption, too, presents problems. Rational forward-looking consumers ought to change their spending patterns only in response to unexpected news about their lifetime income, and save sudden windfalls (like covid stimulus cheques) lest they are offset by some future sudden costs. In reality, people often overreact to windfalls and underreact to persistent economic changes. And random “shocks” may in fact carry useful information: a one-off prize, like the Nobel, might presage a future of lucrative speaking gigs, for instance. Even for prize-winning economists, it can be hard to extract the signal from the noise.
The Nobel arrives as Mr Woodford’s framework comes under new theoretical pressure. The neo-Wicksellian advice to central banks is to communicate in advance what they would do in response to a boom or bust. The market can then anticipate interest rates in real time—and it can do so better the more a central bank reveals about its “reaction function”. Yet the Fed’s new chair, Kevin Warsh, worries that this leads to a “hall of mirrors” in which markets watch the central bank and the central bank watches markets. A bit of uncertainty about how rates change is good, he argues.
Then there is the new economic reality. Central bankers are coping with supply-side shocks from a pandemic to wars in Ukraine and now Iran. High debt burdens in rich countries raise the spectre of interest rates being used to manage the cost of borrowing rather than inflation. Rate-setters must make uncomfortable decisions about how much inflation and joblessness to tolerate in order to keep the economy stable. New Keynesian theory is one thing; the practice of political economy is quite another.

epub_86.title: AI companies want to become frontier scientific researchers
epub_86.text:
AI companies want to become frontier scientific researchers
Science & technology
| Lab work
AI companies want to become frontier scientific researchers
Better AI models may be their reward
Oct 15th 2026
SIR DEMIS HASSABIS says he started Google DeepMind to create “the ultimate tool for science”. In the years since, DeepMind’s research has graced the cover of Nature nine times. At the beginning that was for breakthroughs in AI itself, but its more recent successes have come from applying AI to other areas of scientific endeavour. Its protein-folding model AlphaFold, for example, earned Sir Demis a share of a Nobel prize in 2024.
DeepMind’s peers are catching up. This autumn, OpenAI reshaped the terrain of mathematics, first by
solving a landmark Millennium Prize problem
and then by publishing solutions to more than 300 open questions in a single day. Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s boss, declared in September that the company had discovered a potential successor to CRISPR, a gene-editing technique, using its Claude model, promising that AI-powered biology is on an “exponential trend”.
Smaller companies are joining in: in 2024 Sakana AI, a Tokyo-based research group, unveiled an “AI scientist” which its creators claimed could complete all the tasks required to write a scientific paper. In a peer-reviewed article published in Nature this March, Sakana reported that the AI scientist wrote a paper which passed the first round of peer review for a top-tier AI conference—a hurdle which defeated almost a third of the human-written papers.
Such work was initially welcomed by the broader scientific establishment. But the growing pace of AI-powered discovery has put many on edge. Part of what unnerves researchers is the extent to which AI companies are not merely providing a tool for discovery but choosing to wield it themselves. This is unusual: AI companies are content to sell their services to everyone from accountancies to media outlets without operating in those industries themselves. Why, then, is the situation so different with science?
What the labs say implies that they see pushing the frontiers of science as simply a good thing to be doing—or, more cynically, a good thing to be seen doing. Much of the scientific work at the biggest AI companies is promoted as research for its own sake. Sir Demis’s lofty goals came about, he told The Economist, because he wanted “to understand what’s going on here in the universe”. Practical applications, as for all good scientists, were almost secondary.
DeepMind’s peers echo the message. “We just genuinely care about this endeavour,” says Mark Chen, OpenAI’s chief research officer, dismissing accusations that the company’s scientific efforts are corporate philanthropy. Many of the company’s researchers were scientists or mathematicians before moving to the corporate sector, says Mr Chen, and they still yearn for the beauty of a new discovery.
The prospect of profit doesn’t hurt, though. Isomorphic Labs, a spin-out of DeepMind founded by Sir Demis, is the exemplar. The company seeks to use DeepMind’s technology to develop novel therapies for cancers, as well as cardiovascular and immune conditions. It has developed its own technology,
an updated version of AlphaFold 3
, with the ability to do for biochemical reactions what its predecessor did for protein folding. If the gambit pays off, then Isomorphic will begin to show a financial return as its candidate molecules, of which it has 17 under development, begin to be turned into real medicines by pharmaceutical companies around the world.
Praise and profits, strong motives though they are, are only part of the story. The real reason AI labs are so keen to invest in science is probably because it is the best way to improve their models.
In the early days of large language models (LLMs), scientific aptitude was one of the benchmarks used to test how models surpassed their predecessors. But that test was no trickier than a high-school science quiz. Today’s best models, by contrast, are capable of handling postgraduate level questions, scoring a little over 50% on “humanity’s last exam”, a quiz spanning all domains designed to be as hard as a knowledge-based test can be (see chart).
This rapid progress means AI labs are running out of data on which to test their models. The logical next step is for AI models to do novel research themselves. “Science and mathematics”, says Pushmeet Kohli, the head of Google DeepMind’s science team, “act as the playground, the grand challenges that we give to AI to drive innovation.”
Unsolved questions in mathematics are particularly valuable, since any answers models find can be formally proven and verified. The frontier of AI development relies on a technique known as “reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards”—labs train AI models by giving them tasks in domains which have objectively correct answers, and reward them for success. There has been speculation that OpenAI’s latest dump of maths papers may be the by-product of one such training run. “Provide a formal proof of this unsolved problem” could be the hardest verifiable challenge humanity has to offer.
Pushing models to be world-leading in mathematics, however, does not necessarily mean they will be more competent at other tasks. Churning through scientific problems may make the intelligence of AI systems still more “jagged”, meaning they show superhuman potential in some domains while making laughable errors in others (if less frequently than they once did). Whether AI models with scientific ultra-smarts go on to develop general competency is an “existential” question, according to one company insider, with ramifications for the future of humanity.
There are reasons to think the intelligence of models trained this way may be less jagged than expected. Mr Chen, of OpenAI, invokes the “bitter lesson” of AI science: that bigger, architecturally simpler systems turn out to be better than ones with baroque additions designed to aid specialisation. According to Rich Sutton, the AI researcher who first used the phrase, AI systems in domains from chess to speech recognition got better once researchers stopped trying to dictate how their models should approach the task.
Recent work bears that out. Preliminary research led by Yong Liu from Shanghai Jiao Tong University found that training systems—without micromanagement—to fold proteins appears to make them better at everything else, too. A version of Alibaba’s open-source Qwen AI trained on questions and answers related to protein folding displayed improved capabilities in such areas as spatial, graph, scientific and general reasoning.
The upshot is that OpenAI is, Mr Chen says, “bitter lesson-pilled”: the company has bet big that the best way to build a model for any one task is to build a model that can handle all tasks. Not everyone agrees. DeepMind, for example, has had success developing specialised models, not least AlphaFold.
But the bitter lesson is coming for it, too. The company’s “co-scientist”, released in May, is a general system, using multiple instances of its Gemini chatbot to generate new hypotheses, ponder them internally, and improve them. This struck many as being a pivot from the company’s prior approach. (The tool was released shortly before Sir Demis moved into a new role as chief scientist of Alphabet, DeepMind and Google’s parent company.) Dr Kohli characterises the changes as an expansion of its scientific work.
If the bitter lesson continues to hold, it could reshape scientific endeavour. Building a small, focused machine-learning system is within the scope of many researchers. An AI-powered supernova detector, for instance, took “just 15,000 examples and the computing power of my laptop” to train, according to Héloïse Stevance, a physicist at Oxford University. But building a frontier LLM takes terabytes of data, and a server farm’s worth of compute—enough to render it out of reach of all but a few of the richest companies in the world.
And better models might offer a prize that is worth throwing capital towards. A good AI scientist may also prove to be good at developing better AI systems. Making model training more efficient and AI chips less power-hungry are goals upon which companies from Sakana to DeepMind have set their sights. Jack Clark, a co-founder of Anthropic, predicts that this task will be fully within the capabilities of AI systems by 2028. A future of AI scientists making more AI scientists beckons.

epub_87.title: AI’s transformation of mathematics is a turning point for science
epub_87.text:
AI’s transformation of mathematics is a turning point for science
Science & technology
| The end of mathematics?
AI’s transformation of mathematics is a turning point for science
Other disciplines should take heed
Oct 15th 2026
“SOMETIMES PEOPLE have the wrong idea of maths and think that it will be overtaken by computers,” said the mathematician Alain Connes in 2000. He was describing why a team of esteemed mathematicians were offering $1m rewards for solutions to seven intractable mathematical conundrums. These Millennium Prize problems, said Dr Connes, “are totally inaccessible to computers”.
But computers got better. In early September OpenAI, an American firm, claimed one of its internal AI models had solved a Millennium Prize problem: the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, which relates to the motion of fluids. It was only the second of the lot to be conquered and the first to fall to a machine. Mathematicians had been wrestling with this one for at least a century. The AI solved it in 88 hours.
Then came what Álvaro Lozano-Robledo, a mathematician at the University of Connecticut, has called “possibly the single most important day in the history of mathematics thus far”. On October 6th OpenAI released a torrent of 719 papers detailing solutions the same model had found to at least 372 other long-standing open problems. No field of research has ever experienced an event like it.
Many mathematicians are not celebrating. “The shock is immense,” wrote Hugo Duminil-Copin, a mathematician at the University of Geneva, who won a Fields Medal (maths’ most distinguished prize) in 2022. “I am paralysed.” In a statement published soon after the Navier-Stokes announcement—and since endorsed by more than 8,000 researchers—Dr Duminil-Copin and 27 fellow Fields medallists described the situation as a “severe misalignment of AI in mathematics”. They worry about the risks posed by solutions divorced from human understanding. Left unchecked, says Martin Hairer of EPFL in Lausanne, Switzerland, another signatory, AI would “sterilise the field”.
That AI’s mathematical breakthroughs have prompted such reactions is, on its face, odd. Having answers to long-standing questions is an advance for humanity. Mathematicians also have a vested interest in resisting disruption to their careers. Their case is not entirely special pleading, though—and offers a preview of the uproar that could soon break out across science.
The objecting mathematicians argue that focusing on solutions neglects the importance of questing for them. Tackling open problems spurs on the invention of new tools and techniques, some of which might later prove useful beyond their initial purpose. For example imaginary numbers, which when squared have values less than zero, were described by 16th-century mathematicians as being as “subtle as they are useless”. They now underpin electrical engineering and quantum physics.
OpenAI’s new papers have failed, the mathematicians allege, to provide them with surprising ideas or new lines of inquiry. AI is not very good at explaining how it arrives at its results, says Luis Martínez-Zoroa, a mathematician at CUNEF University in Madrid and a leading expert on the Navier-Stokes problem. He describes the AI’s 166-page paper outlining its working as “a bit of a Frankenstein of different parts of research” that is far from clear.
Mathematics is not the only field facing disruption. An analysis of 41.3m papers from disciplines across the natural sciences, co-authored by James Evans at the University of Chicago and published in January, found that researchers are adopting AI at an accelerating rate (see chart). AI has already dramatically changed how theoretical physicists work, according to David Tong of the University of Cambridge. “In terms of calculating, it’s just obvious you turn to an LLM,” he says. “That wasn’t true three months ago.” On September 25th Anthropic, another AI firm, announced that its model, Claude, had pushed the frontier in calculating the interactions between certain sets of particles.
Scientists adopting AI appear to be finding success: Dr Evans’s study showed that those who use the technology publish more and attract more citations. Yet, while a boon for individuals, AI use shrank the range of topics studied by almost 5% and cut scientists’ engagement with each other’s work by 22%. That aligns with the findings of a recent survey of over 600 scientists conducted by Google. Almost half of the respondents said AI pushes them towards safer, more incremental projects that are guaranteed to produce publishable results in short order. Only 28% thought AI was enabling them to pursue more speculative work.
Other risks arise as AI plays an ever bigger role in science, says Hector Zenil, a computer scientist at King’s College London. Writing in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence, in February, Drs Zenil and Evans envisage a future in which AI models (with some robotics thrown in, too) close the scientific loop, meaning they become capable of autonomously taking measurements, forming hypotheses, testing them in the lab and evaluating their findings before beginning the process again. The researchers warn that could push science into strange new territory where machine-driven research ceases to be legible to humans.
It may still be possible, in such a world, to check the machines’ results are correct, and perhaps even make use of them. Scientists, says Dr Zenil, might thus become like archaeologists, following up AI discoveries and trying to work out how they were achieved. Dr Tong, who is optimistic that AI will be a force for good, nonetheless warns that “I’m not sure we’re really prepared for what’s coming in six months or a year.” Theoretical physics is a close relative of mathematics, so is the most ripe of the sciences for similar disruption.
Mathematicians are not jobless yet, though. The very opacity of OpenAI’s results promises plenty of work verifying AI’s methods and identifying which approaches prove most fruitful. What’s more, say mathematicians, good as AI is at problem-solving, it still struggles with creative work; whether an AI could have invented imaginary numbers, for instance, remains unclear. Yet as Dr Connes is finding out, scientists underestimate the potential of the technology at their peril.

epub_88.title: AI will make it possible to design and build organisms from scratch
epub_88.text:
AI will make it possible to design and build organisms from scratch
Science & technology
| The life fantastic
AI will make it possible to design and build organisms from scratch
Synthetic biology has arrived at last
Oct 15th 2026
Twenty years ago, The Economist ran a story about a factory that could make dragons. It was an April Fool, based on the idea that living cells could be modelled accurately inside computers. At the time, that idea was a fantasy. But the flourishing of artificial intelligence in the intervening decades appears to have brought it closer to reality. A sign of progress came on October 7th, when the Virtual Biology Initiative (VBI), a project to collect the data needed to create predictive models of how cells behave and change, announced that it had received commitments worth $800m since its launch in April.
The VBI’s goals are medical. Predictive models will let researchers design more effective drugs that are more likely to pass successfully through clinical trials. But, if that works, future generations of models might be used to design modified versions of existing organisms, such as crop plants—and perhaps, eventually, entirely new living things.
The technology that has made such advances conceivable is deep learning, wherein large neural networks are trained to tackle complex problems. It is this technique that underpins the foundation models that power the chatbots marketed by firms such as Anthropic, Google and OpenAI. To such models, the long-chain molecules at the heart of biology (nucleic acids and proteins) are no different from  the chains of words in human writing. Letting foundation models loose on them was thus an obvious idea. And it is proving extraordinarily productive.
In the words of Adrian Woolfson, the business brain behind Genyro, a bio-startup in San Diego, “Biology is now computable, predictable and therefore designable.” It is also instantiable. Evo 2, for example, a foundation model partly invented by Brian Hie, of the Arc Institute in Palo Alto, can analyse DNA segments up to 1m base-pairs long (the size of a small bacterial genome). By studying the order of chemical bases paired together in that molecule’s double helix, it can predict how changes to that order might affect its parent organism. It is able to do this because it was trained on DNA sequences collected from over 100,000 species, in the way that chatbots are trained on text.
In January Dr Woolfson’s scientific partners, Kaihang Wang and Noah Robinson, of the California Institute of Technology, unleashed on the world a high-fidelity, high-efficiency DNA-assembly system called Sidewinder. Sidewinder can piece long stretches of DNA together (currently up to 12,500 base pairs) with high accuracy. That is enough, by itself, to synthesise the genomes of small viruses. It also simplifies the construction of yet-longer stretches, such as bacterial genomes and small artificial chromosomes.
Combined with Evo 2 (Dr Hie is another of Genyro’s founders) the firm now has the tools needed for Dr Woolfson to put his money where his mouth is. He hopes to do so by synthesising, among other things, an artificial wheat chromosome carrying genes for heat- and drought-resistance.
Evo 2 is by no means the only genomic foundation model out there. DeepMind, Google’s AI lab, has created one called AlphaGenome. It is more of a specialist than Evo 2. AlphaGenome was trained almost exclusively on human genomes, as was Genos, an offering from BGI Research, in Shenzhen, China.
Deep-learning models are available, too, for those studying particular groups of non-human species. Plants, fungi, bacteria, viruses and vertebrate animals are all served in this way. Conversely, Basecamp Research, a company in London, is casting the net wider. Its model is trained on samples that attempt to capture all the DNA in, say, a water sample from a particular place, in order to study—with a view to creating new antibiotics—the chemical warfare going on between the microbes therein.
And that is only genomics. Deep-learning models of various sorts can also handle other biological molecules, especially proteins. They are able to work out how natural proteins, which are long chains of chemical links called amino acids, fold up, which is crucial to understanding how they work. They can also predict what changing particular amino acids will do, and even design proteins from scratch, with particular purposes in mind—from better antidotes to snake venom to bespoke enzymes for novel chemical reactions.
DeepMind also has one of these, called AlphaFold 3. And its spin-off, Isomorphic Labs—which has the modest mission statement “Solve all disease”—plans to use both that and AlphaGenome in drug-discovery partnerships with three larger, longer-established pharma firms: Novartis, Eli Lilly and Johnson & Johnson. The pharma firms will provide the targets. Isomorphic will use its AI to suggest drug candidates. The pharma firms will then test its suggestions experimentally.
Other established pharma companies are doing similar AI work in-house. Roche, Novo, GSK and AstraZeneca all either own or have stakes in supercomputers for that purpose. Indeed, Lilly itself has hedged its bets by building one, called LillyPod, independently of Isomorphic. This will apply the deep-learning approach to data from the company’s 150-year-old archive, which is replete with unpublished failures as well as published successes. That should yield insights unavailable to those relying solely on the published scientific literature, with its bias towards what worked.
In the field of agriculture, meanwhile, AI is being brought to bear on several hitherto-intractable problems. One such is polyploidy, a phenomenon common in plants in which an organism has multiple sets of similar chromosomes. Several important crops, including wheat, cotton and potatoes, are polyploid. This makes it hard to determine which genes are responsible for what effects, and thus know where to make advantageous genetic edits.
Appropriate AI can sort out what’s what. It can also help make sense of plant immune systems, which have evolved independently of those in animals but are similarly complex. That should allow them to be tweaked to farmers’ advantage. And there are even attempts to use AI to tinker with the fundamentals of photosynthesis, to try to make it more efficient—a long shot, given that evolution has had several billion years to optimise it, but one that would be of incalculable value if it could be pulled off to increase yields.
The big prize, though, will be to combine the approaches to biology enabled by AI to devise computer models of how cells work. The VBI is a step towards this.
The initiative itself is a coalition of public, academic and private research organisations led by Biohub, an organisation in San Francisco set up by Mark Zuckerberg, boss of Meta, and his wife Priscilla Chan. DeepMind, Isomorphic Labs and the Arc Institute are among its members. The aim is to gather, in AI-friendly format, the vast amounts of new biological data needed to create predictive models. Though these will not replicate all aspects of cellular behaviour they will respond like real cells to simulated disease and treatment.
That should greatly speed up medical research and drug testing. Virtual cells with different genomes, for example, might indicate which are likely to respond well to a drug even before clinical trials start. That would make such trials more of a formality, rather than the nail-biting, years-long exercise they currently are.
To understand enough biology to make such a virtual cell will require looking at, and building models to handle, a lot more than just the composition of individual DNA and protein molecules. These new models will need to know where those molecules are, how they interact with each other and with the other molecules of biochemistry (such as lipids and sugars) and how this whole network responds to signalling molecules such as hormones.
Biohub will sponsor the development of tools to do this, such as cryo-electron tomography, which can resolve what is happening inside a cell at close to atomic detail. Meanwhile, in a collaboration also announced on October 7th, America’s Department of Energy (DoE) and National Institutes of Health (NIH) will chip in too. The NIH will contribute $500m-worth of already-collected data that Biohub will attempt to standardise, and the DoE will spend a similar sum on computing and other resources needed for the endeavour.
Virtual cells will still be just computer models. Synthetic biology’s masterpiece—in the word’s original sense of a work created to prove mastery—will be to create completely novel organisms from scratch.
Depending on how you define the words “organisms” and “novel”, this may already have happened. In September 2025 Dr Hie and some of his colleagues at the Arc Institute announced that they had used Evo 2 and its predecessor, Evo 1, to design and synthesise 16 viable viruses based on, but significantly different from, a bacteriophage called Phi-X174 that is one of virology’s workhorses.
Bacteriophages, as their name suggests, prey on bacteria. Intriguingly, some of Dr Hie’s novelties had higher fitness than their wild equivalents. Cocktails of them proved able to overcome the normal resistance to viruses shown by three different strains of E. coli, a gut bacterium that also has workhorse status. This is of particular interest because custom-built phages might have medical applications. So-called phage therapies, in which hostile bacteria are kept under control by viruses rather than chemical antibiotics, were once widely regarded as eccentric, but are now under active consideration.
Back at Genyro, no one could accuse Dr Woolfson of thinking small. He hopes the combination of biological foundation models and cheap, large-scale DNA synthesis will enable the exploration of the myriad possibilities offers that natural selection has not yet discovered—what he calls “the whole of DNA space.”
This would, presumably, start with creatures that, though novel, still had, like Dr Hie’s phages, a recognisable resemblance to something natural. But, just as natural selection, proceeding one step at a time, went from microbes to humans via fish, amphibians, mammal-like reptiles and monkeys, so AI-driven incremental change might result in applications that sound, today, like fantasy. Growing buildings rather than constructing them, perhaps? Delivery drones with wings instead of propellers? Off-road cars with legs instead of wheels?
And DNA space itself may prove bigger than it looks at first sight. AI-designed artificial cells might assist the extension of biochemistry, and therefore synthetic biology, by rewriting the genetic code itself. Natural proteins employ only 20 types of amino acid, but DNA would have the ability to encode three times as many if the machinery of protein synthesis could be re-wired to eliminate duplicates. That might permit all sorts of useful chemistry that is currently not seen in nature.
It could also, though, unleash accidental monsters. Dr Hie and his colleagues chose phages for their work on synthetic viruses in part because they pose no conceivable threat of turning into pathogens. And the creators of Evo 2 made sure when they were training it that none of the viruses in the databases were pathogenic, lest the model accidentally learn to do something dangerous. As the technology spreads, though, risks will proliferate.
Like AI itself, then, the biology that ai will enable offers possible worlds that are both wonderful and terrifying. The next time you read a story about a dragon factory in an issue of The Economist, don’t be so sure that we’re joking.

epub_89.title: Could AI help scientists with their paperwork?
epub_89.text:
Could AI help scientists with their paperwork?
Science & technology
| Stop the slop
Could AI help scientists with their paperwork?
Yes—but that amplifies existing problems
Oct 15th 2026
THE STEREOTYPE of a scientist is someone who wears a white coat and toils in a laboratory, doing experiments with test tubes. In reality, researchers spend a surprising amount of time doing paperwork: writing grant applications, drafting and reviewing scientific papers, and reading new results in journals. If there is one thing that modern artificial-intelligence systems are good at handling, however, it is language. So could AI make scientists more productive by handling some of these tasks, freeing them to spend more time on actual research? That is possible. But AI has also made it easier to produce low-quality and even fraudulent science, which is overwhelming systems of moderation and peer review. Which trend will win out?
A survey of Australian scientists found that they spent between one and three months a year, or 16% of their time on average, preparing research proposals. Other studies have shown that a typical grant application takes around 34 days of work to prepare, and the success rate is only around 20%. So it is hardly surprising that around a quarter of researchers are using AI tools to speed up the process, according to a survey published in April by Elsevier, a publisher of scientific journals. James Wilsdon, who studies research policy at University College London, gives the example of a researcher he spoke to at an Ivy League university. Having previously spent one day a week writing grant proposals, the researcher now spends 45 minutes, thanks to AI. “The extra capacity that is being unlocked by all of this is immense,” says Dr Wilsdon.
A similar transformation is under way at a later stage of the scientific process: the drafting of papers describing research outcomes, and their vetting by peers for inclusion in scientific journals. As with grant proposals, the use of AI tools has made papers easier to write. Since the launch of ChatGPT in 2022 submissions to journals in the Science family  and uploads to arXiv, the world’s largest preprint server, have grown (see chart). Fields like computer science, which rely less on experiments and lab work, have seen the biggest increases. From 2025 to 2026, paper submissions to the International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML) doubled to 24,000.
At first glance this may seem like a boon for science. More research should be a good thing. But AI-written papers are not necessarily better. One analysis of 2.5m biomedical science papers, published in the Lancet in May, found that the rate of fabricated citations increased 12-fold between 2023 and early 2026 to around 0.5%, probably as a result of increasing AI use. Examinations of papers in “predatory journals”, where authors pay for publication, find around 90% are AI-generated. “There’s been a very measurable increase at the bottom of the quality spectrum,” says Paul Ginsparg, the founder of arXiv.
A surge in bogus papers is a problem. For one thing, estimates Simon Linacre of Cabells, a company that classifies journals, fees to predatory journals amount to roughly $120m each year—money which could be spent on research. Bogus findings that are discovered erode public trust. Those that are not can cause real-world harm. In one notorious case, studies based on fabricated data were used to justify the widespread clinical practice of giving starch infusions to ill patients undergoing surgery. It took many years before their kidney-damaging properties were identified. AI may accelerate the spread of such misinformation too. In a recent demonstration, researchers based in Sweden uploaded two papers to a preprint server documenting a fictional eye disease called bixonimania. Within weeks AI chatbots, like Gemini and ChatGPT, were discussing the condition as if it were real.
AI advances have also made it harder for reviewers to tell at a glance if a paper is slop. AI models can nowadays easily mimic the jargon, tone and style that signal expertise in a field. A study published in Science in December found that, before large language models (LLMs), the sophistication of writing in a paper was generally a good guide to its scientific quality. Now that relationship has reversed.
AI tools can help with the problem they have caused, by detecting things like manipulated images, inconsistencies in the text or fully AI-generated content. More than half of reviewers were already using such tools in 2025, according to a survey carried out by Frontiers, another scientific publisher. With appropriate safeguards, AI could improve the peer-review process, says James Zou of Stanford University. Last year he conducted a study involving 40,000 reviews, half of which were written by humans, and half by humans who used AI. He found that AI-assisted reviewers were better at objective tasks such as finding inconsistencies and technical errors, while humans were better at subjective tasks such as assessing the novelty and impact of the research.
Funding organisations may be able to adopt similar solutions. One research foundation in Barcelona, for example, now uses AI to cull the least promising 20% of submissions, to reduce the load on its human assessors. But, says Dr Wilsdon, the whole idea of using written proposals to allocate funding may be obsolete. Writing in Nature, he and his colleague Geraint Rees, of University College London, conclude that the least-bad option may be to allocate funding using a combination of AI analysis, detailed scrutiny of applicants’ records and in-person interviews.
These ideas risk biasing grants towards existing institutions and researchers. That is ironic, because of the erstwhile hope that AI would democratise science, by helping non-native English speakers improve their writing. This has happened, but non-Anglophone researchers who use AI are no more likely to be published in leading journals now than they were previously. Indeed, in an effort to cope with rising submissions, arXiv has set up a system to flag to its moderators papers from new authors or those of unknown provenance.
Early-career scientists may also suffer. Drafting papers is part of how scientists hone their thinking. Many researchers worry about the risk of “cognitive surrender” whereby relying heavily on LLMs prevents students from developing a deep understanding of their subject.
The flood of papers also makes it harder for researchers to find the ones that matter. Dr Zou says he can read only about 100 papers a year in depth, out of tens of thousands published in his fields of interest. Fortunately, the deluge might be made easier to handle by AI tools creating personalised digests based on a researcher’s interests. Dr Zou is experimenting with ai agents that identify papers of potential interest to him, summarise them, find links to other papers, and then suggest new avenues for research.
Many researchers argue that AI has simply made existing problems in academia worse. To secure positions and win grants they are often judged on the number of papers they have published. This can encourage scientists to prioritise quantity over quality. There is evidence that AI-assisted submissions have risen fastest at institutions that reward productivity most directly. “AI is just the accelerant”, says Ivan Oransky, a founder of RetractionWatch, a database that documents dodgy publications. “The kindling is the publish-or-perish culture.” If scientists want to fix the problems caused by AI slop, fixing incentives is the place to start.

epub_90.text:
Do you need to walk 10,000 steps a day?
Science & technology
| Well Informed
Do you need to walk 10,000 steps a day?
How fast you walk may be as important as how much
Oct 15th 2026
“WALKING IS MAN’S best medicine,” said Hippocrates, an ancient Greek physician. Or so the story goes. Whether the phrase originated with him is disputed. But it does contain a kernel of truth. Walking is a form of exercise that is free, requires no equipment and is easy for most people to incorporate into their days. But how many steps should one walk—and at what speed—to unlock its benefits?
Conventional wisdom sets 10,000 steps per day as a good target. The source of that number, though, is as questionable as Hippocrates’s quotation. Its origins lie not in a clinical trial, but a Japanese advertising campaign for a pedometer launched ahead of the 1964 Tokyo Olympics (10,000, in Japanese Kanji, also looks a little like a person walking). Those committed to getting their steps in should not shy away from the 10,000 mark. But in terms of scientific research, the number barely has a leg to stand on.
A study published in Lancet Public Health in 2025 considered 57 papers published since 2014 to assess the connection between different daily step counts and various health outcomes. Walking more was found to be beneficial across the board. Taking 7,000 steps a day, in contrast to 2,000, brought about a 47% lower risk of premature death, a 25% lower chance of developing cardiovascular disease and a 14% reduction in the risk of diabetes. Even a little goes a long way: going from 2,000 daily steps to 4,000 resulted in a 36% drop in mortality risk over the years tracked.
But the benefits eventually taper off. “What we see with most of the health outcomes is a diminishing return on investment after 7,000,” says Melody Ding, an epidemiologist at the University of Sydney, who led the study. Extra steps keep helping, but beyond around 7,000 per day, they are scarcely worth the effort. The jump from 7,000 daily steps to 10,000, for example, led to only a 2% further reduction in mortality risk.
Step count is only one measure. Another is intensity, which scientists generally quantify using cadence: the number of steps taken per minute. According to Dr Ding, the evidence for an ideal cadence is harder to pin down. Still, she says, sports science generally suggests that as far as physical activity is concerned, the more intense, the better: “If people can get the heart rate up, or a little bit out of breath,” she says, “that would definitely have health benefits.”
That aligns with the findings of Emmanuel Stamatakis of Monash University, in Melbourne. Writing in the British Journal of Sports Medicine in September, Dr Stamatakis and his colleagues tracked the effects of step count and intensity on the health of 64,743 participants for around eight years, using data from UK Biobank, a large data set. As with step count, quicker cadences were generally beneficial. Those who walked fewer than 5,000 brisk steps per day achieved, on average, a similar reduction in mortality risk to those who walked between 5,000 and 7,500 steps. But diminishing returns applied here, too. The paper suggests the sweet spot, therefore, is 7,500-10,000 daily steps, with frequent bursts at 100 steps a minute.
Any reasonable amount of walking is better than none. But for those unable to walk much, upping the pace might be a way to increase the benefits. “And if you don’t have enough opportunities,” says Dr Stamatakis, “create them.” Rather than parking right outside the supermarket, for example, stop around the block and do a walking sprint in.

epub_92.title: Squeeze into those skinny jeans: millennial culture is back
epub_92.text:
Squeeze into those skinny jeans: millennial culture is back
Culture
| Party like it’s 1999
Squeeze into those skinny jeans: millennial culture is back
A tech-powered 2000s revival represents the biggest nostalgia boom yet
Oct 15th 2026
The entertainment industry has caught a millennium bug. Arriving in cinemas in November is “Focker-in-Law”, the latest follow-up to “Meet the Parents” (2000), in which Ben Stiller struggled with his girlfriend’s difficult dad. (In the new film Mr Stiller, now 60, plays the father.) No Doubt, whose hits in the 1990s included “Just a Girl”, recently finished a comeback residency at the Sphere in Las Vegas. Meanwhile home audiences can look forward to reboots including “The Inbetweeners”, a popular television series from 2008, and “Tomb Raider”, a classic game of the 1990s that will be re-released in souped-up form in February 2027.
Millennial culture is back, faster than you can say “oat-milk latte”. Millennials, who are now aged 30-45, are nearing the peak of their spending power—and entering management-level jobs where they can call the shots on new creative projects. The result is that their formative era, the late 1990s and 2000s, is back in fashion. It may seem like only yesterday that millennials were being mercilessly mocked by Gen Z on social media over everything from their grey home interiors to their too-tight trousers. But now they are taking their revenge. “The 2000s called—skinny jeans are back,” declared Vogue, a fashion bible, earlier this year.
Every generation has its revival, as its members grow up and recreate the culture of their youth. The 1990s saw a 1970s resurgence, as middle-aged boomers made nostalgic films such as “The Brady Bunch Movie” and “Dazed and Confused”. Before that there was an outbreak of ’50s nostalgia in the 1970s, with shows like “Happy Days”, “M*A*S*H” and the movie “Grease”. A series of 1950s rock’n’roll revival concerts brought back stars like Chuck Berry and Bill Haley & His Comets, filling venues such as Madison Square Garden.
Yet social and economic changes are combining to quicken and amplify these cultural revivals. The upshot is that the new millennial moment may be the most powerful wave of nostalgia yet, reaching more people than ever before.
One reason is a new creative conservatism, caused by old media’s pinched economics. Cinema-going has fallen sharply since the pandemic (though recently it has
become cool again
), and social apps are eating into TV viewing. Risk-averse Hollywood executives are therefore falling back on reliable intellectual property. As they run out of superheroes, they are scouring their back catalogues. Earlier this year “The Devil Wears Prada 2” out-grossed the 2006 original. In September Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman returned after 28 years for a sequel to “Practical Magic”. Next year a “Baywatch” reboot will squeeze new bodies into the red swimsuits that graced TV sets in the 1990s.
The revival is not limited to Hollywood. Indian moviegoers flocked to “Border 2”, the sequel to a hit war film of 1997, after its release in January. Japan’s anime studios have also been cranking out remakes, such as “Hell Teacher” and “Yaiba: Samurai Legend”, aimed at middle-aged millennials who enjoyed the originals in their youth.
Meanwhile, a live-events boom has helped get the music industry into nostalgia mode. Concerts are larger and more lucrative, so retired musicians have greater incentive to get back on the road. Oasis, who provided the soundtrack to older millennials’ teenage years in the 1990s, recently announced a second leg of their comeback tour, which was the second-highest grossing concert tour of 2025. Other millennial-era artists, from My Chemical Romance to Shania Twain, are back on stage. The Dixie Chicks have reformed (now known as just the Chicks—some millennial names have aged better than others).
Social change has further fuelled the millennial boom. The rise of “kidults”, who splurge on toys and fun experiences for themselves, has swollen the market for nostalgic playthings. This year Bandai is celebrating the 30th anniversary of its Tamagotchi, a “digital pet” craze of the 1990s, by re-releasing its original model. In August Lego launched a $200 “X-Files” set.
Kidult behaviour is perhaps clearest in gaming, where millennials have carried their teenage hobby into middle age. Some 43% of 35- to 44-year-olds in rich countries own a games console, according to GWI, a research company. Sony is courting them with a remake of the “God of War” trilogy, a PlayStation hit from 2005. Nintendo’s remake of “The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time” (1998) will be out in November. Its Switch console can emulate older Nintendo machines, allowing parents to play N64 classics when their children have gone to bed. The rise of millennial executives may also explain a rash of films based on classic games, from last month’s “Resident Evil” to a “Zelda” movie due out next year.
Perhaps the biggest booster of nostalgia, however, is technology that has made older content permanently accessible. On streaming platforms, hit shows never really go away, allowing millennial series such as “Friends” and “Gilmore Girls” to find a new generation of fans. Streaming services like Disney+ and HBO Max use original shows to attract new subscribers, but more than 90% of viewing on their platforms is of older “catalogue” shows, according to Luminate, an analytics firm.
Streaming libraries also make it easy to hear the sounds of the past. The fastest growth in music streaming is in titles from the 1990s and 2000s, according to Luminate. Among Americans aged 13-24, the share who listen mainly to music from the 2020s fell from 55% in 2021 to 44% in 2025. Millennial stars are selling the rights to their back catalogues while they are hot: Britney Spears, 44, cashed out last year for a reported $200m. Even new acts often have a millennial sound, from “nu-metal”-inspired bands like Spiritbox and Loathe to pop artists like Addison Rae (who has attributed her “Y2K” style to a youth spent watching stars such as Ms Spears on MTV).
Social media mean that the nostalgia machine is not just stronger: it is also running faster. Whereas boomer-era nostalgia relied on slow-moving channels, like the months-long TV commissioning process, today fashions can be virally rediscovered in an instant. The result is that trends are sometimes getting a second wind within a decade. A popular meme earlier this year declared that “2026 is the new 2016”, with Gen Zs expressing nostalgia for ten-year-old cultural phenomena such as Pokémon Go, a smartphone game.
“Everything goes viral so fast, and it burns so bright,” says one Hollywood agent. “But it burns very quickly.” That means the millennial revival may be the strongest so far—but also that it could be short-lived. Don’t throw away those baggy jeans just yet.

epub_93.title: What’s behind the big interest in miniatures?
epub_93.text:
What’s behind the big interest in miniatures?
Culture
| In the palm of your hand
What’s behind the big interest in miniatures?
Nostalgia and a desire for control are fuelling a boom in small things
Oct 15th 2026
A charming Victorian home with four bedrooms and two bathrooms has just hit the market for only £1,150 ($1,500), plus shipping. Newly renovated by the previous owner, this “dream house” promises hardwood floors, marble accents and a “gorgeous wraparound front porch”. The one catch: it is just 54 inches wide by 42 inches tall. At least it has a low heating bill.
Miniatures are having a huge moment. Hobbyists are jumping on the model bandwagon as collectors, makers or both. Attendance at dolls’ house conventions is booming. Miniatures.com, one of America’s leading small-creation retailers, has seen more than a tripling of net sales over the past two years. The International Guild of Miniature Artisans—“miniature” referring to the size of the craft, not to the artisans themselves—saw “a record number” of new people attend their annual art course, according to Audrey Tripp, the director.
The resurgence of this whimsical pastime reflects growing enthusiasm for “grandma hobbies”, with people embracing hands-on, analogue activities. The tiny trend offers a “kind of escapism”, says Steve Putnam, a miniaturist and collector. Stuck at home during covid, many young people rediscovered their childhood dolls’ houses, or needed a hobby that did not take up much space. Miniatures provide the freedom to “create anything because it’s so small”, says Mr Putnam.
The ability to control a world appeals during times of instability, too: hence the construction boom in dolls’ houses. “I can’t afford to have this massive dream home, but I’m going to make it from scratch,” says Hannah Lemon, the winner of the second season of “Best in Miniature”, a Canadian reality TV series.
Designing miniatures is no small feat. A recent exhibition at the Museum of the City of New York displayed a replica of the city made from balsa wood, cardboard and glue, which stretched 50 by 27 feet. It took Joe Macken, the artist, 21 years to craft it by hand. Elisabeth Sherman, the curator, says that with the rise of technology “we have a real human desire for things that we can touch, things that we can make ourselves.” The intricate craft forces creators and viewers to slow down.
The final reason for this uptick is technology itself. The rise of 3D printing and laser-cutting has enticed new artisans to the field. Though traditionalists sometimes gripe about these tools, claiming they cut corners (literally) and do not produce high-quality work, most think they have helped craftsmen’s speed and productivity. They have also lowered prices, bringing more people into the thrall of collecting. It’s a small world, after all.

epub_94.title: How erectile dysfunction led a KGB spy into the arms of MI6
epub_94.text:
How erectile dysfunction led a KGB spy into the arms of MI6
Culture
| Another spy and traitor
How erectile dysfunction led a KGB spy into the arms of MI6
In “Redwood” Ben Macintyre shows how personal struggles help recruit informants
Oct 15th 2026
VLADIMIR KUZICHKIN, a KGB spy who defected to Britain after a harrowing escape from Iran in 1981-82, asked for two things: a horoscope and a circumcision. “Recruiting a vetted circumciser had been hard enough,” writes Ben Macintyre, a historian, but “locating a security-cleared astrologer was impossible”.
“Redwood” is the gripping tale of Kuzichkin’s recruitment into MI6. (“Redwood” was his code name.) It is Mr Macintyre’s latest true-life spy thriller: earlier narratives have looked at Kim Philby, an MI6 officer who defected to the KGb, among others. It succeeds, like his other books, in melding spies’ psychology with an up-close look at the tradecraft of espionage. Each of his protagonists has helped turn the cogs of history at a pivotal moment.
So it went with Kuzichkin (pictured left). A senior officer of the KGB rezidentura in revolutionary Tehran, he arrived as the Shah’s old order broke down and a new, chaotic regime was taking shape.  He was aggrieved by the corruption and barbarity of the KGB and the Soviet regime. But his path to treason was personal, hastened by erectile dysfunction and his failing marriage. He turned to MI6 for help. The service dispatched red pills—vitamin placebos, designed to placate the desperate KGB officer, who later thought circumcision, on an astrologically favourable date, would solve his medical problem. His recruitment was sealed over gallons of vodka.
Espionage is often a high-stakes game in which hundreds of people and advanced technology might support a single operation. But “Redwood” shows how it can also be amateurish, bumbling and improvised. Ian McCredie, Kuzichkin’s MI6 case officer (pictured right), tried to confound Iranian eavesdroppers by blasting Persian radio and running the taps. As Kuzichkin escaped via Turkey, MI6 worried about the prospect of a KGB snatch squad. Their answer was to send an officer armed with a large brass lamp to thump any assailants.
“Redwood” also highlights how spies are not always whom you expect. The KGB was convinced that the flamboyant British ambassador, Nicholas Barrington, was the MI6 head of station in Tehran, rather than the dull Mr McCredie. In fact, Barrington “regarded MI6 in much the same light as the people who cleaned his toilet…and swept the tennis courts”. He had no interest in overseeing their work.
Kuzichkin’s secrets may have changed the course of Iranian history. America and Britain, worried by the possibility of a Soviet-backed communist coup in Iran, decided to share Kuzichkin’s intelligence on communist activities with Iran’s regime. Some 4,000-12,000 people were executed in the purges that followed, destroying much of the opposition and consolidating the Islamists’ grip on power.
Kuzichkin, “haunted” by their slaughter, died in 2009. MI6 did not co-operate in “Redwood”, but Mr McCredie spoke at length to the author. Other living MI6 officers appear under flimsy pseudonyms. Their candour may have caused some discomfort inside the service. But the result is another first-rate spy story.
