epub_95.title: With Elizabeth Holmes, can you ever really see everything?
epub_95.text:
With Elizabeth Holmes, can you ever really see everything?
Culture
| Mirror, mirror
With Elizabeth Holmes, can you ever really see everything?
A riveting new documentary, “You Can See Everything”, is Shakespearean in ambition and nuance
Oct 15th 2026
THERE IS nothing more seductive than the idea of unfettered access. When a subject is mysterious, slippery and high-profile, it is even more enticing. The longer a person is in front of a camera, the likelier one is to spot an inconsistency or a lie, or feel resolved they have found out the truth. For truth-telling was surely the goal of Nathan Fielder, a Canadian film-maker and comedian, when he entered Elizabeth Holmes’s home for 34 days before she reported to federal prison in Texas in May 2023. She had been sentenced to more than 11 years for fraud and conspiracy related to her blood-testing startup, Theranos.
“You Can See Everything”, Mr Fielder’s documentary, is an enthralling display of the tension between observer and observed. (It opens in American cinemas on October 16th and in British ones in November.) Mr Fielder and his co-director, Lance Oppenheim, moved in with “Liz”—as well as her partner, Billy Evans, and their two young children—in their oceanfront cottage in San Diego. Subjects who throw open their door would seem to have nothing to hide. But is their openness itself a disguise? The documentary keeps viewers guessing—and riveted.
It is a film of two acts. In the first, viewers witness a brilliant and surreal sequence of intense and often uncomfortable scenes: Ms Holmes insisting that she has not once told a lie in her entire adult life, for example, and Mr Fielder quizzing Mr Evans on whether he has been scammed by Ms Holmes. Time and again Mr Fielder tries to pin his subject down on matters big and small, such as whether Theranos’s device really could “perform any test” (she says she was misinterpreted) or whether she understands the joke in a famous comedy routine (apparently not). Often she obfuscates; her replies sound like the “Glomar” response the CIA gives in testimony (neither denying nor confirming the existence of material).
By the time Ms Holmes reports to prison, Mr Fielder remains baffled by her. But is she being careful because she is a liar? Or is she so universally believed to be a liar that she deeply fears making even the smallest error in anything she says? Many film-makers might have ended the project on that ambiguous note. Mr Fielder, instead, ambitiously embarks on an elaborate second adventure, enlisting the help of others who have been sucked into Ms Holmes’s orbit, to try to solve the riddle. This makes for spectacular theatre. Mr Fielder apes tactics from Shakespeare, staging a play within a play (within a play).
The film echoes other great works of the “journalist and the murderer” genre. Just as Sarah Koenig of the hit podcast “Serial” struggled with the “bare fact of why on earth would a guilty man agree to let me do this story, unless he was cocky to the point of delusion”, Mr Fielder cannot understand why Ms Holmes would let him so far in unless she truly believed people have the wrong perception of her. Yet  intimacy with charming and potentially dishonest subjects breeds a new suspicion: that the journalist or film-maker has been taken in, and that neither subject nor narrator can be trusted.
John Carreyrou, the reporter at the Wall Street Journal who helped uncover Ms Holmes’s fraud, described in his excellent book, “Bad Blood”, how “she emitted a reality distortion field that forced people to momentarily suspend disbelief.” By the conclusion of “You Can See Everything” Mr Fielder appears to believe in at least a little of what Ms Holmes is selling: that she loves her partner and her family, for instance, even though she gave up the last remaining days she would spend with them during their childhoods to make this film. Perhaps believing her makes Mr Fielder a fool. But in the process of potentially being duped, he has also revealed just how brilliant a film-maker he is, too.

epub_96.title: “Musk” reminds you how much you already know about Elon
epub_96.text:
“Musk” reminds you how much you already know about Elon
Culture
| Back Story
“Musk” reminds you how much you already know about Elon
It is hard to make a fresh documentary on a ubiquitous subject, Alex Gibney’s gruelling film shows
Oct 15th 2026
You may not be a fan of Elon Musk. Perhaps you’re not even very interested in him. But if you watch “Musk”, a gruelling new documentary, you will realise that, osmotically, you have come to know a lot about the sometime trillionaire. This is a compliment to his influence and ubiquity. It is less positive news for the documentary itself, even for the whole documentary genre.
In “Musk”—out now in American cinemas and screened at the BFI London Film Festival—Alex Gibney, an Oscar-winning director, sets out to discover how Mr Musk has “assumed so much power, and why had we given it to him?” Using interviews with former colleagues and partners (business and romantic), the first half of the film chronicles Mr Musk’s breakneck rise, from PayPal to Tesla’s electric vehicles, the satellites of Starlink and reusable rockets of SpaceX.
After a ten-minute interval, the second half covers his plunge into politics and AI. Mr Gibney shows how pandemic rules and the gender transition of one of his many children nudged Mr Musk rightwards. Posing as a “free-speech absolutist”, he buys Twitter and tries to run it like Tesla. Then, after Donald Trump installs him at DOGE, he tries to do the same with the federal government. Maybe one day the brain chips that are among his side hustles will let people download this saga in an instant. For now, it lasts almost four hours.
In a parade of talking heads, the missing face is Mr Musk’s. He declined to be interviewed and called Mr Gibney a “douche” and “crackpot”. The director’s solution is to create a somewhat flattering digital avatar which mouths things Mr Musk has said in public. This is fitting, reasons Mr Gibney, since Mr Musk has questioned whether what seems to be real life is actually a simulation run by future beings. (Popular among pretentious adolescents, the notion that you may only think you’re here was zapped by René Descartes nearly 400 years ago.)
Viewers may instead conclude that they’ve been living inside a giant documentary about Elon Musk—since so much of this one feels so familiar. As the deepfake Musk-bot attests, there is an awful lot of him on the record already. Here he is mucking about with a chainsaw and Argentina’s president. Here he is in the White House with his young son, X.
What feels fresh? Mr Gibney speculates about the possible abuse of data harvested by Mr Musk’s pimply underlings at DOGE. You may be shaken (if not surprised) by reflections from some of his offspring’s mothers. “If you were my employee,” he reportedly told Justine Musk, his first wife, “I would fire you.” After he let her go, one of the women he took up with was Ashley St Clair, a former MAGA influencer, who says: “Elon is a nuke.”
The film revisits Mr Musk’s unhappy childhood in South Africa, where he was bullied at school and belittled by his sinister father, Errol, who pops up on camera to rationalise his abrasive parenting style. Observers may wonder how a person as rich and powerful as Mr Musk can be so thin-skinned and needy that he frets over the traction gained by his tweets. The explanation, “Musk” suggests, lies in a kind of arrested development and a yen for affirmation.
Beyond its bloat and paucity of revelations, the problem with “Musk” is that it wavers between two damning—but different—analyses. One is that Mr Musk is an uncompromising fanatic who takes reckless risks in pursuit of his goals, whether autonomous cars or humanity’s glorious “multiplanetary” future. On this reading, his story’s underlying theme is the cost and virtue of doubt: how a lack of it can fuel stellar success but also be a dangerous flaw.
The other, contradictory critique is that Mr Musk is a grifter, who takes credit for things he didn’t do or that may never happen (like colonising Mars). Accordingly, his main talents are self-promotion and securing government contracts and credits; he hitched his rocket to Mr Trump’s wagon out of venal self-interest and fear of regulatory trouble. In which case, the lesson is that his acolytes and investors are chumps.
The ultimate moral of this documentary may be less about him than about documentaries. In the over-exposed age of social media and rolling news, it is hard to make a revelatory one on a marquee subject. As for Mr Musk: audiences will blink out of the cinema, wishing his robot project had produced AI usherettes to deliver ice-creams to their seats—and hoping not to hear about him for a while. In that they are, once again, liable to be disappointed.

How Donald Trump remade America’s government
Culture
| Axes of Elon
How Donald Trump remade America’s government
DOGE was a huge missed opportunity
Oct 15th 2026
It was during the early months of the pandemic, and Donald Trump was vexed. Experts had told him that hydroxychloroquine, a malaria drug, was no good as a treatment for covid-19. He summoned Francis Collins, the head of the National Institutes of Health, to put him straight. The president had compelling anecdotal evidence. “Get me Jack Nicklaus!” he shouted to a flunkey. Mr Nicklaus was an 80-year-old ex-professional golfer. He had caught covid, taken hydroxychloroquine and recovered, he told Dr Collins. “There, you see!” said Mr Trump. “You see!”
Dr Collins, who discovered the gene for cystic fibrosis, tried to respond tactfully. No disrespect to Mr Nicklaus, arguably the greatest golfer in history, but most people who contract the virus get better. Only a double-blind randomised controlled trial can reveal whether a drug actually works, and such trials had shown that this one did not. Mr Trump never summoned Dr Collins for a private meeting again.
To govern well requires finding accurate information and analysing it rationally. Mr Trump’s scorn for such principles has increasingly infected the federal government. During his first term, Dr Collins merely had to endure a nutty lecture from Robert F. Kennedy junior about how vaccines cause autism. In his second term RFK junior is the health secretary, Dr Collins was pushed out and
measles is spreading
among unvaccinated American kids.
In “Blockers” Michael Lewis tells the stories of federal workers who tried to resist Mr Trump’s assault on the bureaucracy. Most are low-key, diligent and startled to be told by Elon Musk and his Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) that their offices are hotbeds of fraud, waste and wokery.
Mr Lewis is a journalist who spins technical topics into entertaining tales; previous works have taken on Wall Street (“Liar’s Poker”) and data and baseball (“Moneyball”). He concedes that waste in government is a real problem. Employees are too hard to sack. He tells the story of Maxine, an air-force employee who parked close to a fire hydrant, was asked to move, refused, accidentally reversed into a cop and drove off. The ensuing car chase shut down an air base during a war. When she was fired, she filed a grievance and won. When she eventually returned to work, she found that two higher-ranking officers were doing her job in addition to their own. When she found out they were paid more than her, she claimed discrimination (she was black) and sued for a pay rise.
Reform was—and is—needed. Unfortunately, Mr Trump’s hatchet men did not understand the machine they were trying to re-engineer. They “thought in stereotypes”, writes Mr Lewis. The typical DOGE person was a 25-year-old techie “dying to breathe the same air as Elon Musk and only just now grokking the fact that the United States government had three branches”. They were mainly “white guys easily bent out of shape by…the idea of people who were not white guys having unfair advantages”. They had “a simple picture in their heads of ‘the bureaucrat’, and that person looked a lot like Maxine”.
So DOGE started slashing. It attempted to fire all the probationary staff—the recent hires who were mostly either young or had urgently needed skills. Permanent staff were offered hefty payouts to quit. Many who could easily find other jobs accepted; the less capable ones stayed. A return-to-the-office rule was enforced mindlessly. DOGE killed a study of how wildfires spread into suburbs, because the only computers powerful enough for its modelling were not in a government office.
DOGE
failed to make the state smaller
, despite Mr Musk’s ambitious promises. But it did make it dumber. Colette Delawalla, a clinical psychologist, was told that her application for a research grant would fail because it contained the word “translate” (which includes “trans”) and “bias” (an essential term in statistics that is also used in complaints about racism).
It made it crueller, too. Mr Musk was outraged that the United States Institute of Peace was paying a former member of the Taliban. The man was supplying vital intelligence. After Mr Musk outed him on X, the informant’s family was rounded up and tortured. The Trump revolution also made government less accountable, by suppressing evidence that his policies were hurting people. After he cut food subsidies for the poor, a survey measuring hunger was scrapped.
Most disturbing of all, in Mr Lewis’s telling, Mr Musk’s tech-savvy footsoldiers saw the law as an obstacle to work round, rather than a guide. Mr Lewis tells the story of Kathleen Walters, the chief privacy officer at the Internal Revenue Service (IRS). DOGE had sent an email to every federal employee ordering them, on pain of dismissal, to each list five things they had accomplished in the previous week. Since violating taxpayers’ privacy is a crime, many at the IRS risked prison if they responded—and the sack if they didn’t.
Ms Walters locked horns with Gavin Kliger, a young hoodie-clad DOGE staffer. Mr Kliger showed up at the IRS demanding access to all its systems and taxpayer data. This was plainly illegal. Even worse was an effort by a Trump appointee to make the IRS share with the immigration authorities personal data about millions of illegal immigrants who had filed tax returns.
The IRS had spent decades reassuring such people that, if they wanted to pay taxes and build a record of civic virtue that might one day help them win legal status, their privacy would be respected. Mr Trump wanted their addresses so he could shackle and deport them. An acting IRS commissioner, who had been in the job for only an hour, sent out the request on a Friday night, doing an end run around the woman whose job it was to say no.
Alerted by a colleague, Ms Walters called the acting commissioner from outside a pizza restaurant, and warned her that the plan was unlawful. Two months later, after having spent an evening hiding from Mr Kliger in a darkened conference room, Ms Walters quit. Later, in Texas, teams of ICE agents showed up in a Latino neighbourhood knowing exactly which doors to jimmy open. A court ruled that the IRS data-sharing with ICE was illegal, but for many of its victims—and for trust in the system—it was too late.

epub_101.title: Annie Dillard wanted to know the mind of God

Annie Dillard wanted to know the mind of God
Obituary
| Creation and destruction
Annie Dillard wanted to know the mind of God
The nature writer and “theologian” died on September 15th, aged 81
Oct 15th 2026
She could never forget the moth. It hatched from a cocoon kept by her teacher in a Mason jar, a huge Polyphemus silk moth with, potentially, velvety brown wings bearing a bright blue eyespot. At the moment of hatching, its wings produced a hardening varnish that would enable them to spread. Then it could fly. But the jar was too small, and the varnish worked too fast. The moth, when released on the street, could only walk. But it struggled gamely on with its useless lumps of wings, heading somewhere. In Annie Dillard’s mind, it was still going.
She was the only one to see it as it went. She was often a sole observer, quietly noting. A goldfinch shaking a seeding thistle until the down floated, “blind and sweet”, all over the landscape. A mosquito biting a poisonous copperhead. A leaf still curled like a thin, pale flame in its bud on a tulip tree. Frogs leaping like flares through a mesh of blue-green algae, “surfacing to awareness”. Another frog on the bank of Tinker Creek, stock still, as a giant water bug slowly liquidised its insides and sipped its life away.
It was Tinker Creek that made her famous. The book she wrote about her thoughts and sightings there, “Pilgrim at Tinker Creek”, won her a Pulitzer in 1975, when she was only 28. She was the youngest woman to win one, and the first in the man’s world of nature-writing. But fame was the last thing she wanted. All she had needed for years was that damp, broken ground near Roanoke, Virginia, the sycamore log on which she sat, the noisy creek with its silvery shiners swarming in the shallows, and the Osage orange tree from which rose, once, a hundred red-winged blackbirds. When the Pulitzer news came, she was washing spinach. She wouldn’t have to do that any more, the pressman said. But she would, and did.
Before too long she fled from the unbearable fussing, decamping with her writer husband to Washington state and the islands off the coast.  From her various exile places she produced essays, poetry, philosophy, journalism, two novels and an autobiography. For preference she wrote in very small spaces, usually log cabins, facing away from the view. Inevitably people compared her to Henry David Thoreau, the 19th-century naturalist who had been the subject of her master’s thesis, but she didn’t agree. Unlike him, she didn’t live in most of her cabins; half of “Tinker Creek” had been written, after hours, in a public library. Her favourite writer was not him, but Primo Levi, because he wrote the truth.
Nor did she think of herself as a nature writer. All she saw and noted was part of an overwhelming question: why, among the prodigal beauties and intricacies of the world, was there so much destruction? Why were there thousands of barbules on the wing of a wild goose that any predator might devour? What was the creator—if there was a creator—thinking? Why was there so much care, then none? She loved to watch hatchings and unfoldings. But the hatchlings were immediate food for something else, and each leaf shrivelled in two seasons. This couldn’t all be some cynical show, though she sometimes called it that. Perhaps it was more a case that God could do anything, so he did. Wildly, freely.
And what was she, amid all this? Nothing important. She was not needed in creation. Her life seemed no more than the tunnels made by miner larvae on a leaf, “a faint tracery on the surface of mystery”. Yet she contained multitudes. She could see, with her naked eye, through two million light years as far as the Andromeda galaxy. She could explore endlessly, as she did, and reflect on her explorations. Those were not, in the end, about understanding nature. She was more of a theologian.
Religion didn’t feature much at all as she was growing up, tomboyish and comfortably middle-class, in Pittsburgh. Books did. They swept her away. From the age of five, she reckoned she read 100 books a year. She wanted to know and remember everything: history, geography, geology, minerology, criminology, the names of trees and the names of birds. She read and re-read “The Field Book of Ponds and Streams”. As with her sightings in nature, so with the written word. Someone had to read these books.
On the writing of books, though, she had strong opinions, laid out in 1989 in “The Writing Life”. That life was far from a state of sedentary inspiration. It was arduous, tough and necessarily cruel. The writer’s first line of words was a probe into the unknown, digging a path; once she had arrived in a new, promising place, the path had to be erased. Cut the umbilical cord. Everything written up til then probably had to go, even the favourite passages and the load-bearing walls; even, sometimes, the whole original point of the thing. Ruthlessness was essential; no excess. If a book got stuck, or out of control, it must be visited every day, as if the writer were a lion-tamer with a chair shouting “Simba!” Mastery had to be reasserted, and not just—as she asserted hers—with near-continuous coffee and Vantage cigarettes.
In the middle of “The Writing Life” she recorded a peculiar event: the apparently spontaneous combustion of a typewriter. It was a portable Smith-Corona, so not attached to power. The explosion shook the house, and she raced upstairs to find the device erupting with fire and ash. As she tried to douse the flames, sparks burned holes in her shirt. It might have been a careless cigarette, but she did not say so. In her telling there was just, suddenly, fire.
It was often around. As a child, she wanted to run so fast that she would throw out sparks. At Tinker Creek she saw, at sunset, some divine power “rolling along the mountain ridges like a fireball”. At moments of “seeing truly” the grass was wholly fire, and the backyard cedar became a tree of lights. She felt lifted then, resounding “like a beaten bell”. Yet only she had noticed those things, as only she had seen the death of the Tinker Creek frog, or the crippled moth staggering on. Only she was meant not to miss that horror and that beauty. That was what she was for.
